QA.q: How many calls and emails does it take to get one client?
alts: How much outreach should I do every day?
ek client ke liye kitni outreach karni hai
QA.a: Outbound is a chain of percentages. Do enough volume every day, then fix the weakest link before you add anything new.

QA.q: Why is my offer more important than my script?
alts: My script is good but nobody buys, why?
QA.a: A great script cannot rescue a weak offer. Build an offer around the result the buyer wants and remove every reason it might not work for them.
links: Lesson 1.2: Your offer decides your results

QA.q: How do I deal with rejection?
alts: People keep saying no and I feel bad
rejection se kaise deal karun
QA.a: Detach from the outcome. You are there to find out whether you can help, not to win every call.

QA.q: Why do people really buy?
alts: What makes a buyer decide?
QA.a: People decide with emotion and justify with logic. They buy when they feel the gap, believe you can close it, and trust you more than the alternatives.

QA.q: How should I use this platform to train?
alts: What is the best way to study this course?
QA.a: Skill comes from deliberate, recorded practice. Read less than you practise.
links: Lesson 1.5: How to train with this platform

QA.q: How do I make my offer hard to refuse?
alts: How do I add guarantees, bonuses and urgency to my offer?
QA.a: Once the core offer is right, reverse the risk, add bonuses that kill objections, give an honest reason to act now, and name it so people remember it.
links: Lesson 1.6: Make the offer hard to refuse: guarantees, bonuses, urgency and a name

QA.q: How do I pick a niche?
alts: Which niche should I choose?
How do I niche down?
niche kaise choose karun
QA.a: "I do websites" competes with everyone. "I get dental clinics in Texas more booked appointments from their website" competes with almost no one. Pick one kind of buyer and build everything for them.
links: Lesson 14.1: From a skill to a market: niche down until you're the obvious choice

QA.q: What do buyers weigh when they look at an offer?
alts: How do I make my offer more attractive?
QA.a: Buyers judge an offer on how big the result is, how sure they are it'll happen, how long it takes and how much effort it costs them. Most freelancers only work on the first. The money is in the other three.
links: Lesson 14.2: The four things buyers weigh, and how to move each one

QA.q: How do I build an offer from the buyer's problems?
alts: What should my offer include?
QA.a: Your offer's parts should come from the buyer's problems, not from your skills. Walk through what happens before, during and after they buy, write down everything that could stop them, and turn each one into a solution.
links: Lesson 14.3: List every obstacle, then solve each one

QA.q: Should I do the work for them or teach them?
alts: Done for you or done with you, which is better?
QA.a: The same solution can be delivered in many ways, from you doing everything to giving them a template. Pick the way that's worth the most to the buyer and costs you the least, then cut the rest.
links: Lesson 14.4: Choose how you deliver: done for them, with them or by them

QA.q: How do I turn my service into a product?
alts: How do I package my service?
QA.a: Open-ended work ("we'll do whatever you need") is hard to sell and hard to deliver. A package with a fixed result, a fixed scope, a fixed time and a fixed price is easy to say yes to and easy to repeat.
links: Lesson 14.5: Turn a service into a product

QA.q: How do I get clients with no case studies?
alts: I have no proof or results yet, what do I do?
mere paas koi case study nahi hai
How do I sell with no experience or portfolio?
QA.a: No case studies doesn't mean no proof. You can show your thinking before they pay, borrow proof from your process, and get your first results by offering a small number of clients a deal in exchange for a case study.
links: Lesson 14.6: Proof when you don't have any yet

QA.q: How do I write my offer on one page?
alts: Where do I put my final offer together?
QA.a: Bring everything together into one page you can read on a call, paste into an email and hand to a setter. If it doesn't fit on one page, it isn't clear enough yet.
links: Lesson 14.7: Workshop: build your offer on one page

QA.q: How much should I charge?
alts: How do I price my service?
kitna charge karun
What price should I quote a US client?
QA.a: A US business owner isn't comparing your price to Pakistani salaries. He's comparing it to what the problem costs him. Price against that, charge enough to do the job properly, and stop competing on cheap.
links: Lesson 15.1: Price for the result, not your hours

QA.q: Retainer or commission, which pricing model should I use?
alts: Should I charge per result or monthly?
QA.a: How you charge matters as much as how much. Retainers, setup fees, pay-per-result and commission each share risk differently. Pick the one that fits your stage and the buyer's fear.
links: Lesson 15.2: Pricing models for service businesses

QA.q: Should I offer a guarantee?
alts: What guarantee can I safely give?
QA.a: A guarantee moves the risk from the buyer to you. Done well, it brings in more clients than it ever costs in refunds. Done badly, it can sink you. Here's how to choose one and write it so it works.
links: Lesson 15.3: Risk reversal you can afford

QA.q: What small first offer gets a client in the door?
alts: How do I make it easy to say yes the first time?
QA.a: The hardest sale is the first one. Make the first step small, safe and useful, so a stranger can say yes without much risk. Then earn the bigger sale by delivering.
links: Lesson 15.4: The first sale: offers that get them in the door

QA.q: How do I upsell after a yes?
alts: What do I offer when they say no to the main offer?
How do I add add-ons?
QA.a: The best moment to offer more is right after someone says yes. The best moment to offer something smaller is right after someone says no. Plan both before the call.
links: Lesson 15.5: More from every yes: add-ons and smaller options

QA.q: How do I get clients to pay every month?
alts: How do I make my offer recurring?
QA.a: One-off projects mean you start from zero every month. Monthly clients stack up. Build a reason to stay into the offer from the start, and reward clients who commit for longer.
links: Lesson 15.6: Make it recurring: keep clients paying every month

QA.q: How do I name my offer?
alts: How do I test if my offer works?
QA.a: A clear name makes an offer memorable. A good presentation makes the price feel small. And a few weeks of honest testing tells you whether the offer, the message or the market needs fixing.
links: Lesson 15.7: Name it, present it, test it

QA.q: What kind of market should I target?
alts: Who should I reach out to?
QA.a: The fastest way to improve a bad call is to call a better-fit person. Pick a market that is in pain, can pay, is easy to find and is growing.
links: Lesson 2.1: Choose a target worth calling

QA.q: How do I build a clean lead list?
alts: How big should my list be?
lead list kaise banaun
QA.a: A smaller, accurate list beats a huge dirty one. Work every list completely before building the next.

QA.q: How do I research a prospect quickly?
alts: What should I look up before contacting someone?
QA.a: One relevant detail turns a stranger's call into a reasonable call.

QA.q: How do I plan my day for outreach?
alts: How should I time block my prospecting?
QA.a: What you schedule gets done. Protect a daily outreach block and hit the same number every day.

QA.q: What are the ways to get clients?
alts: What are the main lead sources?
QA.a: There are only four ways to get attention: warm outreach, cold outreach, content and paid ads. Master one, then add the next.
links: Lesson 2.5: The four lead sources and where outbound fits

QA.q: What is a lead magnet?
alts: What free thing can I give to open a conversation?
QA.a: A lead magnet solves one small piece of the buyer's problem for free, so they see you can solve the rest.
links: Lesson 2.6: Lead magnets: give value that opens doors

QA.q: How do I get clients from people I already know?
alts: What is warm outreach?
How do I ask for referrals from friends?
QA.a: The people who already know you are your fastest first clients. Reach out personally, give value, and ask for help or introductions.

QA.q: What are buying signals?
alts: When is the best time to contact a business?
QA.a: The best time to contact a business is right after something changes: they hire, open a branch, get bad reviews or start running ads. A message that mentions the change gets read. A message that could go to anyone gets deleted.
links: Lesson 2.8: Signals: reach out when something just changed

QA.q: How do I personalise messages at scale?
alts: How much personalisation do I need?
QA.a: You don't need to write every message from scratch. Make every message relevant to the segment, then add a personal line only where it earns its time. Personalise the problem, not the compliment.
links: Lesson 2.9: Personalise at scale: the relevance ladder

QA.q: How do I combine email, calls and LinkedIn in one sequence?
alts: What is a multichannel sequence?
Which channel should I use first?
QA.a: Most replies come after the second or third touch, and often on a different channel from the first. Plan one sequence per lead that mixes email, calls, LinkedIn, video and DMs, then stop the moment they reply.
links: Lesson 2.10: Design one sequence across every channel

QA.q: What do I say in the first ten seconds of a cold call?
alts: How do I start a cold call?
call shuru kaise karun
QA.a: Interrupt the 'salesperson' pattern: sound calm and human, give a clear reason, and ask a question that makes 'no' easy.

QA.q: What are good cold call openers?
alts: What opener should I use?
QA.a: Match the opener to what you know, then move from situation to problem with two or three easy questions before you ask for anything.
links: Lesson 3.2: Openers that earn a second sentence

QA.q: How should I sound on a call?
alts: How much should I talk on a call?
How do I fix my tone and pace?
QA.a: How you say it matters as much as what you say. Talk less than half the time, slow down, and use your tone on purpose.
links: Lesson 3.3: Tone, pace and talk ratio

QA.q: How do I handle the first objection on a cold call?
alts: They object straight away on the call, what do I do?
QA.a: Early objections are reflexes, not decisions. Defuse them calmly, then ask one question that gets them talking.

QA.q: How do I get past the gatekeeper?
alts: The receptionist won't put me through
What do I say to the receptionist?
How do I get past the receptionist?
QA.a: The person who answers is part of the team. Be direct, friendly, honest and calm, as if you belong.

QA.q: What do I say in a voicemail?
alts: Should I leave a voicemail?
QA.a: Short, specific voicemails as part of a planned sequence. Follow up with value and neutral language, never with 'just checking in'.

QA.q: What words should I avoid on a sales call?
alts: How do I stop sounding like a salesperson?
QA.a: Words that sound like selling create resistance. Speak like a calm expert, keep the outcome open, and walk the call from opener to booked meeting.
links: Lesson 3.7: Neutral language, status and the full call

QA.q: Do you have cold call scripts I can copy?
alts: Give me a call script
cold call ki script chahiye
QA.a: A talk track is not a script you read word for word. It's the shape of a good call, with lines you can adapt. Here are six for common situations, built on two openers that work: asking permission and leading with a problem.
links: Lesson 3.8: Talk tracks you can copy: six calls from hello to booked

QA.q: How does cold email work?
alts: What are the rules for cold email?
QA.a: Cold email is a short, relevant note to a business contact, sent from a healthy domain, with an honest way to opt out.
links: Lesson 4.1: How cold email works, and the rules

QA.q: How do I set up cold email so I land in the inbox?
alts: How many domains and mailboxes do I need?
QA.a: Use separate sending domains, authenticate them properly, warm up slowly and keep volume low per mailbox.
links: Lesson 4.2: Set up so you land in the inbox

QA.q: How do I build an email list?
alts: How do I verify email addresses?
QA.a: One narrow list, one clear persona, every address verified.
links: Lesson 4.3: Build and clean an email list

QA.q: How do I write my first cold email?
alts: What should a cold email say?
cold email kaise likhun
QA.a: Short, about them, and easy to answer. Name a problem other owners have, offer something useful, and ask a question with an easy no.

QA.q: How many follow-up emails should I send?
alts: How do I follow up on a cold email?
QA.a: Most replies come from follow-ups. Four to five short emails over two to three weeks, each with a new reason to reply, never 'just checking in'.

QA.q: How do I handle replies to my cold emails?
alts: Someone replied to my email, what now?
QA.a: Reply fast, stay calm, ask one question, and move interested people to a call. Treat every no, referral and opt-out with the same respect.

QA.q: How do I measure my cold email results?
alts: What should I test in my emails?
QA.a: Track replies and booked calls, change one thing at a time and test with enough volume.
links: Lesson 4.7: Measure and improve your emails

QA.q: Why are my emails going to spam?
alts: How do I fix deliverability?
meri emails spam mein ja rahi hain
QA.a: If your emails land in spam, nothing else matters. Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft now enforce strict sender rules, and they can reject mail outright. Set up properly, send slowly, and watch a few numbers every week.
links: Lesson 4.8: Deliverability in 2026: the rules and the numbers to watch

QA.q: Show me cold email examples
alts: Do you have cold email templates?
Is there a swipe file of emails?
QA.a: Short beats long. Problem beats pitch. A question beats a meeting request. Here are ten emails for different niches and situations, each under about 80 words, with notes on why they work.
links: Lesson 4.9: A swipe file: ten cold emails and why they work

QA.q: How does social media outreach work?
alts: How do I get clients from social media?
QA.a: Social outreach is a conversation, not a pitch. Notice, connect, talk, then move to a call.

QA.q: How do I set up my profile to attract clients?
alts: What should my LinkedIn profile say?
QA.a: Before you message anyone, make your profile answer three questions: who you help, how, and why they should trust you.

QA.q: How do I do outreach on LinkedIn?
alts: What do I write in a LinkedIn connection note?
linkedin se client kaise milega
QA.a: Warm up, send a short connection note, start a conversation, then move off the platform.

QA.q: How do I get clients from Facebook?
alts: How do I use Facebook groups for outreach?
QA.a: On Facebook, give value in groups first, then message people who already know your name.
links: Lesson 5.4: Facebook outreach: groups, pages and Messenger

QA.q: How do I get clients on Instagram?
alts: What do I send in an Instagram DM?
QA.a: Warm up with follows, story views and real comments, then send a short DM that refers to something they posted.

QA.q: What is a good daily routine for social outreach?
alts: How long should I spend on social outreach each day?
QA.a: Thirty focused minutes a day, a simple tracker and a clear follow-up rhythm beat sporadic bursts.
links: Lesson 5.6: A daily social outreach routine

QA.q: What are the LinkedIn limits?
alts: How many connection requests can I send on LinkedIn?
Can I send voice notes on LinkedIn?
QA.a: LinkedIn rewards people who show up, not people who blast invitations. Stay well inside the limits, warm people up with comments, keep notes short, and use voice notes once you're connected.
links: Lesson 5.7: LinkedIn in 2026: limits, comments first, and voice notes

QA.q: Why send a personal video?
alts: Do video messages work for outreach?
QA.a: A 45-second video made for one person shows effort, proves you looked, and stands out from text.
links: Lesson 6.1: Why short personal videos get replies

QA.q: What do I say in an outreach video?
alts: How do I script a Loom video?
QA.a: Hook with their name, show one specific thing, give one insight and make one small ask.

QA.q: How do I record an outreach video?
alts: What equipment do I need for video outreach?
QA.a: A basic laptop, a quiet room and one clean take is enough. The thumbnail and the link placement matter more than polish.
links: Lesson 6.3: Record it: setup, thumbnails and sharing

QA.q: How do I send and follow up on an outreach video?
alts: How do I make many videos quickly?
QA.a: Place the link with one line of context, follow up when it is watched and batch the process.
links: Lesson 6.4: Send, follow up and scale

QA.q: What is an SOP?
alts: How do I write my own SOPs?
What daily schedule should I follow in US hours?
QA.a: An SOP is a written routine: what to do, in what order, how long it takes and how you know it's done. It turns good days into normal days, and it lets you hand work to someone else later.
links: Lesson 16.1: How to use these SOPs, and write your own

QA.q: How do I build 200 leads in a day?
alts: What are the steps to build a lead list?
QA.a: A clean, researched list is half the result. This SOP takes you from a niche to 200 verified leads with a signal column, in about five to six focused hours.
links: Lesson 16.2: SOP: build 200 leads in a day

QA.q: What are the steps to set up cold email from zero?
alts: How long does cold email setup take?
QA.a: Do the setup once, properly, and your emails reach the inbox for months. Rush it and nothing you write will be seen. Allow about three weeks from buying domains to your first real send.
links: Lesson 16.3: SOP: set up cold email from zero

QA.q: How do I launch an email campaign?
alts: What do I check before sending a campaign?
QA.a: A campaign launch is a checklist, not a guess. Check the list, the copy and the setup before you press send, then watch the first two days closely.
links: Lesson 16.4: SOP: launch an email campaign

QA.q: How do I run a daily calling block?
alts: What is the routine for making calls every day?
QA.a: Calls work when they're done in one protected block at the right time, with the list ready, the opener practised and every result logged. This SOP turns 90 minutes into the most productive part of your day.
links: Lesson 16.5: SOP: the daily calling block

QA.q: What is the daily social and video routine?
alts: What do I do every day on LinkedIn and Instagram?
QA.a: Thirty to forty-five minutes a day on LinkedIn, Instagram or Facebook, plus a few personal videos, builds warm conversations that cold email can't. Do it in the same order every day.
links: Lesson 16.6: SOP: the daily social and video block

QA.q: How fast should I answer replies?
alts: What are the steps to turn replies into meetings?
QA.a: A reply is the most valuable thing your outreach produces, and it goes cold fast. Check twice a day, answer positive replies within hours, and move every interested person to a booked time.
links: Lesson 16.7: SOP: handle replies and book meetings

QA.q: How do I review my outreach each week?
alts: What should I check every week?
QA.a: Once a week, look at the numbers, find the one weakest step and change one thing. This 45-minute habit is what separates people who improve from people who just stay busy.
links: Lesson 16.8: SOP: the weekly outreach review

QA.q: What makes a good appointment?
alts: When is a meeting worth booking?
QA.a: An appointment is worth booking only when the right person, with a problem they admitted in their own words, agrees to a specific time for a clear reason.
links: Lesson 7.1: What a good appointment is

QA.q: How do I qualify a prospect?
alts: What questions do I ask before booking a meeting?
QA.a: Qualify by asking, not interrogating. Five light questions tell you whether a meeting is worth booking.

QA.q: How do I book the meeting?
alts: They are interested, how do I get them on a call?
meeting kaise book karun
QA.a: Book live, for a specific time, with a reason that is about them, and get a small commitment before you hang up.

QA.q: How do I stop no-shows?
alts: What reminders should I send before a meeting?
They booked but did not show up
QA.a: No-shows come from forgetting, weak commitment and doubt. Confirm in their words, send something worth watching, and remind at the right moments.
links: Lesson 7.4: Show rate: confirmations and no-shows

QA.q: How fast should I call a new lead back?
alts: What is speed to lead?
QA.a: A lead who just reached out is warmest in the first minutes. Waiting is a choice that costs money.
links: Lesson 7.5: Speed to lead and missed calls

QA.q: What are the US calling rules?
alts: Is cold calling legal in the US?
What is the TCPA?
What are the do not call rules?
QA.a: Consent, do-not-call lists, calling hours and recording laws decide how you may call. Check them before you dial.
links: Lesson 7.6: US calling rules you must know

QA.q: How do I book meetings through DMs?
alts: How do I hand a lead over to the closer?
QA.a: Setting works the same in DMs as on the phone: open, connect, find the problem, invite. Then hand the closer everything they need so the prospect never repeats themselves.
links: Lesson 7.7: Setting by message, and the handoff to the closer

QA.q: Why does discovery matter?
alts: What is a discovery call for?
QA.a: People believe what they say, not what you say. Discovery is where the buyer convinces themselves that the problem is real, costly and worth fixing now.
links: Lesson 8.1: Why discovery decides the deal

QA.q: What questions do I ask on a discovery call?
alts: In what order do I ask discovery questions?
discovery call mein kya poochun
QA.a: Connect, understand the situation, uncover the problem, picture the outcome, weigh the cost of doing nothing, then check commitment. In that order.

QA.q: How do I start a discovery call?
alts: How do I find out who makes the decision?
QA.a: Agree how the call will go, explore the pain past the surface, and find out how and with whom the decision gets made, before you present anything.
links: Lesson 8.3: Frame the call, find the pain, settle the decision

QA.q: What is gap mapping?
alts: How do I show the gap between where they are and where they want to be?
QA.a: Map where they are, where they want to be, what is in the way and what the gap costs. Then say it back and get a yes.

QA.q: What are reflective questions?
alts: How do I get people to talk themselves into changing?
QA.a: Short, neutral questions with an easy 'no' lower resistance and get people to argue for change themselves.
links: Lesson 8.5: Reflective questions that move people to think

QA.q: How do I listen better on sales calls?
alts: What are mirrors and labels?
QA.a: The most powerful discovery tools are the quietest. Repeat, name, wait, and listen to how they say it, not just what they say.
links: Lesson 8.6: Listening: mirrors, labels and silence

QA.q: How do I present my solution?
alts: Should I explain how my service works in detail?
QA.a: People buy the destination, not the flight. Present what their life and business look like after, then only as much of the 'how' as they need to believe it.
links: Lesson 9.1: Sell the outcome, not the process

QA.q: How do I present on a sales call?
alts: price kab batani hai
When do I reveal the price on a call?
QA.a: A ten-minute presentation built from their words and numbers beats a thirty-minute demo. Commit them to the solution before you say the price.

QA.q: What are the seven buying beliefs?
alts: How do I check a deal is ready before the price?
QA.a: Before you present, check that all seven buying beliefs are in place and the deal is real. Gaps found early are easy. Gaps found after the price become objections.
links: Lesson 9.3: Check the deal before the price

QA.q: How do I write a proposal?
alts: Should I email my proposal?
proposal kaise banaun
QA.a: Present the proposal live, never just by email. One page, their gap, a clear recommendation, a confident price and an agreed decision date.
links: Lesson 9.4: Proposals that get a yes

QA.q: How do I sell when there is more than one decision maker?
alts: How do I get the partner involved early?
QA.a: Most decisions involve more than one person. Bring the other decision makers in early, and help your contact sell it inside.

QA.q: How do I close a deal?
alts: How do I ask for the sale?
deal close kaise karun
QA.a: When the buyer holds all seven beliefs, the close is a calm question. Most 'closing problems' are discovery problems found too late.

QA.q: What are the steps of a full sales call?
alts: How do I run a sales call from start to finish?
QA.a: Clarify why they're here, name the problem, review what they've tried, paint the outcome, commit to the solution, state the price, handle concerns, reinforce the decision.
links: Lesson 10.2: The full sales call, step by step

QA.q: What is behind an objection?
alts: How do I find the real objection?
How do I handle objections?
QA.a: Objections come from circumstances, other people or self-doubt. Defuse, separate money from belief, find the real concern, and resolve that one.
links: Lesson 10.3: What is behind an objection

QA.q: How do I negotiate?
alts: They want to negotiate, what do I do?
QA.a: Negotiate from understanding, not pressure. Label, ask, trade, and be willing to walk away.

QA.q: What are the principles of influence?
alts: How do I persuade people ethically?
QA.a: Six well-studied principles of influence. Use them to help people decide, never to trap them.
links: Lesson 10.5: Six principles of influence, used ethically

QA.q: How do I follow up on a quiet deal?
alts: They went quiet after the proposal
client ne jawab dena band kar diya
QA.a: Most deals need several touches. Follow up with value and their own words, ask neutral questions, and close the file gracefully.
links: Lesson 10.6: Follow-up that wins quiet deals

QA.q: What are the most common objections and answers?
alts: What are the five big objections?
QA.a: Price, 'I need to think about it', 'I need to talk to my partner', timing and 'send me something' cover most stalls. Prepare calm, honest answers for each.
links: Lesson 10.7: The five big objections, answered

QA.q: What do I do after they say yes?
alts: How do I collect payment on the call?
QA.a: The sale isn't finished at 'yes'. Take payment on the call, reinforce why they decided, and start onboarding before you hang up.
links: Lesson 10.8: After the yes: reinforce, collect and onboard

QA.q: What are the pipeline stages?
alts: How do I set up my pipeline?
QA.a: Clear stage definitions make forecasts honest and next actions obvious.

QA.q: What numbers should I track every week?
alts: What is a good scoreboard?
QA.a: Measure the same numbers every week, compare with healthy ranges, and fix the weakest stage first.

QA.q: What is a follow-up cadence?
alts: How often should I follow up?
How many times do I follow up?
QA.a: A planned sequence of varied, value-led touches beats chasing whenever you remember.

QA.q: How do I review my own calls?
alts: How do I score my calls?
QA.a: Score calls against specific behaviours, not feelings. Fix one behaviour at a time.

QA.q: How do I train a team?
alts: How do I hire and scale outreach?
QA.a: Write the process down, hire for behaviour, train daily with roleplay and call review, and scale only what already works.

QA.q: What tools do I need?
alts: What software do I need to start?
konse tools chahiye
QA.a: Buy one tool per layer, start with free or low-cost options and add a tool only when its absence hurts.
links: Lesson 12.1: The whole stack on one page

QA.q: Which lead data tools should I use?
alts: How do I verify and enrich leads?
QA.a: Choose where your leads come from, then verify and enrich them before they reach any sending tool.
links: Lesson 12.2: Lead data and enrichment tools

QA.q: Which email sending tools do I need?
alts: What email infrastructure do I need?
QA.a: Domains, mailboxes and a sending platform form the engine. Build it in the right order and monitor it weekly.
links: Lesson 12.3: Email infrastructure and sending tools

QA.q: Which tools should I use for social and video?
alts: Should I automate LinkedIn?
QA.a: Run LinkedIn, Facebook and Instagram by hand first. Add tools for finding, scheduling and recording, not for blasting.

QA.q: How do I call the US from Pakistan?
alts: How do I get a US number?
What do I need for calling?
pakistan se US call kaise karun
QA.a: A good number, a reliable internet connection, a proper headset and a dialer that records and logs make calls consistent.

QA.q: They said: It's too expensive.
alts: It's too expensive.

client bolta hai bohat mehnga hai
It costs too much
QA.a:
What it usually means: Usually doubt about the result, sometimes a real cash problem. Find out which before you answer.

A reply to adapt: "That's fair, it's a real investment. Setting the price aside for a second: do you feel this would actually fix [the problem]? [If yes:] Then it's about the money, not whether it works. You said [the problem] costs about [their number] a month. How does the price look next to that?"

Then ask: Expensive compared to what?

QA.q: They said: Someone can do it cheaper, or for free.
alts: Someone can do it cheaper, or for free.
They found someone cheaper
koi aur sasta kar raha hai
QA.a:
What it usually means: They think the work is simple and the cost is only the setup.

A reply to adapt: "Could be, and if it works out, great. The cost is rarely the setup. It's the tuning and support after, and what it costs you when it doesn't work. What would happen if the cheaper option missed calls for a month?"

Then ask: Who would fix it when something goes wrong?

QA.q: They said: What does it cost? (asked too early)
alts: What does it cost? (asked too early)
They ask how much it is straight away
How much is it?
pehle hi price pooch raha hai
QA.a:
What it usually means: Price-shopping before they know if it fits.

A reply to adapt: "Fair question. It depends on [volume and what you need], so I'd rather not guess. Can I ask two quick questions, and then give you a real number?"

Then ask: How many [calls / leads / jobs] a month do you handle?

QA.q: They said: I can't commit to a long contract.
alts: I can't commit to a long contract.
QA.a:
What it usually means: Fear of being stuck if it doesn't work. A trust and risk concern, not a price one.

A reply to adapt: "Completely fair. If it's not working, you shouldn't be stuck with it. We can start month to month with a clear measure for the first 30 days, so you only stay if it works. [ADD only terms you offer.]"

Then ask: What would you need to see in 30 days to feel good about continuing?

QA.q: They said: Can you give me a discount?
alts: Can you give me a discount?
They want a discount
They ask for a lower price
discount maang raha hai
QA.a:
What it usually means: Testing for flexibility, or cash is genuinely tight.

A reply to adapt: "I keep pricing the same for everyone, so it stays fair. If budget is the issue, I can change the scope, start smaller or spread the setup. What matters most to you: the full coverage, or a lower monthly number?"

Then ask: If the price were right, would you start this week?

QA.q: They said: We don't have the budget.
alts: We don't have the budget.
They have no budget
budget nahi hai
QA.a:
What it usually means: Either money is truly short, or the problem doesn't feel worth funding yet.

A reply to adapt: "Understood, no pressure. Can I ask: if money weren't a factor at all, would you want to go ahead? [If yes:] Then let's look at what's possible: a smaller start, payment terms, or timing. [If unsure:] Then let's talk about that first, because budget won't fix doubt."

Then ask: If budget weren't an issue, how would you feel about it?

QA.q: They said: How do I know you're legit?
alts: How do I know you're legit?
They think I'm a scam
They don't trust me
Is this a scam?
QA.a:
What it usually means: You're new or unknown, and they're risking money.

A reply to adapt: "Fair to ask, I'd ask the same. You don't have to take my word for it: [ADD real proof, a live demo on your numbers, a small pilot, a written agreement]. What would you need to see to feel comfortable trying a first step?"

Then ask: What would give you confidence to try a small first step?

QA.q: They said: I tried something like this before and it didn't work.
alts: I tried something like this before and it didn't work.
QA.a:
What it usually means: They were burned, and expect the same again.

A reply to adapt: "Thanks for telling me, that's really useful. What happened? [Listen fully.] So the problem was [their words]. Here's how we handle that part differently. Does that address it, or is there more to it?"

Then ask: What specifically didn't work last time?

QA.q: They said: What if it doesn't work for me?
alts: What if it doesn't work for me?
They worry it won't work
QA.a:
What it usually means: Fear of a loss they can't recover. The likelihood belief is weak.

A reply to adapt: "That's the right question. Let's define what 'working' means for you, put a date on checking it, and [ADD only the guarantee you can honour]. Would that make it feel safe enough to try?"

Then ask: What would 'working' look like for you?

QA.q: They said: Can I talk to a customer of yours?
alts: Can I talk to a customer of yours?
QA.a:
What it usually means: They want proof from someone like them.

A reply to adapt: "Yes, where I can. [ADD references you have permission to share.] If I don't have one in your exact situation yet, I'll tell you straight and we can start with a small pilot so you judge for yourself."

Then ask: What would you want to ask them?

QA.q: They said: That sounds too good to be true.
alts: That sounds too good to be true.
QA.a:
What it usually means: Something earlier sounded like hype.

A reply to adapt: "You're right to be careful. Here's exactly what I can and can't promise: [honest scope]. Which part sounds the least believable? Let's look at that one."

Then ask: Which part sounds the least believable?

QA.q: They said: Why should I pick you over a bigger company?
alts: Why should I pick you over a bigger company?
QA.a:
What it usually means: They're comparing credibility and risk.

A reply to adapt: "Good question. A bigger company gives you a brand. I give you [speed / direct access / a setup built for your business]. Honestly, if a brand is what matters most, a bigger company might be better. What matters most to you?"

Then ask: What matters most to you in who you work with?

QA.q: They said: Just send me some info.
alts: Just send me some info.
They said send me an email
They just want information by email
bolta hai email kar do
Send me some details
QA.a:
What it usually means: A polite way to end the call, or quiet interest. Find out which.

A reply to adapt: "Happy to. So I don't send you something useless, what would you want it to show you? [If they answer:] Honestly, five minutes now would answer that better than a PDF. [If not:] No problem, I'll send it and follow up Thursday."

Then ask: What is the one thing you would most want to see?

QA.q: They said: We're slammed right now.
alts: We're slammed right now.
They are too busy
They said they have no time
abhi time nahi hai
QA.a:
What it usually means: No bandwidth to think about it.

A reply to adapt: "Totally get it. Out of curiosity, when you're this busy, what happens to the calls you can't pick up? [Listen.] That's usually when it costs the most. Setup takes [time] and one short call from you. Would 15 minutes next week be easier?"

Then ask: When is it a little quieter for you?

QA.q: They said: Call me back in a few months.
alts: Call me back in a few months.
They said not right now
Maybe next quarter
baad mein call karna
QA.a:
What it usually means: Not a priority, or a polite brush-off.

A reply to adapt: "Sure. So I don't call at a bad time again, what will be different in a few months? [Listen.] And meanwhile, what happens to [the problem]? [If it's real:] Is waiting worth that? [If not:] OK, I'll call on [specific date]."

Then ask: What would need to change for this to become a priority?

QA.q: They said: I need to think about it.
alts: I need to think about it.
They said let me think
sochna hai bol raha hai
They want time to think
QA.a:
What it usually means: There's one unspoken concern: price, whether it works for them, or timing.

A reply to adapt: "Of course, it's worth thinking about. Usually when someone says that, there's one part they're not sure about. Is it the price, whether it'll work for you, or the timing? [If they won't say:] Picture six months from now. If nothing changes, where are you? And if you'd started today?"

Then ask: Is it the price, the results, or the timing?

QA.q: They said: It's our busy season, ask me after.
alts: It's our busy season, ask me after.
QA.a:
What it usually means: A real constraint, or a delay.

A reply to adapt: "Makes sense. If the busy season is when [the problem] costs the most, would you rather have it fixed before the rush, or after it's already cost you? What would starting in two weeks look like?"

Then ask: What would you need to be ready before the rush?

QA.q: They said: I need to talk to my partner.
alts: I need to talk to my partner.
They need to ask their wife or husband
partner se poochna hai
QA.a:
What it usually means: A real second decision maker, or cover for their own doubt.

A reply to adapt: "Of course, they should be part of this. If it were only up to you, would you go ahead? [Listen.] What do you think they'll ask first? It might be easiest if I join for ten minutes so they can ask me directly. Tonight or tomorrow morning?"

Then ask: If it were only up to you, where would you be?

QA.q: They said: I'm not the one who handles that.
alts: I'm not the one who handles that.
QA.a:
What it usually means: A gatekeeper, or no authority.

A reply to adapt: "No problem, thanks for telling me. Who would be the right person? I'll keep it short for them. What's the best time to reach them, and can I mention you pointed me their way?"

Then ask: What's the best way to reach them?

QA.q: They said: I have to run it by my team.
alts: I have to run it by my team.
QA.a:
What it usually means: A group decision, or a delay.

A reply to adapt: "Makes sense. Who's on the team, and what will they care about most? I can do a short call with them, or give you a one-page summary that answers their questions. Which would help more?"

Then ask: Can I join a short call with the team?

QA.q: They said: We already have a provider.
alts: We already have a provider.
They already have someone
They already use another company
pehle se kisi ke saath kaam kar rahe hain
QA.a:
What it usually means: They think the problem is solved.

A reply to adapt: "Good, that's probably part of why you've got the business you have. Out of curiosity, how well does it handle [the specific gap, e.g. nights and weekends]? If it's covering everything, I'll leave you alone."

Then ask: Is that for everything, including [the gap], or mostly [the easy part]?

QA.q: They said: We don't have that problem.
alts: We don't have that problem.
They say they don't need it
They don't need my service
QA.a:
What it usually means: They don't see the gap, or it's genuinely small.

A reply to adapt: "That's great if so. Most owners don't see it because it never shows up on a report. Would it be a bad idea to check, say, how many calls went to voicemail last week? If it's close to zero, you're right and I'll get out of your hair."

Then ask: How would you know if it were happening?

QA.q: They said: Someone in the office handles it.
alts: Someone in the office handles it.
QA.a:
What it usually means: A person covers it, so it feels solved.

A reply to adapt: "Good, that's a real strength. What happens when they're busy on another call, off shift or out sick?"

Then ask: How much comes in after hours or at lunch?

QA.q: They said: We've got enough work already.

QA.a:
What it usually means: Growth isn't the goal right now.

A reply to adapt: "Good problem to have. Is the aim more about keeping the work you've got more profitably, and getting some evenings back? That's often where [offer] helps most."

Then ask: What would you change about the work you have today?

QA.q: They said: If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
alts: If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
QA.a:
What it usually means: Change feels risky.

A reply to adapt: "Agreed, no point fixing what works. Can I ask one thing: of the last ten [calls / leads], how many turned into a booked job? [Listen.] Is that where you'd want it?"

Then ask: What would 'broken' look like for you?

QA.q: They said: Will it work with my software?

What it usually means: They don't want a tool that breaks how they work.

What it usually means: Legal worries.

Then ask: Do you have a recording policy we should follow?

What it usually means: Fear of lock-in.

Then ask: Would you like to see that clause?

dilchaspi nahi hai

What it usually means: Bad timing, or a brush-off.
