L.t: How cold email works, and the rules
L.idea: Cold email is a short, relevant note to a business contact, sent from a healthy domain, with an honest way to opt out.
L.md:
## What cold email is good for
Cold email reaches decision makers who never pick up the phone. It scales, it leaves a written trail, and it works well beside calls and social messages. It is weaker for complex pitches, so keep the goal small: **get a reply, then get a short call.**

## The simple model
Replies come from four things multiplied together:
**deliverability x right person x relevant message x easy ask.**
If any one is near zero, the result is near zero. A perfect email that lands in spam gets nothing. A perfect inbox placement with a vague message gets nothing too.

## Set honest expectations
Reply rates vary a lot by list, offer and message. Treat any benchmark you read as a rough guide, and measure your own. A realistic early target is a steady trickle of replies and a few booked calls per few hundred emails, then improve from there.

## The rules you must follow
!> General information, not legal advice
!> Check your own situation with a qualified attorney.

- **United States (CAN-SPAM):** applies to commercial email, including business to business. Use your real name and a truthful from line, a subject that is not misleading, a valid physical postal address, and a clear way to opt out. Honour opt-outs promptly (the law allows up to 10 business days, so do it the same day). Penalties apply per email.
- **Mailbox provider rules:** Google and Yahoo tightened requirements for bulk senders in 2024. They expect proper authentication (SPF, DKIM and DMARC), easy unsubscribe for bulk marketing mail and low spam complaint rates (under 0.3 percent, and ideally far lower).
- **Other regions:** the UK, EU and Canada have stricter consent rules for some recipients. Canada's anti-spam law is especially strict. If you email outside the US, check the rules first.

## A simple compliance habit
Put a one-line opt-out and your company name and address in every email. Keep a suppression list of everyone who asks to stop, and never email them again.

> The two-sentence summary
> Send a short, honest, relevant email to a real business contact. Make it easy to say no, and respect it.
L.drill: Write your sender identity (name, company, address, opt-out line) and a suppression list in your sheet. Then list the countries of the prospects you plan to email and note which rules apply.
quiz: Which part of the simple model can ruin an otherwise perfect email?
Poor deliverability, so it lands in spam
If the email never reaches the inbox, the rest does not matter.
What should you do when someone asks to stop receiving your emails?
Add them to a suppression list and never email them again
Ask them to fill a form

L.t: Set up so you land in the inbox
L.idea: Use separate sending domains, authenticate them properly, warm up slowly and keep volume low per mailbox.
L.md:
## Never send cold email from your main domain
If your main domain gets flagged, your normal business email suffers too. Buy one to three look-alike domains for sending (for example, if your brand is acme.com, use tryacme.com or getacme.com), and redirect them to your main website.

## Mailboxes
Create two or three mailboxes per domain, each with a real person's name. A common approach is to use a mainstream mailbox provider for each. Spreading volume across several mailboxes keeps each one well below the limits where problems start.

## The three DNS records
| Record | What it does | Plain meaning |
|---|---|---|
| SPF | Lists which servers may send for your domain | "These servers are allowed to send as me" |
| DKIM | Adds a signature to each email | "This email was not altered, and really came from me" |
| DMARC | Tells receivers what to do if SPF or DKIM fail | "Check my mail and report problems" |

Set all three up before you send anything. Your email provider has step-by-step guides. A free tester, such as a mail-tester or DNS checker, will confirm they work.

## Warm up before you send
New mailboxes have no reputation. Warm-up means sending and receiving small, natural volumes of email for two to four weeks, so inbox providers learn your mailbox is real. Most sending platforms include a warm-up feature. Keep it running even after you start sending campaigns.

## Keep volume low
A common rule of thumb is to start with 10 to 20 cold emails a day per mailbox and rise slowly toward 30 to 50 only if bounce and spam rates stay healthy. Spread sends across the working day, not in one burst.

## Technical choices that help
- **Plain text** emails with no heavy design.
- **Zero or one link** in the first email. Add your domain's signature, no images.
- **No open tracking.** It adds a hidden image and is unreliable. Track replies, which are what matter.
- **Custom tracking domain** if you do track clicks.
- **Verify every email address** before sending, so your bounce rate stays under about 2 percent.

## Watch the health signals
Check bounce rate, spam complaints and replies weekly. If bounces rise or replies fall, pause the mailbox and fix the cause before sending more.

!> Do not rush this
!> Skipping setup is the most common reason cold email fails. A week of setup saves months of damage.
L.drill: Work through the Cold email pre-flight checklist. Do not send a single campaign email until every box is ticked.
quiz: To protect your main domain's reputation
If a sending domain is flagged, your main business email stays safe.
To build a sending reputation before real campaigns
New mailboxes have no reputation, so they need a few weeks of natural activity.

L.t: Build and clean an email list
L.idea: One narrow list, one clear persona, every address verified.
L.md:
## One list, one persona
Do not send the same email to plumbers, dentists and gyms. Build one list for one type of business and one type of role, so the message can be specific. Aim for 200 to 500 contacts per campaign.

## Where to find emails
- Company websites (contact pages and team pages).
- Business directories and map listings, then the company website for the address.
- Professional networks, for names and titles.
- Data tools that provide company and contact details. Check their terms and the law in the target region.

## Prefer a named person
An email to a named decision maker beats one to a generic mailbox. If you only find a generic address, such as info@, it can still work for small businesses where the owner reads everything, but expect lower replies.

## Verify before you send
Run every address through an email verification tool. Remove invalid addresses, spam traps and risky ones. Treat "catch-all" domains carefully: they accept everything, so you cannot be sure the mailbox exists. Send to them in small amounts or skip them.

## Clean the data
- Remove duplicates and anyone on your suppression list.
- Use the person's first name as they use it, and the business name in the form people say it ("Apex Plumbing", not "APEX PLUMBING LLC").
- Add one personal line per lead for your best prospects (a trigger, a review, a hire).

## Segment by quality
| Tier | What it means | What to send |
|---|---|---|
| A | Strong fit and a clear trigger | Personal email, maybe a short video |
| B | Good fit | Template with one personalised line |
| C | Maybe | Template only, or skip |

> Rule of thumb
> If you would not be comfortable reading the email aloud to the person on a phone call, the list is wrong.
L.drill: Build a 200-contact list for one persona. Verify every address and mark each lead tier A, B or C. Count how many remain after cleaning.
quiz: Why verify email addresses before sending?
To keep bounce rates low and protect your reputation
Because it is a legal rule
High bounce rates damage your sender reputation.
Why keep one list for one persona?
So the message can be specific and relevant
Specific messages get more replies than generic ones.

L.idea: Short, about them, and easy to answer. Name a problem other owners have, offer something useful, and ask a question with an easy no.
L.md:
## The shape of a good cold email
Aim for **50 to 90 words**. Read it on your phone. If it needs scrolling, cut it.

1. **Subject:** short, lowercase, like a colleague wrote it ("after-hours calls", "question about apex").
2. **First line:** why you're writing to *them*: a trigger, an observation, or a problem other owners like them have.
3. **The problem:** one likely pain, in plain words.
4. **Something useful:** a free audit, a short demo, a result. Only what is true.
5. **One easy question:** low friction, with an easy no.
6. **Signature and opt-out line.**

## Ask small, give first
A cold email that asks for a 30-minute meeting asks a stranger for a lot. One that offers something useful asks for very little:

| Ask | Friction |
|---|---|
| "Can we book a 30-minute demo?" | High |
| "Worth a 10-minute look on Thursday?" | Medium |
| "Mind if I send a 40-second demo of how your after-hours calls could be answered?" | Low |
| "Is this even a problem for you, or am I off base?" | Lowest |

Start low. Book the meeting in the second or third message, once they've replied.

## A worked example
**Subject:** after-hours calls

Hi Dave,

A few of your reviews mention it's hard to reach Apex after 5 pm. Most plumbers I talk to lose jobs that way, mostly from people who never leave a voicemail.

I recorded a 40-second demo of how those calls could be answered and booked for Apex. Want me to send it over, or is this not really a problem for you?

Sam
If you'd rather not hear from me, reply "stop" and I won't email again.

## Neutral beats hype
Words like "revolutionary", "skyrocket", "guaranteed results" and "limited time" read like an ad and trigger spam filters and suspicion. Write the way a calm expert talks. "Not sure if it's relevant, but..." gets more honest replies than "You need this."

## Three first-line types
| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| Trigger | "Saw you're hiring a dispatcher." |
| Observation | "Your site says 24/7, but a couple of reviews mention missed calls." |
| Problem other owners have | "Most plumbers I talk to lose jobs on calls after 5." |

## What to avoid
Long company introductions, attachments, images, more than one link, fake "Re:" subjects, fake urgency, and anything you couldn't say out loud on a phone call.

!> Be truthful
!> Never claim a relationship, a result or a client you don't have.

call.meta: To an owner of a plumbing company

Proves you looked at their business, in one line.

quiz: About how long should a cold email be?
Short emails get read and answered.
Which ask has the lowest friction?
Is this even a problem for you, or am I off base?
An easy question with an easy no is the simplest thing to reply to.
Why offer a demo or audit in the first email?

L.idea: Most replies come from follow-ups. Four to five short emails over two to three weeks, each with a new reason to reply, never 'just checking in'.
L.md:
## Why follow-ups matter
People are busy. Many replies arrive after the second, third or fourth email. One email is a lottery ticket. A short sequence is a process.

## A five-email sequence
| Day | Email | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | First email | Observation, problem, something useful, easy question |
| 4 | Follow-up 1 | One new fact or question: "Most plumbers find about half of after-hours callers never leave a voicemail. Does that match what you see?" |
| 8 | Follow-up 2 | Different angle: a different problem, a real result, or the lead magnet again in a new form |
| 13 | Follow-up 3 | Very short and neutral: "Is fixing after-hours calls on your list at all, or should I leave it?" |
| 18 | Close-out | "I'll stop reaching out. If missed calls ever become a headache, reply here." |

## Every follow-up brings something
Never "just checking in" or "bumping this to the top of your inbox". Each email adds a new fact, a new question, a different benefit or a lower-friction ask.

## Short and neutral works late in the sequence
After a few emails, a one-line neutral question often gets the reply long emails didn't: "Did you already sort out after-hours calls, or is it still an issue?" It's easy to answer, and both answers are useful.

## Same thread
Reply in the same thread with the same subject to keep context.

## Timing
Send in the recipient's working hours. Mid-week mornings often work well, but test with your own data. Space emails further apart as you go.

## Stop rules
Stop immediately when someone replies, books or opts out. Never send a "follow-up" after a no.

## Combine channels
Pair email with a call, a social message or a short video. A call the day after email two often lifts response from people who ignored the emails.
L.drill: Build the five-email sequence in the Cadence builder. Write every email in your own words with no 'just', make the fourth under 20 words, and load it for a small test list.
quiz: Add something new: a fact, question, benefit or easier ask
A new reason gives a new chance to reply.
Why send a very short neutral question late in the sequence?
It's easy to answer and both answers are useful
Low effort to reply means more replies.
When they reply, book or opt out
A reply or opt-out ends automation immediately.

L.idea: Reply fast, stay calm, ask one question, and move interested people to a call. Treat every no, referral and opt-out with the same respect.
L.md:
## Speed matters
A reply is a warm lead. Answer within the hour during working time. A reply that sits for a day cools fast.

## Positive reply: one question, then book
**They say:** "Sure, send the demo."
**You say:** Send it, then: "Here it is. Out of curiosity, roughly how many calls come in after you close in a busy week?" When they answer: "Worth 15 minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2 Eastern to see what it'd look like on your numbers?"

Ask one question before the booking ask, so the meeting is about their problem, not your product.

## "Send me more info"
"Happy to. So I send the right thing, what's the main thing you'd want to know?" Then: "Honestly, 10 minutes on a call would answer it better than a brochure. Thursday or Friday?"

## "Not interested" or "Not now"
Defuse and leave an easy door open: "No problem at all. Is it that missed calls aren't really an issue for you, or just not the right time?" Then do what they say.

## "We already have someone"
"Good, that's probably why you've got the business you have. Do they cover nights and weekends too, or mostly daytime?"

## "Who is this?" or "How did you get my email?"
Be honest: "I found your business on [source] and wrote because [reason]. If you'd rather not hear from me, I'll remove you right away."

## "Wrong person"
"Thanks for telling me. Who would be the right person to ask about after-hours calls?" Referrals from these replies are often warm.

## Out-of-office
Pause the sequence and resume after their return date.

## Unsubscribe or "stop"
Remove them from every list and sequence at once. A brief reply is fine: "Done, you're removed. Sorry for the interruption."

## Angry replies
Don't argue. Apologise briefly, remove them and move on.

## Keep a reply log
Tag each reply as positive, neutral, negative, referral or opt-out. Your **positive reply rate** tells you if the email works.
L.drill: Write your reply to each of the nine reply types above. Save them as snippets in your sending tool.
quiz: A prospect replies 'sure, send the demo'. What do you do?
Send it and ask one question about their situation, then offer a time
One question keeps the conversation about their problem, then you book.
How fast should you answer a positive reply?
Within the hour in working time
Speed turns interest into a booked call.
What do you do with an opt-out?

L.idea: Track replies and booked calls, change one thing at a time and test with enough volume.
L.md:
## Metrics that matter
| Metric | What it tells you | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| Bounce rate | List quality | Keep under about 2% |
| Spam complaints | Message and targeting problems | As close to zero as possible |
| Reply rate | Interest and deliverability | Rising |
| Positive reply rate | Real interest | Rising |
| Booked calls | The result | Your funnel number |

## Why not opens?
Open tracking is unreliable, because many mail apps load images automatically, and it can hurt deliverability. Judge your emails by replies.

## Diagnose with the funnel
- **Few replies, low bounces:** the message or the list needs work.
- **Many bounces:** your list or verification is poor.
- **Replies, but few positive:** targeting is off, or the offer is weak.
- **Positive replies, few booked:** reply faster and ask better.

## Test one variable at a time
Change one thing per test: the subject, the first line, the ask or the offer. Send at least 100 to 200 emails per version before you decide. Small samples mislead.

## A weekly routine
1. Check mailbox health and bounces.
2. Review replies and tag them.
3. Pick the weakest metric.
4. Launch one test.
5. Log the result.

## Stop rules for campaigns
Pause a campaign if bounces climb above your limit or a mailbox gets complaints. Fix first, then resume at a lower volume.

> Keep a swipe file
> Save your best emails and the replies they got. After ten campaigns you will have your own proven templates.
L.drill: Set up a one-page tracker for your next campaign: sent, bounced, replies, positive replies, booked. Plan your first test and write down what you expect to happen.
quiz: Which metric should you trust more than opens?
Replies measure what you want, and opens are unreliable.
How should you run a test?
Change one thing and send enough volume
One variable and enough volume gives a result you can trust.

L.t: Deliverability in 2026: the rules and the numbers to watch
L.idea: If your emails land in spam, nothing else matters. Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft now enforce strict sender rules, and they can reject mail outright. Set up properly, send slowly, and watch a few numbers every week.
L.md:
## What changed
Over the last two years, Google, Yahoo and Microsoft moved their sender rules from advice to enforcement. Mail that fails them can now be rejected outright, not just moved to spam. Assume the strict rules apply to cold email even at low volume.

## The must-haves
| Rule | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** | All three set up on every sending domain, passing and matching the domain in your From address |
| **A DMARC policy** | Start with monitoring, then move to a stricter policy once everything passes |
| **Low spam complaints** | Google asks senders to stay below 0.1% and never reach 0.3% in Postmaster Tools |
| **Easy opt-out** | A clear way to stop emails, honoured quickly. US law (CAN-SPAM) also requires a physical address and no misleading subject lines |
| **Valid addresses** | Verify every list. Keep bounces under about 2% |

## The setup most cold emailers use
- **Separate domains** that look like your brand (yourbrand-mail.com, getyourbrand.com). Never your main domain.
- **Two or three mailboxes per domain**, on a proper email provider.
- **Warm up for two to three weeks** before the first campaign.
- **Send around 20 to 30 cold emails a day per mailbox** to start. Many practitioners cap at about 50. Need more volume? Add mailboxes, don't push each one harder.
- **Plain text, no images, few or no links in the first email**, and no open tracking. Tracking pixels and links can hurt inbox placement.

## Numbers to check every week
| Number | Healthy | Act now if |
|---|---|---|
| Bounce rate | under 2% | above 3%: stop, re-verify the list |
| Spam complaints | under 0.1% | approaching 0.3%: pause that domain |
| Reply rate | 1–3% is typical; top senders do better | under 0.5% for 300+ sends: fix list or message |
| Positive replies | a third or more of all replies | mostly negative: fix targeting |
| Inbox placement test | most land in the main inbox | many in spam or promotions: pause and check setup |

The average sender gets roughly one reply per 100 to 150 contacts. Good targeting and a short, relevant email can get you several times that.

## When something goes wrong
1. **Pause** the affected mailbox or domain. Don't keep sending into a problem.
2. **Check** authentication with a free checker, and look at Postmaster Tools.
3. **Clean** the list: re-verify, remove role addresses and anyone who bounced.
4. **Warm back up** at low volume for a week before you send again.

!> Laws and platforms change
!> These are general guidelines as of 2026, not legal advice. Check your email provider's current rules and the latest US and provider requirements before each new campaign.
L.drill: Run the Cold email pre-flight checklist for your domains. Write down your current bounce rate, complaint rate and daily volume per mailbox, and fix anything outside the healthy ranges before your next send.
quiz: What happens to mail that fails the providers' sender rules now?
It can be rejected outright, not just sent to spam
It goes to the promotions tab only
Enforcement has moved from spam folders to outright rejection.
You need to send more emails a day. What's the safe move?
Push each mailbox to 200 a day
Spread volume across more mailboxes instead of overloading each one.
Your bounce rate jumps to 5%. What should you do first?
Send more to make up for it
High bounces damage your domain. Stop, clean the list, then restart slowly.

L.t: A swipe file: ten cold emails and why they work
L.idea: Short beats long. Problem beats pitch. A question beats a meeting request. Here are ten emails for different niches and situations, each under about 80 words, with notes on why they work.
L.md:
## What the best cold emails have in common
- **Short**: emails under about 50 to 80 words tend to get more replies. They're read on a phone.
- **About them**: more "you" than "we".
- **One problem**, not a list of services.
- **An easy ask**: "worth a look?" or "is this on your radar?" instead of "book a 30-minute call".
- **Plain**: no images, no links in the first email, written like a person.

## 1. Signal: hiring (clinics)
> Subject: front desk
> Hi Dr. Patel, saw you're hiring a second receptionist. When clinics grow, calls often slip through at lunch and after 5. We help clinics catch those with online booking and a missed-call text-back. Worth a look at how many you're missing?

*Why it works:* a real signal, one problem, a low-effort question.

## 2. Problem question (home services)
> Subject: after-hours calls
> Hi Mike, quick question: what happens to calls that come in after your office closes? Most HVAC owners I speak with lose a few jobs a week to voicemail. If that's you, I can show you what it's costing on your numbers. Open to it?

## 3. Review-based (restaurants)
> Subject: your Tuesday reviews
> Hi Sara, noticed a few reviews say Tuesdays are quiet and service is great. We help family restaurants fill weekday tables with local ads. Want three ad ideas written for your menu? No call needed.

*Why it works:* offers something useful before asking for time.

## 4. Free audit (websites)
> Subject: 3 things on your site
> Hi Tom, I looked at your booking page on my phone and found three things that probably cost you appointments. I recorded a two-minute video showing them. Want me to send it?

## 5. Agency to agency (B2B)
> Subject: referrals
> Hi Lisa, most agency owners tell me referrals are great but impossible to plan around. We set up outbound that books 8 to 12 qualified calls a month alongside referrals. Is a steady calendar a priority this quarter, or not really?

## 6. Follow-up with new value
> Example
> Hi Mike, one more idea on after-hours calls: a simple text that goes out within a minute of a missed call gets a lot of those callers back. Happy to show you how it'd look for you.

## 7. Follow-up with a question
> Example
> Hi Sara, is filling weekdays a priority right now, or is it more of a summer project?

## 8. Breakup
> Example
> Hi Tom, I haven't heard back, so I'll assume the timing's off. Should I close this out, or check back in a few months?

*Why it works:* gives a polite way out, which often prompts a reply.

## 9. Reactivating an old lead
> Example
> Hi Dave, we spoke in March about missed calls and you said to check back after the busy season. Is it worth picking this up again?

## 10. Referral ask from a contact
> Example
> Hi Ahmed, quick favour: do you know anyone who runs a clinic or a dental practice in the US? I've built something that helps them book more patients online and I'm looking for two more to work with.

## Adapt, don't copy
Change the problem, the niche and the details to match your offer. Read each email out loud. If it sounds like an advert, cut it until it sounds like a note from a person.

!> Honest claims only
!> Only use numbers and results you can back up. Lines like "8 to 12 calls a month" in these examples are placeholders. Replace them with your real results, or remove them.
L.drill: Pick three emails from this file that fit your niche. Rewrite each for your offer in under 80 words. Paste them into the message builder (cold email) and check the word count and warnings.
quiz: Which ask usually gets more replies in a cold email?
Worth a look at how many you're missing?
Visit our website to learn more
A low-effort question is easier to answer than a meeting request from a stranger.
Why does the breakup email often get a reply?
It gives a polite way out, which feels safe to answer
People reply when it's easy and low pressure, even if the answer is 'later'.
An example email mentions '8 to 12 calls a month'. You have no results yet. What do you do?
Replace it with your real results or remove it
Only use claims you can back up.

L.idea: Social outreach is a conversation, not a pitch. Notice, connect, talk, then move to a call.
L.md:
## Why use social platforms
Prospects spend time on social platforms and often reply there faster than by email or phone. Messages feel personal, and a profile gives them a way to check you are real.

## The arc: notice, appreciate, ask, then set
1. **Notice.** Find a real reason to reach out: a post, a hire, a review, a shared group.
2. **Appreciate.** One genuine line about it. Not flattery, just something true.
3. **Ask.** One easy question about their work, with an easy no. Listen.
4. **Set.** Move through situation, problem, impact and desire before you invite them to a call (the five DM setting stages in lesson 7.7).

Give before you ask. Offering something useful (a missed-call check, a 40-second demo, a quick tip) earns replies that pitches never get (lesson 2.6).

## Pick the platform by audience
| Platform | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| LinkedIn | Professionals, agency owners, managers, B2B | Best for names, titles and company search |
| Facebook | Local business owners, trades, community groups | Groups and business Pages are where owners spend time |
| Instagram | Visual and local businesses, solo owners | Warm-up matters, since DMs from strangers land in a requests folder |

## Warm beats cold
A message from someone they have seen before gets replies. Spend a few days following, liking and leaving a thoughtful comment before you message.

## The rules of the road
- **Platform rules:** each platform restricts scraping and heavy automation, and can limit or close accounts that break its terms. Start manual, stay under limits and do not send identical messages in volume.
- **Honesty:** use your real identity. Do not fake profiles or claim a relationship you do not have.
- **Respect a no:** one polite follow-up, then stop.
- **Privacy:** only use information they have made public, and do not repeat private details back to them.
- **Laws:** anti-spam and marketing laws can still apply to messages. Check the rules where you and your prospect are.

## How much to send
Quality over volume. Twenty thoughtful messages a day, with real notes, beat two hundred copies.

> A good first message
> It is short, about them, contains no pitch, and ends in a question they can answer in five words, including "no".
L.drill: Choose the platform where your ideal prospect is most active. Find 10 prospects there and write the one real reason you would message each.
quiz: What is the first step of the arc?
Notice a real reason to reach out
A genuine reason makes the message relevant.
How should you start on a platform where you are a stranger?
Warm up by following and commenting thoughtfully
Send the same message to everyone

L.idea: Before you message anyone, make your profile answer three questions: who you help, how, and why they should trust you.
L.md:
## Why profiles matter
Almost everyone you message will look at your profile first. If it looks empty, odd or promotional, the message dies.

## LinkedIn
- **Photo:** clear, friendly, face visible, plain background.
- **Headline:** who you help and the result. "I help plumbing companies answer every call and book more jobs" beats "Sales professional".
- **About:** four short paragraphs. The problem you solve, how you do it, who it is for, how to contact you. Write in first person.
- **Featured:** one proof item (a short case, a demo video, a checklist). Only use real work.
- **Activity:** a few useful posts or comments, so the profile looks alive.

## Facebook
- Use a clean personal profile with a professional photo, or a business Page for your company.
- Add a short intro and a link to your site. Set old posts that look unprofessional to private.
- Join relevant groups as yourself, not as a brand.

## Instagram
- Switch to a business or creator account.
- **Bio:** what you do, who for, and one call to action. Keep it under three lines.
- **Photo:** face or clean logo.
- **Highlights:** "Results", "How it works", "About". Use real material.
- Post enough that the grid is not empty, such as short tips or behind-the-scenes clips.

## One consistent identity
Use the same name, photo and one-line promise across all platforms. A prospect who sees you in three places trusts you more.

## Proof without inventing anything
If you have no client results yet, show a process, a sample audit, a demo or your own learning in public. Put placeholders in your plan for real proof, and replace them the moment you have it.

!> Never fake proof
!> No invented testimonials, logos, numbers or follower counts.
L.drill: Rewrite your headline or bio in one sentence that names who you help and the result. Check it with a stranger: can they tell what you do in five seconds?
quiz: What should a LinkedIn headline say?
Who you help and the result
A specific promise tells a prospect why to reply.
What if you have no results to show yet?
Show your process, a sample or a demo, and add real proof later
Honest proof of work still builds trust.

L.idea: Warm up, send a short connection note, start a conversation, then move off the platform.
L.md:
## Find the right people
Use search filters: job title, industry, location and company size. A paid navigator tool helps with filters and saved lists, but the free search is enough to start. Save your list in a sheet so you never message the same person twice.

## Warm up for two or three days
View their profile, like a post and add one useful comment. People are more likely to accept someone they have seen.

## The connection note
Keep it short. The note has a strict character limit, so aim for under 200 characters. Do not pitch.

**Examples**
- "Hi Dave, I work with plumbing companies on after-hours calls. Saw your team is growing. Would be good to connect."
- "Hi Maria, I enjoyed your post on hiring techs. I help local trades with phones and bookings. Happy to connect."
- No note is fine too, and sometimes accepted more often than a salesy one.

## Message one, after they accept
Thank them and ask one easy question. No link, no pitch.
"Thanks for connecting, Dave. Curious: when a customer calls after hours, what usually happens to the call?"

## Message two, after they reply
Go one layer deeper, in their words: "Makes sense. Of the ones that hit voicemail, do many end up calling someone else first?" Then: "Is that something you'd want to fix, or just part of the business?"

## If they don't reply, after 3 to 4 days
Add value with an easy no: "Most owners I speak with find about half of after-hours callers never leave a voicemail. Does that match what you see, or not really?"

## The invite, once they've described the problem
"Not sure we're a fit, but happy to show you how two other plumbers handle it. 15 minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?" Or offer a short demo video first.

## Voice notes and InMail
Short voice notes can feel warm. Paid direct messages can reach people you are not connected to, but use them for your best prospects only.

## Stay safe
- LinkedIn limits how many connection requests you can send, and watches for automation and copied messages. Commonly cited guidance is to stay well under 100 requests a week.
- Third-party automation tools break the platform's terms and can get an account restricted. Start manual.
- Vary your messages and write each first line for the person.

## Sequence at a glance
Day 1 connect, day 2 or 3 after accept: message one, day 6 to 7: message two, day 12 to 14: message three or a polite close.

call.title: LinkedIn conversation, annotated
turns: Hi Dave, I work with plumbing companies on after-hours calls. Saw your team is growing. Would be good to connect.
Thanks for connecting, Dave. Curious: when a customer calls after hours, what usually happens to the call?
Invites a reply with no link and no pitch.
Goes to voicemail. We call back in the morning.
Makes sense. Do you find some of them have already called someone else by then?
Lets him state the cost in his own words.
Is that something you'd want to fix, or just part of running the business?
If he says he wants it fixed, that is a commitment in his own words.
I'd fix it if it was easy.
Not sure we're a fit yet, but happy to show you how two other plumbers handle it. 15 minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
Low pressure, specific, and only after he admitted the problem and the desire.

L.drill: Write three connection notes and a three-message sequence for one persona. Send 10 over the week and note acceptance and reply rates.
quiz: What should the first message after connecting do?
A light question starts a real conversation.
When should you invite them to a call?
After they've described the problem and said they'd like it fixed
An invite lands when it's about a problem they admitted.
Why should you avoid third-party automation tools at the start?
They can break platform rules and risk your account
Platforms can restrict accounts that use automation.

L.t: Facebook outreach: groups, pages and Messenger
L.idea: On Facebook, give value in groups first, then message people who already know your name.
L.md:
## Where owners are on Facebook
Many local business owners use Facebook for their business Page and for trade or industry groups. Contractors, for example, often share questions in groups about pricing, staff and software.

## Step 1: Join and listen
Join three to five relevant groups. Read the rules first. Many groups ban promotion, so do not post a pitch.

## Step 2: Be useful
For a week, answer questions, share a useful tip and comment on posts. Your name should be familiar before you message anyone.

## Step 3: Message people who engaged
Message someone who posted a question you can help with, or who replied to your comment.

**Examples**
- "Hi Dave, saw your question about missed calls in the group. A few ideas worked well for other shops. Want me to share, or have you already sorted it?"
- "Hi Maria, loved your post on hiring techs. Do you ever struggle to cover the phones when the team is out?"

## Messaging a business Page
You can message a business through its Page. Use the same rules: short, relevant, no pitch. Ask who handles phones or scheduling, and whether you can send them a short note.

## Messenger basics
Messages from people you are not friends with usually land in a message requests folder. Some will never see yours. Warming up in groups and comments helps a lot.

## What to avoid
- Posting links or ads in groups that ban them.
- Messaging every member of a group.
- Sending the same copy-paste message to many people.
- Scraping group member lists.

## Move off Facebook
Once there is interest, suggest a call or ask for an email: "Easier to show you on a call. Does Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2 work?"

> Be a good guest
> Groups run on trust. One spammy post can get you banned from the whole group.
L.drill: Join three relevant groups. Contribute one genuinely useful comment a day for five days. Then message the first three people who engage with you.
quiz: What should you do first in a Facebook group?
Read the rules and contribute value
Respecting the group's rules protects your access and reputation.
Where do messages from strangers often land?
Many people never check requests, so warm up first.

L.idea: Warm up with follows, story views and real comments, then send a short DM that refers to something they posted.
L.md:
## Who to find on Instagram
Instagram works well for visual and local businesses, solo owners and creators. Find them by location, hashtags, tagged posts and the accounts that follow similar businesses.

## Warm-up first
Spend two to three days following, watching their stories and leaving thoughtful comments (not just emojis). Your name should appear before your DM.

## The first DM
Refer to something real. Keep it short. No link.

**Examples**
- "Hi Dave, loved the bathroom remodel you posted yesterday. Do you handle emergency calls too, or just scheduled jobs?"
- "Hi Maria, saw your story about the busy week. How do you keep up with calls when you are out on jobs?"

## Story replies
Replying to a story is one of the most natural ways to start a chat. Say something specific about the story, then ask a question.

## Message requests
If you do not follow each other, the message goes to the requests folder. A follow and a few likes before messaging help.

## Voice notes
A 15-second voice note can feel personal. Use it for your best prospects and keep it friendly, not salesy.

## When to move
When they've described the problem and said they'd like it fixed: "Easier to show you than type. Not sure it's a fit, but 15 minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?" Or offer a short demo video first.

## Keep it safe
- Do not send identical DMs in bulk.
- Keep daily volume low and spread it out.
- Do not use bots to like and follow at scale.
- Use a business account that is easy to verify as real.

## Do not
Pitch in the first message, send a link to a stranger, tag people in ads or ask for a sale in a comment.
L.drill: Pick 10 local businesses. Follow, watch stories and comment on each for two days. Then send a personal DM to three of them and log replies.
quiz: What makes a good first Instagram DM?
A short message about something they posted
Why avoid sending identical DMs in bulk?
It looks like spam and can get you restricted
Copy-paste volume is exactly what platforms look for.

L.idea: Thirty focused minutes a day, a simple tracker and a clear follow-up rhythm beat sporadic bursts.
L.md:
## The 30-minute daily routine
| Minutes | Task |
|---|---|
| 5 | Reply to everyone who answered. Replies come first |
| 10 | Warm up: comment on posts of tomorrow's targets |
| 10 | Send new notes and first messages (about 10 to 20) |
| 5 | Log everything in your tracker |

## What to track
For each prospect: name, business, platform, date of first touch, stage, next action and a note. A spreadsheet or the Lead tracker is enough.

## Stages
New, warmed, connected, in conversation, call booked, no reply, closed out.

## Follow-up rhythm
- **Day 1:** connect or follow, and engage.
- **Day 3 to 4:** first message after they accept.
- **Day 7:** second message with something useful.
- **Day 10:** a very short neutral question: "Is this even a problem for you, or am I off base?"
- **Day 14:** a polite close or a short video. Then stop.

Never "just following up". Every touch brings a reason: a new fact, their own words, or something useful.

## Combine channels
A LinkedIn message plus an email, or an Instagram DM plus a call, outperforms one channel alone. Always mention the other touch lightly: "I also sent a short email."

## Measure
Weekly: messages sent, acceptances, replies, conversations, calls booked. Divide to find your rates. If acceptances are low, your note needs work. If replies are low, your first message does.

## Account safety checklist
- Real name and photo, complete profile.
- Low, steady volume.
- No scraping, no bots, no copy-paste at scale.
- Two-factor authentication on.
- One person per account, no sharing logins.

## When to stop
If a prospect says no or stops replying after two messages, close it out politely and move on.

> The goal
> Not messages sent. Conversations started, and calls booked.
L.drill: Run the 30-minute routine for five days. At the end, calculate your acceptance rate, reply rate and calls booked.
quiz: What should you do first in the daily routine?
Replies are warm and decay fast.

L.t: LinkedIn in 2026: limits, comments first, and voice notes
L.idea: LinkedIn rewards people who show up, not people who blast invitations. Stay well inside the limits, warm people up with comments, keep notes short, and use voice notes once you're connected.
L.md:
## Know the limits
LinkedIn limits how many invitations you can send, roughly around 100 a week for most established accounts and fewer for new ones. Going near the edge, sending identical messages or using automation that acts like a bot can get your account restricted.

| Account | Safe pace (invitations) |
|---|---|
| New (under 3 months) | 20–30 a week |
| Established | 15–20 a day, up to about 100 a week |
| Any account | Spread across weekdays; avoid sudden jumps |

Free accounts can only add a personal note to a small number of invitations each month. Check what your account allows, and send many invitations without a note if needed: the warm-up and the follow-up message do the work.

## Comments first, connection second
1. **Follow** the person for a few days.
2. **Comment** on one or two of their posts with something useful: a question, an experience, a short tip. Not "Great post!"
3. **Then connect.** They've seen your name and your face. Acceptance rates are higher.

## Keep the first message tiny
After they accept, don't pitch. Thank them, mention something real, and ask a light question.
> Say it like this
> "Thanks for connecting, Lisa. Your post about hiring setters was spot on. Out of curiosity, are you building the outbound side in-house, or still mostly referrals?"

## Voice notes once you're connected
A 30 to 45 second voice note from the LinkedIn mobile app stands out in a sea of text. Say who you are, why you're reaching out, and ask one question. Speak calmly, the way you would on a call. Your communication drills help here.

## Post a little, consistently
Two short posts a week about what you're learning or what you see in your niche make your profile feel real when people check you out. You don't need to go viral. You need to look like a real person who knows the field.

## What not to do
- Pitching in the connection note.
- Long messages with links in the first message.
- Copy-paste messages to hundreds of people.
- Tools that send invitations or messages for you in bulk.

> Move off LinkedIn when it's warm
> Once someone describes the problem, offer a short call and send your booking link. Don't try to close a deal in DMs.
L.drill: Pick ten people in your niche on LinkedIn. Comment usefully on one post from each over the next three days, then send invitations. Write the first message you'll send when they accept, and record one 30-second voice note to practise.
quiz: What's the safest way to grow LinkedIn outreach?
Stay well inside the limits and spread invitations across weekdays
Use a bot to send everything
Send the same message to everyone
Steady, human-paced activity keeps the account safe.
What should you do before connecting with a prospect?
Comment usefully on one or two of their posts
Like every post they've ever made
Useful comments make your name familiar and raise acceptance.
When is a voice note a good idea?
Once you're connected, as a short personal message
A short voice note after connecting feels personal and stands out.

L.t: Why short personal videos get replies
L.idea: A 45-second video made for one person shows effort, proves you looked, and stands out from text.
L.md:
## What the video method is
You record a short screen-and-face video about the prospect's business (their website, their reviews, a missed-call test) using a tool such as Loom. You send the link in an email, LinkedIn message or Instagram DM.

## Why it works
- **Effort is visible.** A video made for them is hard to ignore.
- **Proof you looked.** You show something specific about their business.
- **Trust.** They see and hear a real person.
- **Easy to consume.** Fifty seconds of video beats a paragraph.

## Where it fits
Use video for your **tier A prospects**, the best-fit accounts where one reply is worth real money. Do not send videos to everyone, since each takes a few minutes to make.

## Three good uses
1. **Audit video:** "I looked at your site and Google listing and here is one thing I noticed." This works like a lead magnet: it reveals a problem they couldn't see (lesson 2.6).
2. **Demo video:** a 60-second look at how your solution would work for them.
3. **Follow-up video:** a short thank-you or recap after a call.

## What it is not
Not a polished ad, not a long demo and not a pitch. It is a personal note on camera.

## Expectations
Videos usually raise reply rates compared to plain text, but results depend on the list, the offer and the video. Test it against text on the same segment.

## A fair warning
Show only information that is public or that they gave you. Do not share private data on screen or imply you have access to things you do not.

> Think of it as a handshake
> The goal is a reply: "Thanks, interesting. Let's talk."
L.drill: Choose five tier A prospects. For each, write the one specific thing you could show on screen in 20 seconds.
quiz: Each video takes time, so use it where one reply is worth the effort.
What should a prospect video feel like?
A short personal note on camera

L.idea: Hook with their name, show one specific thing, give one insight and make one small ask.
L.md:
## The four-part script
**1. Hook (5 seconds).** Their name and why you made this.
"Hi Dave, I made this quick video for Apex Plumbing."

**2. Show (15 seconds).** Their site, listing, reviews or a test you ran.
"I was looking at your Google listing and noticed three recent reviews say the phone rang out after 5 pm."

**3. Insight (15 seconds).** One observation, one consequence.
"That usually means jobs going to the next plumber who answers. It is fixable without hiring."

**4. Ask (10 seconds).** One small step, with an easy no.
"Not sure if it's a priority for you. If it is, happy to show you what fixing it looks like, 15 minutes this week. If not, no worries at all."

## Total length
About 45 seconds, 100 to 120 words spoken at a natural pace. Under a minute keeps people watching.

## Tone
Talk as you would to a colleague. Smile, vary your voice, and do not read a script word for word. Use bullet points as prompts.

## What to avoid
- A long intro about yourself.
- Reading price or features.
- Criticising their business harshly. Be kind: "an opportunity", not "a mistake".
- Hype words: "revolutionary", "skyrocket", "guaranteed". Speak like a calm expert.
- Fake claims about what you have done for others.

## Template you can reuse
Keep the structure fixed and swap in the **name, the thing you show and the one insight**. That makes the video personal and fast to make.

## Write the line that goes with it
A video link should travel with two lines of text: why you made it, and what you want. Example: "Dave, I made a 45-second video about calls after hours at Apex. Worth a look?"
L.drill: Use the message builder (video message) to write scripts for three prospects. Time yourself reading each. Aim for 40 to 55 seconds.
quiz: What goes first in the script?
Their name and why you made it
Name and reason make it personal immediately.
About how long should the video be?
Short videos are watched to the end.

L.t: Record it: setup, thumbnails and sharing
L.idea: A basic laptop, a quiet room and one clean take is enough. The thumbnail and the link placement matter more than polish.
L.md:
## What you need
- A laptop or phone with a decent camera.
- A headset or an external microphone. Audio matters more than video.
- Light from a window or a small lamp in front of you.
- A recording tool: Loom, or an alternative with a similar screen-and-camera feature.

## Free plans have limits
Many recording tools limit the free plan by video length and number of videos. Check the current limits before you rely on one.

## Record in one take
1. Close other tabs and silence notifications.
2. Open the page you will show.
3. Start recording with your face in the corner bubble.
4. Speak to the camera at the start and the end, and to the screen in the middle.
5. Stop, watch it once, and re-record if the audio or the point is off. Do not over-polish.

## Make a custom thumbnail
A thumbnail with their name on it ("Dave, quick idea for Apex Plumbing") and a screenshot of their site gets many more clicks than a default frame. Create it with a simple design tool and attach it to the link.

## Title and call to action
Title the video with their name. Add a call-to-action button or a booking link under the video, if your tool supports it.

## How to share
- **Email:** paste the link in plain text. Do not embed the video, since embeds can hurt deliverability. A small linked thumbnail is fine for tier A.
- **LinkedIn and Instagram DMs:** paste the link with one line of context.
- Check that it plays on a phone, since many prospects will open it on mobile.

## Privacy and permissions
Only show what is public or what they shared. Blur anything personal. Do not record other people without permission.

## Batch the work
Record in a block: 10 videos in 45 minutes, using the same script with swapped details.

> Done is better than perfect
> A slightly imperfect personal video beats a polished generic one.
L.drill: Record one practice video of your own business to yourself. Watch it, fix the audio and the first five seconds, then record a real one.
quiz: What matters most in a recording setup?
People forgive average video, not bad sound.
How should you share a video in a cold email?
Paste a plain link, maybe with a small linked thumbnail

L.idea: Place the link with one line of context, follow up when it is watched and batch the process.
L.md:
## The message that carries the link
**Email**
Subject: quick video for Apex
"Hi Dave, I made a 45-second video about after-hours calls at Apex. Worth a look? [link]. Sam. If you would rather not hear from me, reply stop."

**LinkedIn or Instagram**
"Hi Dave, made you a quick 45-second video on calls at Apex: [link]. Let me know what you think."

## Follow up when it is watched
Most tools tell you when a video has been viewed. A view is a signal, not an invitation to chase. Follow up within a day:
"Thanks for watching, Dave. Does this match what you see on after-hours calls? Happy to walk through it in ten minutes."

If it has not been watched in three days, send a short text-only nudge: "Did my video arrive okay?" Later in the sequence, a neutral question works well: "Is after-hours coverage on your list at all, or should I leave it?"

## A cadence with video
| Day | Touch |
|---|---|
| 1 | Short text-only email or connection |
| 3 | Video link with one line |
| 5 | Follow-up on the view, or a text-only nudge |
| 9 | Different angle, plain text |
| 14 | Polite close |

## Scale without losing the personal touch
- Use a fixed structure and change only the first line and the on-screen thing.
- Record in batches of ten.
- Use a tracker with columns for prospect, video link, sent date, viewed and reply.
- Review which videos got replies and copy their hooks.

## Measure
Send plain text to half and video to half of a similar list. Compare reply rates and booked calls.

## When not to use video
For low-value leads, very large teams where a stranger's video seems odd, or places where your tool is blocked.

## Be honest
A video is a tool for being personal, not for pretending a relationship that does not exist.
L.drill: Send five videos this week. Log views and replies. Compare to five plain-text messages to a similar group.
quiz: What should you do when a prospect views your video?
Follow up within a day with a light question
A view is a signal that a short, relevant follow-up is welcome.
How can you scale video outreach?
Use a fixed structure and swap personal details, in batches
Send the same video to all
A fixed structure with personal details is fast and still personal.

L.t: How to use these SOPs, and write your own
L.idea: An SOP is a written routine: what to do, in what order, how long it takes and how you know it's done. It turns good days into normal days, and it lets you hand work to someone else later.
L.md:
## Why SOPs matter
Most people know what to do. They just don't do it the same way every day. SOPs remove the daily decisions: you open the page, follow the steps, tick them off. Your results stop depending on your mood.

When you hire your first setter or assistant, these same pages become their training.

## How each SOP in this module is laid out
- **Purpose**: what it's for.
- **When and how long**: how often, and a realistic time.
- **You need**: the tools and inputs before you start.
- **Steps**: in order, each with a clear *done when*.
- **Quality check**: what to look at before you finish.
- **Common mistakes**: what usually goes wrong.

## The SOPs in this module
| SOP | How often |
|---|---|
| 16.2 Build 200 leads in a day | Weekly or when a list runs low |
| 16.3 Set up cold email from zero | Once, then for each new domain |
| 16.4 Launch an email campaign | Each new campaign |
| 16.5 The daily calling block | Every working day |
| 16.6 The daily social and video block | Every working day |
| 16.7 Handle replies and book meetings | Twice a day |
| 16.8 The weekly outreach review | Every Friday or Monday |

## A simple daily schedule
| Time (Pakistan) | What | Why then |
|---|---|---|
| Afternoon | List building, research, writing, video recording | US is asleep; do the prep |
| Early evening | Replies from overnight (SOP 16.7) | Catch up before US mornings |
| Evening to late night | Calling block (SOP 16.5), social block (SOP 16.6) | US business hours |
| Before you stop | Replies again, log your numbers | Nothing waits overnight |

US time zones differ. East Coast mornings start in your evening. West Coast mornings are three hours later.

## Write your own SOPs
When you find a better way to do something, write it down in the same format. Keep it on one page. Update it when it changes. An SOP that nobody follows is worse than none, so keep them short and real.
L.drill: Write your own daily schedule using the table in this lesson, adjusted for the US time zone of your niche. Put the blocks in your calendar for the next two weeks.
quiz: What's the main benefit of an SOP?
It removes daily decisions so the work gets done the same way every day
Routine makes results depend on the process, not on mood.
When should you call US businesses from Pakistan?
During US business hours, usually your evening and night
Call when they're at work: East Coast mornings start in your evening.
What should every step in an SOP have?
Knowing exactly when a step is finished keeps you moving.

L.t: SOP: build 200 leads in a day
L.idea: A clean, researched list is half the result. This SOP takes you from a niche to 200 verified leads with a signal column, in about five to six focused hours.
L.md:
## Purpose
Build a list of 200 businesses in your niche, with a named decision-maker, verified contact details and at least one signal for the best leads.

## When and how long
Once a week, or whenever your active list drops below 100. About 5 to 6 hours. Split it over two sessions if needed.

## You need
- Your niche in two lines (lesson 14.1) and who you serve (offer builder).
- The Lead search builder for search strings.
- A lead sheet or the Lead tracker, with these columns: Business, Website, City, State, Owner or manager, Title, Email, Phone, LinkedIn, Signal, Source, Status.
- An email verification tool.

## Steps
1. **Generate searches** (15 min). Use the Lead search builder for your niche and three to five cities or states. *Done when* you have at least ten search strings.
2. **Collect businesses** (90 min). Use Google Maps, directories and the sources in your niche pack. Add business, website, city and phone. *Done when* you have 250 rows (you'll lose some).
3. **Remove bad fits** (20 min). Delete chains outside your ICP, businesses that look closed, and duplicates. *Done when* every row matches your two-line niche.
4. **Find the decision-maker** (90 min). Website "About" pages, LinkedIn, Google reviews where owners reply. Add name and title. *Done when* at least 70% of rows have a named person.
5. **Find and verify emails** (45 min). Use your data tool, then verify every address. Remove invalid ones; mark risky ones. *Done when* every email is verified.
6. **Add signals** (60 min). Two minutes per lead for the top 100: hiring, ads, reviews, new location (lesson 2.8). *Done when* the Signal column is filled for your best leads.
7. **Sort and tag** (15 min). Signal leads first. Tag each row A (strong fit and signal), B (good fit) or C (weak). *Done when* the sheet is sorted and tagged.

## Quality check
- Pick 10 random rows. Is every one a real business in your niche, with a real person and a working contact?
- Is the bounce risk low? No unverified emails in the A and B rows.
- Do at least 30 rows have a signal?

## Common mistakes
- Buying huge lists and sending to all of them. Small and clean wins.
- Skipping the decision-maker and emailing info@ addresses.
- Building a new list before you've worked through the last one.
L.drill: Run this SOP for your niche, even if only for 50 leads the first time. Time each step, and write down which step took longest so you can speed it up next week.
quiz: What should you do before finding emails?
Remove businesses that don't fit your two-line niche
Cutting bad fits early saves time on every step that follows.
What's the target for named decision-makers?
A named person gets far better results than a generic inbox.
What's the rule before building a new list?
Work through the last list first
Finishing a list gives you real data on what works.

L.t: SOP: set up cold email from zero
L.idea: Do the setup once, properly, and your emails reach the inbox for months. Rush it and nothing you write will be seen. Allow about three weeks from buying domains to your first real send.
L.md:
## Purpose
Set up sending domains and mailboxes that pass the providers' rules and are warmed up for cold outreach.

## When and how long
Once, then again each time you add a domain. About 2 hours of setup, then 2 to 3 weeks of warm-up.

## You need
- A budget for 2 to 3 domains and 4 to 6 mailboxes.
- An email provider and a sending tool with warm-up.
- Access to your domain's DNS settings.
- The Cold email pre-flight checklist.

## Steps
1. **Buy domains** (20 min). Two or three variations of your brand, e.g. getyourbrand.com, yourbrandhq.com. Never use your main domain. *Done when* domains are registered.
2. **Point each domain to your main website** (10 min). So anyone who types it lands somewhere real. *Done when* each redirects.
3. **Create mailboxes** (20 min). Two or three per domain, with real names (sam@, sam.k@). Add a profile photo and a simple signature with your name, company and a physical address. *Done when* each mailbox can send and receive.
4. **Set SPF, DKIM and DMARC** (30 min). Follow your provider's steps for each domain. Start DMARC on monitoring. *Done when* a free checker shows all three passing.
5. **Connect to your sending tool** (15 min). Add every mailbox. *Done when* all show as connected.
6. **Turn on warm-up** (5 min). Let each mailbox warm for 2 to 3 weeks. *Done when* warm-up is running for all.
7. **Set sending limits** (5 min). Start at 15 to 20 cold emails per mailbox per day, rising to about 30 over the next weeks. Turn off open tracking. *Done when* limits are set.
8. **Test** (15 min). Send a plain test email from each mailbox to a Gmail and an Outlook address, or use an inbox placement test. *Done when* tests land in the main inbox.

## Quality check
- All three records pass on every domain.
- Every mailbox has a name, photo and signature.
- Warm-up has run at least two weeks with no problems.
- Daily limits are set and open tracking is off.

## Common mistakes
- Sending from the main company domain.
- Starting campaigns on day 2 of warm-up.
- One mailbox sending 200 emails a day.
- Forgetting the physical address and opt-out line.
L.drill: Work through steps 1 to 4 this week, or check your existing setup against them. Run the Cold email pre-flight checklist and fix every item that fails.
quiz: How long should mailboxes warm up before a real campaign?
Warm-up builds a sending history so providers trust the mailbox.
Why point each sending domain to your main website?
Anyone who types it lands somewhere real, which builds trust
A domain that leads nowhere looks suspicious to people and providers.
What should your starting daily limit be per mailbox?
Start low and raise slowly to protect your domains.

L.idea: A campaign launch is a checklist, not a guess. Check the list, the copy and the setup before you press send, then watch the first two days closely.
L.md:
## Purpose
Launch a new cold email campaign safely and learn from it quickly.

## When and how long
Each new campaign or new segment. About 2 hours to prepare, then 15 minutes a day for the first week.

## You need
- A verified list of one segment (SOP 16.2).
- Warmed-up mailboxes (SOP 16.3).
- Your one-page offer (lesson 14.7) and the email swipe file (lesson 4.9).
- The message builder (cold email) and the pre-flight checklist.

## Steps
1. **Choose one segment and one problem** (10 min). One niche, one problem, one offer. *Done when* you can say it in one sentence.
2. **Write the sequence** (45 min). First email under about 80 words, plus three or four follow-ups, each adding something new (lesson 4.5). *Done when* the whole sequence fits on one screen.
3. **Check the copy** (15 min). Read each email out loud. Check spam words, word count, and that every claim is true. *Done when* nothing sounds like an advert.
4. **Add personal lines** (time varies). Add signal or personal first lines for your A leads (lesson 2.9). *Done when* every A lead has one.
5. **Run the pre-flight checklist** (10 min). Setup, opt-out line, physical address, tracking off, limits set. *Done when* every item passes.
6. **Send a test** (10 min). Send the sequence to yourself on Gmail and Outlook. Check how it looks on a phone. *Done when* it looks like a normal personal email.
7. **Start small** (5 min). Launch to the first 50 to 100 leads, not the whole list. *Done when* the first sends go out.
8. **Watch days 1 and 2** (15 min a day). Check bounces, replies and any spam complaints. *Done when* bounces are under 2% and nothing looks wrong. Then release the rest.

## Quality check
- Every lead in the campaign belongs to one segment.
- First email under about 80 words, no images, no links.
- Bounces under 2% after the first 100.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing niches in one campaign, so you can't tell what worked.
- Launching to 2,000 leads at once.
- Judging after 50 sends. Wait for at least 300 before deciding.
L.drill: Prepare your next campaign with steps 1 to 6. Don't launch until every step is done. Write the date you'll judge the results (after at least 300 sends).
quiz: How many leads should the first send go to?
A small first send lets you catch problems before they hurt your domains.
Why keep one segment per campaign?
So you can tell what worked and for whom
Mixed segments make the results impossible to read.
When can you judge whether a campaign works?
Small numbers are mostly luck. Give it enough sends to see a pattern.

L.idea: Calls work when they're done in one protected block at the right time, with the list ready, the opener practised and every result logged. This SOP turns 90 minutes into the most productive part of your day.
L.md:
## Purpose
Make a focused block of calls that reaches decision-makers, starts conversations and books meetings.

## When and how long
Every working day during US business hours. Usually 60 to 90 minutes, in your evening. Mid-morning and late afternoon in their time zone are often good windows. Test what works for your niche.

## You need
- A calling list of at least 60 leads, sorted by signal (SOP 16.2).
- Your talk track (lesson 3.8) open in front of you.
- A headset and a quiet room.
- Your calling tool and a US number (lesson 12.5).
- Your 30-day plan open at the daily numbers.

## Steps
1. **Warm up** (5 min). Say your opener and your "not interested" reply out loud three times, or run one drill. *Done when* your voice feels calm.
2. **Set a target** (1 min). For example: 50 dials, 5 conversations, 1 meeting. *Done when* the target is written.
3. **Dial in a row** (60–75 min). No email, no social, no breaks between dials. If no answer, leave a 20-second voicemail on the first and third attempts only (lesson 3.6). *Done when* you hit the dial target or the time is up.
4. **Note every call in 10 seconds** (during). Outcome: no answer, voicemail, gatekeeper, conversation, meeting, not interested, wrong person. One line of notes. *Done when* every dial has an outcome.
5. **Send follow-ups** (10 min). Email or text anyone you spoke to, and anyone who asked for information. *Done when* every conversation has a follow-up.
6. **Log the numbers** (2 min). Dials, conversations, meetings into your daily numbers. *Done when* today's log is saved.

## Quality check
- Did you talk more than the owner in any conversation? Listen back to one call this week.
- Did every conversation end with a clear next step or a clear no?

## Common mistakes
- Researching during the block instead of before it.
- Stopping after the first rude hang-up.
- Not logging outcomes, so you can't see what's working.
- Calling outside the allowed hours or calling people who asked you not to. Check the US calling rules (lesson 7.6).
L.drill: Run one calling block today using this SOP, even if it's only 30 minutes. Log every outcome and compare your numbers with your target.
quiz: What should you do during the calling block?
Dial in a row with no other tasks
Back-to-back dialling keeps your energy and numbers up.
When should you leave a voicemail?
On the first and third attempts
A couple of short voicemails help; leaving one every time wastes time and annoys people.
What do you log after every dial?
The outcome and one line of notes
Outcomes show you where the calls are breaking down.

L.t: SOP: the daily social and video block
L.idea: Thirty to forty-five minutes a day on LinkedIn, Instagram or Facebook, plus a few personal videos, builds warm conversations that cold email can't. Do it in the same order every day.
L.md:
## Purpose
Start and continue conversations on social platforms, and send short personal videos to your best leads.

## When and how long
Every working day, 30 to 45 minutes, ideally during US business hours.

## You need
- Your list of target accounts on the platform that suits your niche.
- The message builder (LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram and video).
- A screen recording tool for videos (Module 6).

## Steps
1. **Reply first** (5 min). Answer every DM and comment from yesterday. *Done when* your inbox is clear.
2. **Engage** (10 min). Comment usefully on five to ten posts from prospects. *Done when* ten comments are posted.
3. **Connect** (5 min). Send 10 to 20 connection requests to people you've engaged with before, within platform limits (lesson 5.7). *Done when* requests are sent.
4. **Message new connections** (10 min). A short, light first message to people who accepted. *Done when* every new connection has a message.
5. **Record videos** (10–15 min). Three to five 45-second videos for your A leads, on their website or listing (lesson 6.2). *Done when* videos are recorded and sent with a one-line message.
6. **Log** (2 min). Comments, requests, messages, videos and replies in your daily numbers. *Done when* today's numbers are saved.

## Quality check
- No pitch in any connection note or first message.
- Every video mentions something specific about the business in the first five seconds.

## Common mistakes
- Sending connection requests to strangers with no warm-up.
- Copy-paste messages to everyone.
- Recording one long generic video and sending it to all.
- Spending the whole block scrolling.
L.drill: Run this block today. Set a 45-minute timer and do the steps in order. Log your numbers and note which step felt slowest.
quiz: What do you do first in the social block?
Reply to yesterday's messages and comments
Replies are warm conversations. They come before anything new.
What should the first five seconds of a personal video do?
Mention something specific about their business
Specific details show it was made for them, so they keep watching.
What's a sign the block is going wrong?
You spent most of it scrolling
Without the steps, the block turns into browsing.

L.t: SOP: handle replies and book meetings
L.idea: A reply is the most valuable thing your outreach produces, and it goes cold fast. Check twice a day, answer positive replies within hours, and move every interested person to a booked time.
L.md:
## Purpose
Turn replies on every channel into booked meetings, and close out every other reply properly.

## When and how long
Twice a day: when you start (overnight US replies) and before you stop. 15 to 30 minutes each time.

## You need
- Access to every inbox, LinkedIn, Instagram and missed calls.
- Your booking link.
- The reply guide (lesson 4.6), the [reply handler](#/t/replies) and the Lead tracker.

## Steps
1. **Collect** (5 min). Open every inbox and channel. *Done when* you've seen every new reply.
2. **Sort** (5 min). Tag each one: Interested, Question, Not now, Not interested, Wrong person, Out of office, Unsubscribe. *Done when* every reply has a tag.
3. **Answer Interested first** (10 min). One short reply with a question and two times, plus the booking link (example below). *Done when* every interested person has a reply within a few hours of you seeing it.
4. **Answer Questions** (5 min). Answer briefly, then ask for the call. *Done when* each has a reply.
5. **Close the rest properly** (5 min). Not now: set a reminder for the month they said. Wrong person: ask who handles it. Unsubscribe: remove them from every sequence and channel immediately. *Done when* every reply has an action.
6. **Update the tracker** (5 min). Stage, next step and date for every lead who replied. *Done when* the tracker matches reality.
7. **Confirm booked meetings** (2 min). Send the confirmation and reminders (message builder, meeting reminders). *Done when* every meeting has reminders scheduled.

## Example reply to an interested lead
> Short, one question, two times
> "Great to hear, Mike. Quick question so the call's useful: roughly how many calls do you miss a week? I have Thursday 10am or Friday 2pm your time, or pick a slot here: [link]"

## Quality check
- No interested reply waiting more than half a day.
- Every unsubscribe removed everywhere.
- Every meeting has a confirmation and reminders.

## Common mistakes
- Answering only by email when they replied on LinkedIn.
- Sending a long sales pitch to someone who said "sure, tell me more".
- Forgetting "not now" leads. They're often next quarter's clients.
L.drill: Set up the reply tags in your Lead tracker or sheet. Run this SOP at the start and end of your next working day, and write down how long the reply to your fastest interested lead took.
quiz: Which replies do you answer first?
Interest fades quickly, so these get the fastest response.
What's the best reply to 'sure, tell me more'?
A short reply with one question and two times to talk
Keep it short and move to a booked time.
Someone asks to stop being contacted. What do you do?
Remove them from every sequence and channel immediately
Opt-outs must be honoured everywhere, straight away.

L.idea: Once a week, look at the numbers, find the one weakest step and change one thing. This 45-minute habit is what separates people who improve from people who just stay busy.
L.md:
## Purpose
See what's working, find the biggest leak, and decide one change for next week.

## When and how long
Once a week, same day and time. About 45 minutes.

## You need
- Your daily numbers and the lead tracker.
- Your sending tool's campaign stats.
- The Funnel planner.

## The weekly table
Fill this in first. Every cell needs a number.

| Channel | Touches | Replies or conversations | Positive | Meetings booked | Meetings held |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Email | | | | | |
| Calls | | | | | |
| LinkedIn / social | | | | | |
| Video | | | | | |
| Total | | | | | |

## Steps
1. **Collect the week's numbers** (10 min). From your daily numbers, tracker and sending tool into the table. *Done when* every cell has a number.
2. **Compare to your targets** (5 min). Use the rates you set in the Funnel planner. *Done when* you've marked each rate as above or below target.
3. **Find the biggest leak** (10 min). Where's the largest drop? Use the guide below. *Done when* you've picked one step.
4. **Listen and read** (10 min). Listen to two calls and read ten replies. *Done when* you've written one thing you noticed.
5. **Decide one change** (5 min). One change, for one step, for next week. Write it down. *Done when* it's in your plan.
6. **Plan next week's volume** (5 min). New leads to add, campaigns to launch, blocks in the calendar. *Done when* next week is scheduled.

## Where the leak is
- **Few touches**: a volume problem. Protect your blocks.
- **Touches but few replies**: a list or message problem.
- **Replies but few positive**: a targeting or offer problem.
- **Positive but few booked**: a reply speed or ask problem (SOP 16.7).
- **Booked but few held**: a confirmation and reminders problem.

## Quality check
- You changed only one thing.
- Next week's blocks are already in the calendar.

## Common mistakes
- Changing five things at once, so you never know what worked.
- Judging a channel on a handful of attempts.
- Skipping the review in a good week. Good weeks teach you what to repeat.

> More, better, then new
> If volume was low, the fix is more volume, not new tactics. Only when you're hitting your numbers should you work on making each step better, and only after that try something new.
L.drill: Do your first weekly review this week using the table. Write your one change for next week and put next week's outreach blocks in your calendar.
quiz: You sent plenty of emails but got very few replies. Where's the problem most likely?
Volume is fine; the list or message isn't connecting.
How many changes should you make each week?
One change at a time shows you exactly what made the difference.
Meetings are booked but many don't show. What do you fix?
Show-up rate depends on confirmation and reminders.

L.idea: An appointment is worth booking only when the right person, with a problem they admitted in their own words, agrees to a specific time for a clear reason.
L.md:
## The setter's real job
A setter does not collect meetings. A setter hands the closer a conversation that can end in a decision. Teams split setting from closing so each role can specialise, but the split only works when setters book **quality**, not quantity.

## Five tests of a qualified appointment
1. **Right person**: the decision maker, or someone who will bring them.
2. **Admitted problem**: the prospect described the pain in their own words, not yours.
3. **Fit**: they match your ICP and could afford the solution.
4. **Desire for change**: they said, in some form, "I'd like to fix this".
5. **Specific next step**: date, time, length, purpose and who attends, confirmed live.

Miss any one and the meeting is **soft**. Expect lower show and close rates.

## Pain is admitted, not assigned
"They probably miss calls" is your guess. "We lose maybe 20 jobs a month to voicemail" is their admission. Only admitted pain brings people to a meeting and to a decision.

## The handoff note
Three lines for the closer (lesson 7.7 has the full version):
- **Pain** in the prospect's words.
- **Impact**: any number they gave.
- **Context**: what they use now, who else is involved, how they sounded.

## A bad appointment costs twice
It wastes the closer's hour and it corrupts your numbers: you think the offer converts poorly when the real problem is who was booked.

> Quality check
> Ask the closer to grade every meeting A, B or C within a day, and review the grades weekly with the setter. Pay and praise setters for meetings that show and fit, not just for meetings booked.
L.drill: Write your definition of a qualified appointment using the five tests. Rewrite the last three meetings you booked as handoff notes, and grade each A, B or C honestly.
quiz: Which is NOT one of the five tests?
Call length says nothing about quality.
They described it in their own words
People act on problems they have stated themselves.
What should setters be rewarded for?
Rewarding raw bookings creates soft meetings and no-shows.

L.idea: Qualify by asking, not interrogating. Five light questions tell you whether a meeting is worth booking.
L.md:
## Why qualify on the first call
Booking everyone feels productive, but low-fit meetings drag down show and close rates and waste the closer. A few conversational questions protect everyone's time.

## Five areas, asked like a person
| Area | Question you can actually ask |
|---|---|
| Situation | "How are you handling calls after five right now?" |
| Pain and impact | "Roughly how many slip through in a busy week? What's a typical job worth?" |
| Desire | "Is that something you'd like to fix, or is it just part of the business?" |
| Support | "Who else would weigh in on something like this?" |
| Timing | "If it made sense, when would you want it running?" |

Ask in whatever order fits the conversation. The desire question matters most: owners who say "it's just how it is" rarely buy.

## Money without the awkward question
Don't ask "What's your budget?" early. Ask: "Have you spent money trying to fix this before?" or "What does a missed job cost you, roughly?" Both tell you whether money is a real barrier.

## It's fine not to book
If the pain is weak, the desire is missing or the decision maker won't join, you can:
- Book a call that includes the right person.
- Send one useful thing (a demo or audit) and set a date to follow up.
- Move the lead to a nurture list.

Disqualifying calmly is a sign of expertise, and it raises your status with the prospects who do fit.

## Record the answers
Put the answers in your sheet or CRM so the closer never re-asks them.

call.title: Qualifying while booking
turns: You mentioned the phones are the biggest headache after hours. Roughly how many calls slip through in a busy month?
An estimate he produces is one he believes.
Probably thirty, forty. Hard to say.
