- Keep a do-not-call list and scrub against registries where it applies.
- Disclose recording where required.
- Do not use an AI voice for cold outbound calls without the right consent (lesson 7.6).

## AI calling agents
Platforms such as Vapi, Retell and Bland let you build voice agents that answer calls. They are a good fit for **inbound** calls and for contacts who have given consent. They are not a shortcut for cold outbound.

## A sample setup
1. A US number from a calling app.
2. A USB headset and a wired connection with a backup.
3. The dialer connected to your CRM.
4. Recording on, with disclosure in your opener.
5. A call block schedule that matches your target time zone.

> Test before you dial
> Call a friend in the US at your planned hour. Check delay, echo and audio.
L.drill: Write your calling schedule in Pakistan time for the US time zone you target. Test your number, headset and connection with a friend on a real call.
quiz: Why start a new number with low volume?
To protect its reputation and avoid spam labels
High volume from a new number looks like spam.
How many hours ahead is Pakistan of US Eastern time?
It is 9 or 10 hours depending on daylight saving.

L.idea: One place for every lead and one link for booking. Keep your pipeline simple and your handoff notes complete.
L.md:
## Choosing a CRM
Start with the simplest thing that works:
| Stage | Option |
|---|---|
| First 100 leads | A spreadsheet, or a free CRM tier |
| Growing | A CRM such as HubSpot, Pipedrive or Close |
| Marketing and pipeline in one | An all-in-one platform such as GoHighLevel |

Pick a tool that can send and receive email and calls, log activity and show a pipeline.

## Fields every lead needs
Name, business, phone, email, source, tier, stage, next action, due date, owner and notes.

## Pipeline stages
Use the stages from lesson 11.1 with entry rules based on buyer actions.

## Scheduling
- A booking tool (such as Calendly, Cal.com or your CRM's calendar) with two or three time slots.
- Connect it to your calendar so double bookings cannot happen.
- Set time zones correctly. Show invites in the prospect's time zone.
- Add confirmation and reminder messages (lesson 7.4).
- Use a meeting link and a phone fallback.

## Handoff from setter to closer
A short note in the CRM: pain in their words, impact number, who else is involved, tone, tools they use and the agreed time. The closer should never ask the same discovery questions again.

## Automations worth building
- New lead to CRM with a first task.
- Booked meeting to a reminder sequence.
- Reply detected to a task and an alert.
- No-show to a recovery message.

## Housekeeping
- Review stalled deals weekly.
- Remove or tag dead leads.
- Back up your data monthly.
- Remove access for people who leave.
L.drill: Set up your pipeline stages and a booking link. Create five test leads and run them through the stages to be sure the notes and tasks work.
quiz: What should a handoff note include?
Pain, impact, who else is involved, tools and the time
A full handoff saves the closer from re-asking.
What do you do about time zones in invites?
Set and show the prospect's time zone

L.idea: Automate the boring steps, keep a human in the loop for anything a prospect reads, and never let AI invent facts.
L.md:
## Connector tools
Tools such as Zapier, Make and n8n connect your apps. They move data from one place to another when something happens.

## Five useful workflows
1. **Form to CRM:** new lead creates a contact and a task, and sends a confirmation.
2. **Reply alert:** a positive reply in your sending tool creates a task and pings you.
3. **Booked call:** triggers reminders and a handoff note.
4. **No-show:** triggers a recovery message.
5. **Lead sheet to sequence:** a new verified row is added to a campaign.

## Build slowly
Automate a process only after you have run it by hand a few times. Test with five fake leads before turning it on.

## AI helpers: where they help
- **First drafts:** subject lines, first lines, variations of a message. Always edit.
- **Summaries:** call notes and meeting recaps.
- **Roleplay:** practise objection handling with a general AI assistant playing the prospect.
- **Research:** summarise a company's website. Check key facts yourself.
- **Reporting:** turn numbers into a short plain-language summary.

## Where AI is risky
- It can make up facts. Never send a claim about a prospect without checking it.
- Generic AI text sounds generic. Rewrite it in your own voice.
- Sending large volumes of AI-written, near-identical messages gets you flagged.
- Do not paste private or sensitive customer data into tools you have not checked.

## Human in the loop
Rule: a person reads every message before it goes to a prospect, and a person decides what to do with every reply.

## AI voice and compliance
AI voices on outbound calls fall under strict rules. See lesson 7.6. Using AI to answer inbound calls is a very different matter.

> Test for good automation
> If it fails, would you notice quickly, and would the damage be small?
L.drill: Map one repetitive task in your week as a trigger and an action. Build it with a connector tool, test with five fake leads and write down how you will notice if it breaks.
quiz: When should you automate a process?
After running it by hand successfully
Automating a broken process just breaks it faster.
What is the main risk of AI-written messages?
They can contain invented facts and sound generic
Always check facts and edit in your own voice.

L.idea: Know your numbers weekly, protect every login and review what you pay for each month.
L.md:
## Reporting
A single sheet or dashboard is enough. Track weekly:
- Attempts by channel (calls, emails, social messages, videos).
- Replies or conversations by channel.
- Meetings booked and held.
- Deals won.
- Cost per booked meeting.

Use the daily numbers in your 30-day plan, or a spreadsheet, and connect your CRM when it helps. Do not drown in charts.

## Cost per booked meeting
Add up your monthly tool costs and your time. Divide by the meetings booked. If the cost per meeting rises, find the weak step in the funnel.

## Security basics
- A password manager for every login.
- Two-factor authentication on email, social accounts, the CRM and the sending tool.
- Separate accounts and logins for each tool. No shared passwords.
- Use separate browser profiles for outreach.
- Keep recovery emails and phones up to date.

## Data care
- Store lead data only where you need it.
- Back up your sheet or export your CRM monthly.
- Delete data on request.
- Never paste lists into tools you have not reviewed.

## Access control
When a team member leaves, remove their access to every tool the same day. Keep a list of who has access to what.

## Monthly cost review
List each tool, its purpose, cost, last time you used it and a keep or cancel decision. Cancel anything unused. Switch only if the new tool clearly beats the old one.

## Watch for tool sprawl
If you cannot explain in one sentence why you pay for a tool, cancel it.

## Disaster plan
What if your main domain is flagged, your calling number is spam-labelled or an account is locked? Keep spare domains, spare numbers and a written recovery checklist.

> Keep it boring
> Reliable beats clever. A stack that works every day beats an impressive stack that nobody maintains.
L.drill: Make your monthly tool list with cost and purpose. Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere you can, then cancel one tool you do not need.
quiz: What should you do when a team member leaves?
Remove their access to every tool the same day
What is cost per booked meeting?
Monthly costs divided by meetings booked
It shows whether your system is getting more or less efficient.

L.t: The first 72 hours after the sale
L.idea: The client decides whether they made a good choice in the first three days. Make those days fast, clear and busy with visible progress.
L.md:
## Why the first 72 hours matter
Right after paying, most clients feel a small doubt: "Did I just waste money?" Silence makes that doubt grow. A fast, organised start makes it disappear. Most refund requests and early cancellations start with a slow, quiet first week.

## What happens, and when
| When | What you do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Within 1 hour of payment | Send the welcome email with the onboarding form and the kickoff booking link | Shows they are in good hands, and starts the clock on what you need from them |
| Same day | Send the access checklist (logins, numbers, calendars) | Missing access is the number one cause of slow starts |
| Day 1 to 2 | Hold the kickoff call | Agrees goals, the scoreboard and the first win |
| Day 2 to 3 | Send the first progress note, even if small | Proves the work has started |

## The welcome email has four parts
1. **Thanks and confirmation.** One line. No long speech.
2. **What happens next.** Three dated steps, so they know the plan.
3. **What you need from them.** The form and the access list, with a deadline.
4. **How to reach you.** One channel, the hours you reply and your reply time.

## The onboarding form
Ask only what you need to start. Long forms do not get filled in. Group the questions:
- **Business basics:** services, service area, hours, average job value, busiest season.
- **Customers:** who the best customers are, and who they do not want.
- **Goals:** the one number they most want to move in 90 days.
- **Brand and voice:** words they use, words to avoid, examples they like.
- **Access:** who gives you each login, and by when.

> Book the kickoff before the form is done
> Do not wait for a perfect form. Book the call for day 1 or 2 and finish any gaps on the call.

!> Never start work that touches their customers without written approval
!> Scripts, emails and calling agents that speak to their customers must be approved by the client in writing first. Keep the approval email.
L.drill: Open the Client delivery kit. Fill in a real or practice client, then copy the welcome email and the onboarding form. Time yourself: both should be ready to send in under ten minutes.
quiz: When should the welcome email go out?
At the end of the first week
A fast welcome removes the doubt that follows payment.
What is the most common cause of a slow start?
Missing access to logins, numbers and calendars
Ask for access on day one with a clear deadline.
The onboarding form is half done. What do you do?
Book the kickoff anyway and fill the gaps on the call
Momentum matters more than a perfect form.

L.idea: A kickoff call agrees one goal, one scoreboard, who does what, and the first win. Everything after it is measured against what you agree here.
L.md:
## The agenda (45 minutes)
| Minutes | Part | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 5 | Thank you and the plan for the call | They know what the call will cover |
| 5 to 15 | Their goal, in their words | One number to move in 90 days |
| 15 to 25 | How we will measure it | The scoreboard: three to five numbers, where they come from |
| 25 to 35 | Who does what | Owner on their side, owner on yours, how fast each replies |
| 35 to 40 | The first win | Something visible in 14 days |
| 40 to 45 | Recap and next date | Report day and the 30-day review booked |

## Ask for the goal as a number
"More leads" cannot be measured. Ask: "If we sit here in 90 days and you are happy, what number changed?" Write down their exact words and the number.

## Agree the scoreboard
Pick three to five numbers that the client can check. For an AI calling agent: calls answered, jobs booked, after-hours calls caught and the booking rate. For appointment setting: conversations, meetings booked, meetings held and show rate.

## Set the rules for talking
- One main channel for updates, such as email or one WhatsApp group.
- Your reply time on working days, and when you are offline.
- What counts as urgent, and how they reach you for it.

> Agree what success is not
> Ask: "Is there anything that would make you unhappy even if the numbers went up?" You will hear about tone, brand and customer experience. Write it down.

call.title: Kickoff with a plumbing owner
turns: Thanks for making time, Dave. In 45 minutes I'd like to agree on your goal, how we'll measure it and the first win. Sound good?
Saying what the call will cover makes the client relax and keeps you on time.
Sure. I just want to stop missing calls.
If we sit down in 90 days and you're happy, what number changed?
This turns a feeling into something both sides can check.
I guess booked jobs from calls we used to miss. Maybe 15 more a month.
Fifteen extra booked jobs a month. I'll put that at the top of every report. Who on your side should I send it to, and who approves anything that talks to your customers?
Naming the approver early prevents delays later.
Send it to me and my office manager, Linda. I approve scripts.
Great. First win: in 14 days, every after-hours call is answered and you get a text summary of each one. I'll report every Monday, and let's book our 30-day review now.
A visible early win builds trust before the bigger results arrive.

L.drill: Write the goal question and the first-win sentence for one real or practice client. Say both out loud until they sound natural.
quiz: What is the best way to ask for the client's goal?
Ask what they want in general
Ask what number changed if they are happy in 90 days
Skip it and start the work
A number gives both sides something to measure.
How many numbers should the scoreboard have?
Few enough to read in a minute, enough to show the full picture.

L.t: The first 30 days: early wins and the 30-60-90 plan
L.idea: Plan the first 90 days in three blocks and make sure the first block delivers something the client can see.
L.md:
## Three blocks
| Block | Focus | What the client should see |
|---|---|---|
| Days 1 to 30 | Set up and first win | The system is live, the first results are reported |
| Days 31 to 60 | Improve | Weak numbers improved, tests started |
| Days 61 to 90 | Scale and prove | Results against the goal, the case for renewal |

## Early wins are visible, not big
An early win is something the client notices without being told: a booked job from a missed call, a meeting on their calendar, a reply from a prospect they wanted. Small and visible beats large and invisible.

## Protect the plan from surprises
- **Write down the assumptions.** For example: "Assumes 40 or more inbound calls a month."
- **Flag risks early.** If a number looks off in week 2, say so in week 2, not at the review.
- **Change one thing at a time.** Then you know what caused the result.

> Under-promise on dates, over-deliver on updates
> A plan that slips quietly loses trust. A plan that slips with a clear reason and a new date keeps it.
L.drill: Use the Client delivery kit to create a dated 30-60-90 plan. Add one early win for days 1 to 14 that the client will notice without being told.
quiz: What makes a good early win?
It is large, even if the client cannot see it
The client notices it without being told
Visible beats big in the first month.
A number looks wrong in week 2. When do you tell the client?
In week 2, with what you are doing about it

L.idea: A good report takes one minute to read: the numbers against the goal, what you did, what is next and one thing you need from them.
L.md:
## The one-minute weekly report
1. **Headline.** One sentence: on track, ahead or behind, and why.
2. **The scoreboard.** The three to five numbers, this week and the total so far, against the goal.
3. **What we did.** Three bullets at most.
4. **What is next.** Three bullets at most.
5. **One ask.** The single thing you need from them, with a date.

## Write the bad weeks too
Send the report on the same day every week, especially when the numbers are down. A missing report on a bad week is read as hiding. A clear report with a plan is read as control.

## The monthly review call (30 minutes)
| Part | What to cover |
|---|---|
| Results | The scoreboard against the goal, in their numbers |
| What worked | One or two things to keep |
| What did not | One thing to fix, and the plan |
| Next month | The focus and any change in scope |
| Feedback | "What should we start, stop or keep doing?" |

> Put the money next to the numbers
> Where you can, show what the result is worth: "12 booked jobs at about $450 each is roughly $5,400." Use the client's own job value.
L.drill: Log this week's numbers for a real or practice client in the delivery kit's scoreboard, then open the weekly report template it fills in. Read it aloud. If it takes longer than a minute, cut it.
quiz: What should a weekly report end with?
One clear ask with a date
One ask is easy to act on.
The numbers are down this week. What do you do?
Send it on the usual day with the reason and the plan
Consistency on bad weeks builds trust.

L.idea: Renewals are won at the 60-day mark, not the week the contract ends. Upsell only after the first goal is on track.
L.md:
## The renewal timeline
| When | What you do |
|---|---|
| Day 60 | Review results against the goal. Ask: "If we keep going, what would you want next?" |
| 30 days before the end | Send the renewal email with results, the plan for the next term and the price |
| 14 days before the end | Renewal call if there is no reply |
| End date | Thank you, or a clean handover |

## When to offer more
Offer an upsell only when two things are true: the first goal is on track, and the client has a new problem you can solve. Good upsells extend what already works:
- AI calling agent: add outbound follow-up calls, review requests or a second location.
- Appointment setting: add a new channel, a new market or a reactivation campaign.
- Agency services: add reporting, a landing page or a new campaign.

## Ask for referrals at the high point
The best moment is right after a visible win, such as a strong monthly review. Make it specific: "Who else do you know who runs a service business and misses calls after hours?"

> Never upsell to fix a result you have not delivered
> If the main goal is behind, fix that first. Selling more to an unhappy client speeds up the cancellation.

call.title: Renewal conversation at day 60
turns: Before we look at next month, here is where we are: 22 meetings booked against a goal of 30 by day 90, and a 78% show rate.
Starting with their numbers keeps the call about value, not price.
That's better than I expected, honestly.
Glad to hear it. If we keep going for another term, what would you want next?
Let them name the next goal
When the client names the next goal, renewal becomes their idea.
We're opening in a second city in spring.
Then the next term could add the second city from March. I'll send the plan and price this week, and we can confirm on our call on the 20th.
The extra scope comes from their plan, so it does not feel like a push.

L.drill: For one client, write the day-60 question and a referral ask. Use the renewal email template in the delivery kit for the 30-day notice.
quiz: When is a renewal really won?
Around day 60, when results are reviewed
Start the renewal conversation well before the end date.
When is an upsell a bad idea?
When the main goal is behind
When the client names a new problem
When it extends what already works
Fix the main result before selling more.

L.t: Saving a client who wants to leave
L.idea: Most cancellations show warning signs weeks earlier. Spot them, call instead of emailing, listen first, then offer a fix, a pause or a smaller plan.
L.md:
## Warning signs
| Sign | What it often means |
|---|---|
| Slower replies, missed calls | Lost interest or too busy to see the value |
| Questions about the contract end date | Already thinking of leaving |
| New person involved, such as a partner or finance | Someone is questioning the cost |
| Late payments | Cash pressure or doubt about value |
| Results flat for four or more weeks | The plan needs to change |

## The save call
1. **Call, do not email.** Tone matters, and email feels final.
2. **Thank them and listen.** "Thanks for being straight with me. Can you walk me through what is not working?"
3. **Clarify the real reason.** Ask until you reach it: results, cost, fit, timing or trust.
4. **Agree what you heard.** Repeat it in their words.
5. **Offer one fitting option.** Fix the problem, pause, a smaller plan, or a trial period with clear goals.
6. **Accept a no gracefully.** Ask for feedback and permission to check in later.

## Match the offer to the reason
| Reason | Offer |
|---|---|
| Results | A 30-day fix plan with one changed thing and a clear check date |
| Cost | A smaller plan, or a pause, not a large discount |
| Timing or season | A pause with a restart date |
| Fit or trust | A frank talk. If it is not a fit, help them leave well |

## Leave well when they go
Hand over everything they paid for, thank them in writing and ask for honest feedback. Clients who leave on good terms come back and send referrals.

!> Do not trap clients
!> Never refuse to hand over their data, logins or numbers, and never make cancelling hard. It damages your name and can break consumer and contract rules.
L.drill: Use the churn-save script in the delivery kit. Roleplay it out loud with a partner for each reason: results, cost and timing.
quiz: A client asks when the contract ends. What should you do?
Treat it as a warning sign and book a call
Questions about the end date usually come before a cancellation.
The client says the cost is too high. What is usually the best offer?
A smaller plan or a pause
A smaller scope keeps the relationship without cheapening your price.
What is the first step on a save call?
Listening first finds the real reason.

L.t: Delivery SOPs and handoffs for agency teams
L.idea: When a team delivers, the process lives in writing. A one-page SOP for each repeated task and a clean sales-to-delivery handoff keep quality the same, whoever does the work.
L.md:
## What deserves an SOP
Anything you do more than twice a month for clients: onboarding, campaign setup, weekly reports, monthly reviews, script updates, cancellations.

## The one-page SOP format
| Part | What to write |
|---|---|
| Purpose | One line: why the task exists |
| Owner | Who does it, who checks it |
| Trigger | When it starts, such as "the client pays" |
| Steps | Numbered, one action each, with the tool used |
| Done means | How you know it is finished and right |
| Time | How long it should take |

## The sales-to-delivery handoff
Before the kickoff, the closer passes this to the account owner, in writing:
- What the client bought: scope, price, term and start date.
- Why they bought: the pain and the goal, in the client's own words.
- What was promised: dates, deliverables, any special terms.
- Risks: worries they raised, people who doubted, any deadlines.

The account owner reads it before the kickoff, so the client never repeats themselves.

## Capacity: know when you are full
Set a maximum number of clients per account owner, and track it. Taking one client too many lowers results for every client. Hire or pause sales before you reach the limit, not after.

> Record once, use many times
> Record a short screen video for each SOP. New team members learn faster from a video plus a one-page checklist.
L.drill: Write a one-page SOP for your weekly report, using the format above. Then fill in the handoff note for your most recent sale.
quiz: What must the closer pass to delivery before the kickoff?
Scope, the client's reasons, what was promised and any risks
A written handoff means the client never repeats themselves.
When should you hire or pause sales?
Before account owners reach their client limit
Plan capacity ahead, or every client suffers.

PB.title: Cold call to a plumbing owner, 7:40am
PB.situation: Dave runs a 6-truck plumbing company in Fort Worth. You found him on Google Maps: 4.7 stars, 300 reviews, two reviews this month mention "couldn't get through".
PB.goal: Book a 15-minute call to show him his own missed-call numbers.
PB.setting: Tuesday, 7:40am Texas time, his mobile. He is in the truck between jobs.
prep: Read his last 10 Google reviews and note any about slow callbacks.
Know his service area and whether he offers 24/7 emergency service.
Have two meeting times ready before you dial.
turns: Dave, it's Sam. We haven't spoken. I'm calling because plumbers in Fort Worth tell me they lose jobs when nobody can pick up after hours. Is that something you deal with, or not really?
Name, honesty about being a stranger, one reason, one question. About 12 seconds. "Or not really" lets him answer without feeling pushed.
I mean, sometimes. We're slammed right now.
Makes sense, busy is good. When the crew's on jobs, what happens to a call that comes in at 7 in the evening?
Agree, then ask about one moment
Don't argue with "slammed". Ask about a specific moment in his week; it gets a story, not a brush-off.
Goes to my cell. If I'm under a sink, voicemail.
And of the people who hit voicemail, roughly how many call back?
Moves from how it works to whether it works. Let him say the number.
I saw a couple of reviews this month saying people couldn't get through. Is that the same thing?
Specific research shows you're not reading a script. Phrase it as a question, never an accusation.
Yeah, that was a Saturday. Nobody was on.
If it's, say, twenty calls a month that don't call back, what's a normal job worth to you?
His numbers, not yours. A cost he works out himself is one he believes.
Four, five hundred. More for water heaters.
So somewhere around eight to ten thousand a month walking to the next plumber on Google. Does that sound about right, or am I off?
Inviting him to correct you makes the number his.
I don't want to pitch you on the phone while you're driving. Can I show you what those calls look like on your numbers? Fifteen minutes. Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
Respects his situation, names the length, and gives a choice instead of a yes/no.
Done. What's the best email for the invite? I'll text you a reminder Wednesday too.
Get the email and send the invite before you hang up. Mention the reminder so it isn't a surprise.
avoid: "How are you doing today?" as the opener. It signals a sales call in two seconds.
Pitching features ("our AI uses natural language...") before he has said the problem.
Giving your own estimate of his losses. Let him supply the numbers.
take: Reason for the call in the first sentence, then a question with an easy no.
Use one thing you found in your research.
Let the owner calculate the cost.
Ask for a short meeting with two times, and send the invite on the call.

PB.title: Roofer, the week after a hailstorm
PB.situation: A hailstorm hit north Dallas 9 days ago. Mike's roofing company has 3 crews. His Facebook page shows he's posting "free inspection" offers.
PB.goal: Book a call about following up on estimates that went quiet.
PB.setting: Thursday, 5:15pm, office line. He picks up himself.
prep: Know the storm date and area (local news).
Look at his Facebook posts for how many inspections he's doing.
Have one question ready about estimates, not leads. Roofers have plenty of leads after a storm.
turns: Mike, it's Sam. We haven't spoken. I know you're buried after last week's hail, so I'll be quick. Roofers tell me the inspections are easy right now, it's following up on all the estimates that falls apart. Is that you, or have you got it covered?
Mentioning the storm proves this isn't a random call. The problem is the follow-up, not getting leads.
Ha. We've done forty inspections since Saturday. Nobody's following up on anything.
Forty in a week is a lot. Of those, how many estimates have gone out?
Maybe twenty-five. The rest are waiting on insurance.
And of the twenty-five, how many have you heard back from?
Shows the gap without you saying it.
Six signed. The rest, no idea.
What's a typical job after a storm like this?
So nineteen estimates sitting at twelve thousand plus. If even three of them are just waiting for someone to call, that's thirty-six thousand. What happens to them right now?
Conservative maths using his numbers. Ends with a question so he talks.
They go to whoever calls them back first. Probably the storm chasers.
That's exactly what I want to show you: a simple follow-up that calls and texts every open estimate on day 2, 5 and 10. Twenty minutes, tomorrow at 7am before the crews go out, or Monday at 5?
Times that fit a roofer's day show you understand his business.
Perfect. I'll send the invite to the email on your website. If you can, have the list of open estimates handy, and we'll use your real numbers.
Asking him to bring data makes the meeting about his money, not your product.
avoid: Leading with "more leads". After a storm, roofers have more leads than they can handle.
Talking down the storm chasers. Let him name the competition himself.
Booking calls during daylight working hours in storm season.
take: Tie the call to what is happening in his week.
Sell what he's short of (follow-up), not what he has (leads).
Offer meeting times that fit his trade.

PB.title: Dental office: the lunch-hour calls
PB.situation: A 3-dentist practice in Phoenix. Their website says "Call to book" with no online booking. The front desk closes 12 to 1.
PB.goal: Book a meeting with the office manager and, ideally, the lead dentist.
PB.setting: Wednesday, 2:30pm, main line. Karen, the office manager, answers.
prep: Check their hours on Google and the website.
Check whether they offer online booking.
Know that new-patient calls are the valuable ones; recall calls matter less.
turns: Hi, it's Sam. I'm looking for whoever looks after the front desk and new-patient calls. Is that you, or someone else?
Asking for a role, not a name, gets you to the right person without pretending you know them.
That's me, I'm the office manager. What's this about?
Thanks, Karen. I work with dental practices on the calls that come in when the desk is busy or closed. I noticed you close for lunch 12 to 1. What happens to new-patient calls in that hour?
A fact from their own website turns a cold call into a relevant one.
They go to voicemail. We call them back after lunch.
How often do you reach them on the callback?
Honestly, maybe half the time. People just book somewhere else.
That's what most practices tell me. Roughly how many new patients do you see a month?
"Most practices tell me" removes any blame from her team.
And what's a new patient worth to the practice over the first year, cleanings, X-rays, the usual?
Dental value is in the first year, not the first visit. Asking this shows you understand the business.
Dr. Patel says about twelve hundred.

So if even four lunch-hour callers a month book elsewhere, that's close to five thousand a year each month you miss them. Would it make sense to look at that with Dr. Patel for fifteen minutes? I can do Thursday at 12:30, while you're closed, or Friday at 4:30.
Ask for the dentist early. Offering the lunch slot is a light, memorable touch.
Friday at 4:30 should work. Let me check with him.
Great. I'll hold Friday at 4:30 and email you both. If it doesn't suit him, just reply with a better time.
Holding a time beats "let me know". The email makes it easy to change.
avoid: Saying "HIPAA compliant" before she asks. Answer it clearly when she does.
Implying her team is failing. They're busy, not careless.
Calling 8 to 9am or 12 to 1pm, the desk's busiest times.
take: Ask for the role, not a made-up name.
Use one fact from their hours or website.
Value new patients over a year, not one visit.
Bring in the decision maker at the booking stage.

PB.title: "Not interested" in the first 10 seconds
PB.situation: Tony owns an HVAC company in Atlanta. It's late July and 98 degrees. He picks up already irritated.
PB.goal: Turn a reflex "no" into a real conversation, or leave on good terms.
prep: Expect the reflex no. It's about the interruption, not your offer.
Know one fact about AC calls in a heat wave (call volume spikes, every company is booked out).
turns: Tony, it's Sam. We haven't spoken. I'm calling because...
Fair enough. Most owners say that before they hear why I called. Can I take 20 seconds to tell you, and then you can hang up on me?
Agree, don't argue. Asking for a short amount of time with an easy way out usually gets a yes.

In a heat wave like this, HVAC companies tell me they're getting more calls than they can answer, and the ones that hit voicemail call the next company. I don't know if that's true for you. Is it, or not really?
The reason fits his week. Ending with "or not really" lets him tell the truth.
I mean, yeah. Phones are crazy. We're booked out four days.
When you're booked out four days, what do you do with the calls you can't take?
We tell them we're booked. Some wait, most don't.
What's a typical AC repair or replacement worth to you right now?
Only one question at a time.
Repairs four hundred. Replacements nine, ten grand.

So one replacement a week lost to "we're booked" is ten grand. Would it be worth fifteen minutes when it cools down, say Thursday at 7am, to see whether some of those could be booked for next week instead of lost?
Respects that he's slammed. "Booked for next week instead of lost" is a benefit he can picture.
Thanks, Tony. I'll text you the invite now. Stay cool out there.
avoid: "I understand, but...". "But" cancels everything before it.
Asking "why aren't you interested?" It puts him on the defensive.
Arguing with the first no.
take: The first no is a reflex. Agree with it, then ask for 20 seconds.
Tie the reason to his season.
If he still says no after the reason, thank him and leave. You'll call again next quarter.

PB.title: "We already have an answering service"
PB.situation: Lisa co-owns an electrical company in Tampa. They pay a live answering service that takes messages.
PB.goal: Find out whether the current setup books jobs or just takes messages, and book a comparison call.
prep: Know the difference between taking a message and booking a job.
Never criticise the other provider.
turns: Lisa, it's Sam. We haven't spoken. I work with electricians on the calls that come in when the team's on jobs. Is that something you think about, or is it handled?
Leaves room for "it's handled" so she relaxes.
It's handled. We have an answering service.
Good, then you already know the calls matter. Can I ask, when they take a call, do they book the job into your calendar, or take a message for someone to call back?
Praise the decision she made. Then ask the one question that matters.
They take a message. We call back in the morning.
How does that go? When you call back the next morning, how many have already found someone else?
Lets her discover the gap herself.
Some. I don't really track it.
Most owners don't, and that's fair. If you had to guess, out of ten messages, how many turn into jobs?
A guess is enough to start a conversation.

That's a useful number. I'm not saying swap anything. Would it be worth fifteen minutes to compare: the calls you got last month, how many became jobs, and what booking them on the spot would change? Friday at 11 or Monday at 2?
"I'm not saying swap anything" lowers the risk. A comparison feels safe to agree to.
I'll bring the questions, you bring last month's call log, and we'll do the numbers together. Sending the invite now.
Makes it a working session, not a pitch.
avoid: "Our service is better than theirs."
Asking which company they use in the first minute.
Giving up at "we already have one". It means she values the problem.
take: "We already have one" means they value the problem. Agree.
Compare messages taken against jobs booked.
Offer a comparison, not a replacement.

PB.title: Gatekeeper and "just send an email"
PB.situation: A pest control company in Charlotte. Linda answers the main line and screens every sales call.
PB.goal: Reach the owner, or get a name and a time to call back.
prep: Know the owner's first name from the website or state licence lookup.
Be ready to say why in one honest sentence.
turns: Hi, it's Sam. Could you help me? I'm trying to reach whoever handles your phones and scheduling.
Honest and polite. Most people like helping.
How you handle calls in spring when the phones get busy. I have two quick questions for the owner.
Short and true. No tricks, no "he's expecting my call".
He's busy. Just send an email.
Happy to. Who should I address it to, and when's he usually in the office?
Accept, then get a name and a time
You agree, and still leave with what you need for the next call.
Ray. He's in Tuesday and Thursday mornings.
Thank you, that's really helpful. And your name, so I can tell him you suggested it?
Linda becomes your ally, not your blocker.
Thanks, Linda. Quick one while I have you: when the phones get busy in spring, is it you picking them all up?
Ask the person who feels the problem
Gatekeepers often feel the problem most. This can turn her into your champion.
It's me and one part-timer. It's a lot.
That's exactly what I want to ask Ray about. I'll send the email today and call Thursday morning. Have a good one.
Specific follow-up shows you mean it.
avoid: Pretending to know the owner.
"It's personal."
Being short with the gatekeeper. She talks to the owner every day.
take: Be direct and respectful.
Turn "send an email" into a name and a time.
Ask the gatekeeper about her own workload. She may be your best ally.

PB.title: When the gatekeeper is the one drowning
PB.situation: A med spa in Scottsdale. Jess runs the front desk alone. Their Instagram has 20,000 followers and lots of DMs asking for prices.
PB.goal: Make Jess your champion and book a call with the owner.
prep: Look at their Instagram comments: are questions being answered?
Know the owner's name (Dr. Reyes) from the website.
turns: Hi, it's Sam. Is this the front desk?
Yes, this is Jess. How can I help?
Jess, I'll be honest, this is a sales call, and I'll be quick. I work with med spas on the calls and DMs that come in faster than the desk can answer. Is that a problem here, or not really?
Honesty disarms. Most gatekeepers expect a trick.
Oh my god. Yes. I'm the only one here on Fridays.
What happens when you're with a client and the phone rings?
People who feel the problem describe it vividly. That becomes your case to the owner.
It goes to voicemail. And the Instagram DMs, I get to them at night if I can.
That sounds like a lot for one person. Does Dr. Reyes know how much comes in?
Shows you're on her side, then brings in the person who decides.
She knows it's busy. I don't think she knows how many we miss.
Would it help if I showed you both, with your own numbers, in fifteen minutes? I'm not asking you to sell it to her. Is there a time she's usually free, maybe Tuesday before the first client?
"I'm not asking you to sell it" removes the burden from Jess.
She's in at 8:30 Tuesdays. First client is 9:30.
Could you pencil in 8:45 Tuesday for fifteen minutes? I'll email you both the invite now.
The gatekeeper can often book the owner's time directly.
avoid: Going around her once she's helped you.
Making promises to her about her workload you can't keep.
take: Honesty about it being a sales call disarms gatekeepers.
If she feels the pain, let her describe it.
Ask her to book the owner's time.

PB.title: Voicemail, then a text that gets a reply
PB.situation: Third attempt to reach the owner of a garage door company in Denver. No answer again.
PB.goal: Leave a voicemail that earns a callback or a text reply.
PB.setting: Wednesday, 7:50am, his mobile. Business number listed on Google (texting only if he has given consent or replies first).
prep: Keep the voicemail under 20 seconds.
Say your name and number slowly, twice.
Check the texting rules for the state before you text (lesson 7.6).
turns: (Voicemail) Hi Carlos, it's Sam, 214-555-0182. I had a quick idea about the stuck-door calls you get at night. I'll try you again Friday morning. Again, Sam, 214-555-0182.
Name, one specific reason, when you'll call next, and the number twice. No pitch, no company name needed.
(Friday call, no answer. No voicemail this time.)
Don't leave a voicemail every time
Two voicemails a week sounds like pressure. Alternate.
Hi Carlos, it's Sam. I called Wednesday about after-hours calls for garage door companies. Quick question: when a door gets stuck at 9pm, who picks up?
Answer who you are in one line, then ask a question about his business, not your product.
Ha, that's most owners I talk to. Worth a 10-minute call to see how many of those you're missing? Monday 8am or Tuesday 5pm?
Keep it as short as his messages.
Booked. Sending the invite to the email on your site.
avoid: Voicemails over 30 seconds.
"Call me back at your earliest convenience."
Texting numbers that haven't replied or given consent.
take: Voicemails are for recognition, not selling.
Say the number twice, slowly.
When they text back, reply with a question about their business.

PB.title: Form lead called back in 3 minutes
PB.situation: Maria owns a 6-chair hair salon in Austin. She filled in a form on your ad: "Get your past clients rebooking".
PB.goal: Book a call before she talks to anyone else.
PB.setting: Saturday, 6:10pm, three minutes after the form.
prep: Call within 5 minutes. Speed is the biggest advantage on inbound.
Have her form answers open.
turns: Hi Maria, it's Sam. You asked about getting past clients rebooking a couple of minutes ago. Is now an okay moment for two quick questions?
Reference what she just did. Ask permission.
Oh, wow, that was fast. Yes, I'm closing up.
Thanks. What made you fill it in today?
Her reason tells you the urgency.
January was slow and I know we have hundreds of old clients who just stopped coming.
Roughly how many clients are in your booking system?
Maybe 1,800. Probably half haven't been in this year.
So if even 5% of those 900 came back once, that's around four thousand dollars, and most of them come back again. Would a 20-minute call on Monday or Tuesday morning work to plan it?
5% is believable. Mention the repeat visits; that's where the value is.
Tuesday at 10. One thing to have ready: can you export your client list from your booking app? I'll show you how if not.
Asking for the list makes the meeting concrete.
avoid: Waiting until Monday to call a Saturday lead.
Pitching price on the first call.
Promising a number of bookings.
take: Call within 5 minutes.
Ask what made them reach out today.
Use small, believable percentages.

PB.title: No-show: rebook without guilt
PB.situation: Greg booked a 15-minute call for 10am. It's 10:08 and he hasn't joined.
PB.goal: Rebook warmly and get the meeting held.
prep: Wait 5 to 8 minutes, then call once.
Have two new times ready.
turns: Hi Greg, it's Sam. We had 10am on the calendar. I figured something came up. Is now still good, or shall we find another time?
Assume the best. Give him an easy way out.
Oh man, I'm sorry, I'm at a job. Totally forgot.
No problem at all, that's the job. Would tomorrow at 7:30am before the day starts work, or Thursday at 5?
Pick times when he isn't on jobs.
Done. I'll text you a reminder tonight with the link. And it'll still be fifteen minutes.
The reminder and the time limit both raise the show rate.
avoid: "I waited for you."
Emailing only. Call within 10 minutes.
Rebooking more than two days out.
take: Call within 10 minutes of a no-show.
No guilt; offer two new times.
Send a reminder the night before.

PB.title: The proposal that went quiet for 10 days
PB.situation: You sent a proposal to a landscaping company 10 days ago after a good meeting. No reply to two emails.
PB.goal: Find out what's really happening, without chasing.
prep: Re-read your discovery notes: what did she say the problem cost?
Be ready for a real no. That's useful too.
turns: Hi Sandra, it's Sam. I sent over the proposal a couple of weeks ago and I haven't heard back, which usually means it's not a priority right now, or something isn't right. Which is it?
Saying what silence usually means, with an easy no, gets the truth faster than "just checking in".
Honestly, my husband thinks it's too much right now.
That's fair, thanks for telling me. When you say too much, is it the monthly price, or doing it now in the busy season?
Timing, mostly. We're slammed until June.
That makes sense. When we spoke, you said you lose about ten quote requests a month in spring. Is that still happening right now?
Bring back the cost she told you, in her words.
Would it help if we started with only the quote follow-ups, which takes nothing from your team, and add the rest in June? Could the three of us talk for ten minutes this week, maybe Wednesday at 6pm?
Smaller start, bring in the partner
A smaller first step answers the timing worry. Including the husband deals with the real decision maker.
Great, I'll send it to both of you.
avoid: "Just checking in."
Dropping the price straight away.
Sending a third email instead of calling.
take: Name what silence usually means and ask which it is.
Separate money from timing.
Bring in the partner who is really deciding.

PB.title: Asking a happy client for an introduction
PB.situation: Dave has been a client for 60 days. Last week he booked 14 jobs from after-hours calls.
PB.goal: Get one warm introduction to another owner.
PB.setting: End of the monthly review call.
prep: Have his result in money ready.
Think of the type of business he'd know (supply-house contacts, other trades).
turns: Before you go, Dave, fourteen jobs from after-hours calls last month at around four hundred each, that's about fifty-six hundred. How does that feel?
Ask for a referral only right after he's said the result out loud.
Honestly, it's the best thing I've done this year.
That's great to hear. Who else do you know, maybe from the supply house or another trade, who has the same problem with calls?
"Who else do you know" with a category is easier than "know anyone?"
Ricky, he does HVAC. He complains about it all the time.
Would you be okay sending him a quick text introducing us? I can write it for you if that's easier.
Offering to write the text removes the effort.
I'll text you three lines now. Thanks, Dave, I'll look after him.
Reassure him the referral is safe with you.
avoid: Asking before he's seen results.
"If you know anyone..."
Contacting the referral before Dave has introduced you.
take: Ask right after he says the win out loud.
Name a category of person.
Write the introduction text for him.

PB.title: Discovery call: the full question sequence
PB.situation: Jen co-owns an HVAC company with 8 techs in Raleigh. She booked 20 minutes after a cold call last week.
PB.goal: Find the problem, its cost and her reason to fix it now, and earn the right to show a solution.
prep: Write down what she said on the cold call.
Have the question sequence open (lesson 8.2).
Don't prepare slides. You'll only show something if she asks.
turns: Thanks for making time, Jen. Here's what I suggest: I ask some questions about how calls work for you now, you ask me anything, and at the end we decide together if a next step makes sense, or not. Is that okay?
Agreeing the plan up front makes it normal to decide at the end.
On the phone you mentioned summer is chaos. Walk me through what happens to a call on a busy July afternoon.
Start from her words and ask for a story.
Two people in the office. If they're both on calls, it rings out. After 6, it goes to my cell.
Open, neutral. Let her judge it.
Not great. My office manager quit in August partly because of the phones.
I'm sorry to hear that. What did that cost the business, beyond the calls?
Bigger than missed calls: people. Let her say it.
Three weeks of chaos, overtime, and I was answering phones instead of running the company.
If you could fix the phones, what would be different next summer?
Have her describe the future in her words.
My team wouldn't burn out, and we'd book every job we can actually do.
What's stopped you fixing it before now?
Brings out the real objection early.
I tried an answering service. Customers hated it, they just took messages.
So you want calls booked, not messages, and it has to sound good to your customers. If that were possible, how soon would you want it in place?
Say back the gap and the conditions. The timing question tests urgency.
Before May. That's when it starts.
Then it makes sense to show you how a booked call would sound for your company. Would you want your co-owner on that call too?
Earn the presentation, bring in the partner
You've earned the right to present. Ask about other decision makers now, not at the end.
avoid: Presenting before you understand the cost.
Asking two questions at once.
Filling silence after a big question.
take: Frame the call so a decision at the end is normal.
Go from situation to problem to consequence to desired outcome.
Find the obstacle early.
Ask about other decision makers before you present.

PB.title: Two owners on the call: spouse and partner
PB.situation: Tom runs the trucks, Amy runs the money. Amy is sceptical; Tom wants it.
PB.goal: Get both of them to agree the problem before you talk about price.
PB.setting: Zoom, Tuesday 7pm, both on camera at the kitchen table.
prep: Plan to ask Amy a question in the first two minutes.
Expect the money question from Amy.
turns: Thanks both of you. Amy, before we start, what would make this call worth your time?
Giving the sceptic the first word turns her into a participant.
Honestly, I want to know what it costs and whether it pays for itself.
That's exactly the right question. Can I ask a few questions first so the answer is about your numbers, not a guess?
Agree with her priority and explain why you need questions first.
Tom, roughly how many calls a week do you miss?
Situation from the one who knows
Tom knows the calls; Amy knows the money.
Amy, what's an average job worth when you look at the books?
Value from the one who knows
Asking Amy for the money number makes her the authority on it.
So fifteen calls, say half real jobs, at three-fifty. That's about twenty-six hundred a week at stake. Amy, does that match what you see?
When the sceptic confirms the number, the decision is mostly made.
Amy: It's in the right range.
Then the question is whether booking even a third of those pays for itself. Shall I show you how that would work, and then the price?
Sets a simple test for the price: does it pay for itself?
avoid: Talking only to the friendly partner.
Answering the price question before you know their numbers.
take: Speak to the sceptic first.
Ask each partner what they know best.
Let the sceptic confirm the number.

PB.title: "That's more than I expected"
PB.situation: You've shown the solution and the price: $497 a month. The owner pauses.
PB.goal: Find out whether it's really the price, and get a decision.
prep: Know the value he agreed in discovery.
Decide in advance what you can trade (term, setup fee), not discount.
turns: Hmm. That's more than I expected.
That's fair. Can I ask, more than you expected compared to what?
Find the comparison: another quote, a budget, or nothing.
I don't know. I thought it'd be like two hundred.
Okay. Setting the price aside for a second, if it were two hundred, would you want to start?
If he says no, price isn't the real issue.

Then let's look at it on your numbers. You said about twenty missed calls a week, and half are real jobs at four hundred. If this books even three extra jobs a month, that's twelve hundred against four ninety-seven. Is that maths right, or am I missing something?
Compare cost with the cost of the problem
Use the number he agreed earlier. End by inviting correction.
So is it the monthly amount, or is it that you're not sure it'll book those three jobs?
I guess I'm not sure it'll work for us.
That's fair. We start with a 30-day pilot on after-hours calls only. If it doesn't book at least three jobs in that time, you can cancel. Does that feel like a fair way to find out?
Reduce the risk, not the price
Lower the risk with terms, and keep the price.
Great. I'll send the agreement now. Shall we set it up this Thursday?
Ask for the decision and the next step together.
avoid: Dropping the price straight away.
Re-pitching all the features.
Talking during the pause after the price.
take: Ask "compared to what?"
Separate money from belief.
Lower risk with terms, not discounts.
Ask for the decision clearly.

PB.title: "Let me think about it"
PB.situation: End of a good meeting with a roofing owner. You've asked for the decision.
PB.goal: Find out what he needs to think about, and agree a clear next step.
prep: Expect it. Most owners say it by habit.
Have a follow-up time ready.
turns: This looks good. Let me think about it.
Of course. Usually when someone says that, something isn't clear yet. Is it the price, the timing, or whether it'll work for you?
Make it normal, then offer the three usual reasons.
Timing, I guess. We've got a lot going on.
That makes sense. If it were three months from now, would it be a yes?
Is timing real, or a polite no?
What would be different in three months?
Honestly, nothing. We'll still be busy.
Then is it better to set it up now, while it's busy, so it's working before the next storm? We can start with estimates only, so it takes nothing from your team.
Turn "busy" into the reason to start.
Okay. Estimates only. Let's do it.
Great. I'll send the agreement now and we'll set it up Thursday.
Agree the next step before you leave.
avoid: "Sure, take your time, call me when you're ready."
Pushing harder or adding fake urgency.
take: Make the stall normal, then ask what's unclear.
Test whether timing is real.
Offer a smaller first step.

PB.title: "Can you do it cheaper?"
PB.situation: The owner wants to go ahead but asks for 30% off.
PB.goal: Keep the price, trade something, and close.
prep: Decide what you can trade: a longer term, upfront payment, a case study.
Never discount without getting something back.
turns: We're in. Can you do it for three-fifty instead of five?
I appreciate you being straight. Before I answer, is the price the only thing between us and starting?
Make sure it's the last issue.

I can't change the monthly price, because it's the same for every client. What I can do is waive the setup fee if you commit to six months, and I'd ask you for a short review once you've seen results. Would that work?
Fairness to other clients is a strong reason. Give something only in exchange.
Six months, no setup fee. Okay.
Great. I'll update the agreement and send it in five minutes.
avoid: Agreeing straight away. It tells him the price was made up.
Discounting the monthly price.
take: Isolate: is price the only issue?
Trade terms, not price.
Get something back for anything you give.

PB.title: LinkedIn: agency owner who accepted your request
PB.situation: Hassan runs a 12-person marketing agency in Dubai. He accepted your connection request. He posts about client churn.
PB.goal: Move from a chat to a 15-minute call without pitching.
prep: Read his last three posts.
Have one sentence about what you do, in his language.
turns: Thanks for connecting, Hassan. Your post about clients leaving after month 3 was spot on. Is that something you're seeing more of this year, or just a few clients?
Shows you read his work. Ends with an easy question.
More this year. Clients want results faster.
Makes sense. When a client leaves, is it usually results, or that they can't see the results?
A smart question earns more replies than a pitch.
Honestly, the second. Reporting is weak.
That's fixable. I help agencies set up weekly reports clients actually read. Worth a 15-minute call to see if it would fit? I'm free Tuesday 11am or Wednesday 3pm Dubai time.
One line about you, then a specific ask in his time zone.
Great, sending an invite. What's the best email?
Book it in a calendar, not in chat.
avoid: A pitch in the first message.
Long messages. Keep each under three lines.
Sending a link in the first message.
take: Start from something he posted.
Ask before you tell.
Move off the platform once there's interest.

PB.title: Instagram: salon owner, story reply
PB.situation: Sofia owns a salon in Miami. You've liked and commented on her posts for two days. She posted a story about an empty Tuesday.
PB.goal: Turn a story reply into a short call about bringing back past clients.
prep: Warm up first: like and comment for 2 to 3 days.
Reply to a story, not out of the blue.
turns: (Story reply) Empty Tuesdays are the worst. Do you usually fill them with regulars, or new clients?
Regulars mostly. But a lot of them haven't been in for months.
Happens to most salons I talk to. Roughly how many clients haven't been back since summer?

If even 20 of them came back for one visit, that's a busy week. I help salons send a friendly win-back message to old clients. Want me to show you what one looks like? 10 minutes, Monday or Tuesday morning?
Use a small number and offer to show, not sell.
Perfect. What's the best number or email for the invite?
avoid: "Hey girl" or overly familiar openers.
Promising a number of bookings.
Messaging her old clients without their consent.
take: Warm up before you message.
Reply to a story with a question.
Keep numbers small and believable.

PB.title: Cold email: positive reply and "who is this?"
PB.situation: Your first email went out Tuesday 7am to plumbing owners. Two replies come in.
PB.goal: Book the interested one within the hour; turn the confused one into a conversation.
prep: Reply within the hour.
Keep replies under 60 words.
turns: Thanks, Ray. Short version: it answers the calls your team can't and books the job into your calendar. Easier to show than explain. 15 minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2? Here's my calendar if neither works: [link]
Don't send a long explanation. Book the call.
(Reply 2) Who is this? How did you get my email?

Fair question, Jim. I'm Sam, I work with plumbing companies in Texas, and your email is on your website. I emailed because plumbers tell me they lose jobs after hours. If it's not relevant, just say so and I won't email again.
Honest and easy to say no
Answer both questions truthfully, then offer an easy way out.
(Jim) Actually it is a problem. What do you charge?
Depends on your call volume, so I'd rather not guess. 15 minutes would tell us both if it's worth it. Thursday at 10 or 3?
Earn the right to answer price
Don't price before you know his numbers.
avoid: Long replies with attachments.
Being defensive when asked how you got their email.
Pricing by email.
take: Reply within the hour.
Answer "who is this?" honestly with an easy no.
Book the call; don't explain by email.

PB.title: Personal video, then the follow-up
PB.situation: You recorded a 45-second video of a roofing company's website and Google reviews for your best prospect.
PB.goal: Get a reply and a short call.
PB.setting: Email, Monday 7am. Your video tool shows he watched it twice.
prep: Record only for your best prospects.
Show something specific: his reviews, his site on a phone.
turns:
Subject: quick video for Apex Roofing

Hi Mike, I made a 45-second video about follow-ups on your estimates after the storm. Worth a look? [link]
No embed, no long text. The video does the work.
(Next morning) Thanks for watching, Mike. Does that match what's happening with your estimates right now? Happy to walk through it in ten minutes.
A light question, not a chase.
Yeah, that's us. Can you do Thursday morning?
Thursday at 7 before the crews go out? Sending the invite now.
Offer a time that fits his trade.
avoid: Videos over 60 seconds.
Saying "I saw you watched it twice".
take: Use video for your best prospects.
Show something specific to them.
Follow up the day after a view.

OBJ.q: It's too expensive.
OBJ.means: Usually doubt about the result, sometimes a real cash problem. Find out which before you answer.
OBJ.reply: That's fair, it's a real investment. Setting the price aside for a second: do you feel this would actually fix [the problem]? [If yes:] Then it's about the money, not whether it works. You said [the problem] costs about [their number] a month. How does the price look next to that?
OBJ.ask: Expensive compared to what?

OBJ.q: Someone can do it cheaper, or for free.
OBJ.means: They think the work is simple and the cost is only the setup.
OBJ.reply: Could be, and if it works out, great. The cost is rarely the setup. It's the tuning and support after, and what it costs you when it doesn't work. What would happen if the cheaper option missed calls for a month?
OBJ.ask: Who would fix it when something goes wrong?

OBJ.q: What does it cost? (asked too early)
OBJ.means: Price-shopping before they know if it fits.
OBJ.reply: Fair question. It depends on [volume and what you need], so I'd rather not guess. Can I ask two quick questions, and then give you a real number?
OBJ.ask: How many [calls / leads / jobs] a month do you handle?

OBJ.q: I can't commit to a long contract.
OBJ.means: Fear of being stuck if it doesn't work. A trust and risk concern, not a price one.
OBJ.reply: Completely fair. If it's not working, you shouldn't be stuck with it. We can start month to month with a clear measure for the first 30 days, so you only stay if it works. [ADD only terms you offer.]
OBJ.ask: What would you need to see in 30 days to feel good about continuing?

OBJ.q: Can you give me a discount?
OBJ.means: Testing for flexibility, or cash is genuinely tight.
OBJ.reply: I keep pricing the same for everyone, so it stays fair. If budget is the issue, I can change the scope, start smaller or spread the setup. What matters most to you: the full coverage, or a lower monthly number?
OBJ.ask: If the price were right, would you start this week?

OBJ.q: We don't have the budget.
OBJ.means: Either money is truly short, or the problem doesn't feel worth funding yet.
OBJ.reply: Understood, no pressure. Can I ask: if money weren't a factor at all, would you want to go ahead? [If yes:] Then let's look at what's possible: a smaller start, payment terms, or timing. [If unsure:] Then let's talk about that first, because budget won't fix doubt.
OBJ.ask: If budget weren't an issue, how would you feel about it?

OBJ.q: How do I know you're legit?
OBJ.means: You're new or unknown, and they're risking money.
OBJ.reply: Fair to ask, I'd ask the same. You don't have to take my word for it: [ADD real proof, a live demo on your numbers, a small pilot, a written agreement]. What would you need to see to feel comfortable trying a first step?
OBJ.ask: What would give you confidence to try a small first step?

OBJ.q: I tried something like this before and it didn't work.
OBJ.means: They were burned, and expect the same again.
OBJ.reply: Thanks for telling me, that's really useful. What happened? [Listen fully.] So the problem was [their words]. Here's how we handle that part differently. Does that address it, or is there more to it?
OBJ.ask: What specifically didn't work last time?

OBJ.q: What if it doesn't work for me?
OBJ.means: Fear of a loss they can't recover. The likelihood belief is weak.
OBJ.reply: That's the right question. Let's define what 'working' means for you, put a date on checking it, and [ADD only the guarantee you can honour]. Would that make it feel safe enough to try?
OBJ.ask: What would 'working' look like for you?

OBJ.q: Can I talk to a customer of yours?
OBJ.means: They want proof from someone like them.
OBJ.reply: Yes, where I can. [ADD references you have permission to share.] If I don't have one in your exact situation yet, I'll tell you straight and we can start with a small pilot so you judge for yourself.
OBJ.ask: What would you want to ask them?

OBJ.q: That sounds too good to be true.
OBJ.means: Something earlier sounded like hype.
OBJ.reply: You're right to be careful. Here's exactly what I can and can't promise: [honest scope]. Which part sounds the least believable? Let's look at that one.
OBJ.ask: Which part sounds the least believable?

OBJ.q: Why should I pick you over a bigger company?
OBJ.means: They're comparing credibility and risk.
OBJ.reply: Good question. A bigger company gives you a brand. I give you [speed / direct access / a setup built for your business]. Honestly, if a brand is what matters most, a bigger company might be better. What matters most to you?
OBJ.ask: What matters most to you in who you work with?

OBJ.q: Just send me some info.
OBJ.means: A polite way to end the call, or quiet interest. Find out which.
OBJ.reply: Happy to. So I don't send you something useless, what would you want it to show you? [If they answer:] Honestly, five minutes now would answer that better than a PDF. [If not:] No problem, I'll send it and follow up Thursday.
OBJ.ask: What is the one thing you would most want to see?

OBJ.q: We're slammed right now.
OBJ.means: No bandwidth to think about it.
OBJ.reply: Totally get it. Out of curiosity, when you're this busy, what happens to the calls you can't pick up? [Listen.] That's usually when it costs the most. Setup takes [time] and one short call from you. Would 15 minutes next week be easier?
OBJ.ask: When is it a little quieter for you?

OBJ.q: Call me back in a few months.
OBJ.means: Not a priority, or a polite brush-off.
OBJ.reply: Sure. So I don't call at a bad time again, what will be different in a few months? [Listen.] And meanwhile, what happens to [the problem]? [If it's real:] Is waiting worth that? [If not:] OK, I'll call on [specific date].
OBJ.ask: What would need to change for this to become a priority?

OBJ.q: I need to think about it.
OBJ.means: There's one unspoken concern: price, whether it works for them, or timing.
OBJ.reply: Of course, it's worth thinking about. Usually when someone says that, there's one part they're not sure about. Is it the price, whether it'll work for you, or the timing? [If they won't say:] Picture six months from now. If nothing changes, where are you? And if you'd started today?
OBJ.ask: Is it the price, the results, or the timing?

OBJ.q: It's our busy season, ask me after.
OBJ.means: A real constraint, or a delay.
OBJ.reply: Makes sense. If the busy season is when [the problem] costs the most, would you rather have it fixed before the rush, or after it's already cost you? What would starting in two weeks look like?
OBJ.ask: What would you need to be ready before the rush?

OBJ.q: I need to talk to my partner.
OBJ.means: A real second decision maker, or cover for their own doubt.
OBJ.reply: Of course, they should be part of this. If it were only up to you, would you go ahead? [Listen.] What do you think they'll ask first? It might be easiest if I join for ten minutes so they can ask me directly. Tonight or tomorrow morning?
OBJ.ask: If it were only up to you, where would you be?

OBJ.q: I'm not the one who handles that.
OBJ.means: A gatekeeper, or no authority.
OBJ.reply: No problem, thanks for telling me. Who would be the right person? I'll keep it short for them. What's the best time to reach them, and can I mention you pointed me their way?
OBJ.ask: What's the best way to reach them?

OBJ.q: I have to run it by my team.
OBJ.means: A group decision, or a delay.
OBJ.reply: Makes sense. Who's on the team, and what will they care about most? I can do a short call with them, or give you a one-page summary that answers their questions. Which would help more?
OBJ.ask: Can I join a short call with the team?

OBJ.q: We already have a provider.
OBJ.means: They think the problem is solved.
OBJ.reply: Good, that's probably part of why you've got the business you have. Out of curiosity, how well does it handle [the specific gap, e.g. nights and weekends]? If it's covering everything, I'll leave you alone.
OBJ.ask: Is that for everything, including [the gap], or mostly [the easy part]?

OBJ.q: We don't have that problem.
OBJ.means: They don't see the gap, or it's genuinely small.
OBJ.reply: That's great if so. Most owners don't see it because it never shows up on a report. Would it be a bad idea to check, say, how many calls went to voicemail last week? If it's close to zero, you're right and I'll get out of your hair.
OBJ.ask: How would you know if it were happening?

OBJ.q: Someone in the office handles it.
OBJ.means: A person covers it, so it feels solved.
OBJ.reply: Good, that's a real strength. What happens when they're busy on another call, off shift or out sick?
OBJ.ask: How much comes in after hours or at lunch?

OBJ.q: We've got enough work already.
OBJ.means: Growth isn't the goal right now.
OBJ.reply: Good problem to have. Is the aim more about keeping the work you've got more profitably, and getting some evenings back? That's often where [offer] helps most.
OBJ.ask: What would you change about the work you have today?

OBJ.q: If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
OBJ.means: Change feels risky.
OBJ.reply: Agreed, no point fixing what works. Can I ask one thing: of the last ten [calls / leads], how many turned into a booked job? [Listen.] Is that where you'd want it?
OBJ.ask: What would 'broken' look like for you?

OBJ.q: Will it work with my software?
OBJ.means: They don't want a tool that breaks how they work.
OBJ.reply: Let me be straight: [ADD the integrations you actually support]. If we can't connect directly, details go to your [calendar / text / email] so nothing is lost. What matters most in how the information reaches you?
OBJ.ask: What matters most in how the information reaches you?

OBJ.q: What about call recording and privacy?
OBJ.means: Legal worries.
OBJ.reply: Good question. Calls announce recording at the start, and we set it up to your requirements. Rules vary by state, so I'd suggest confirming with your attorney. Do you have a policy we should follow?
OBJ.ask: Do you have a recording policy we should follow?

OBJ.q: Who owns the data and the number if I leave?
OBJ.means: Fear of lock-in.
OBJ.reply: You do. It's in the agreement [ADD only if true], and I'd help with the handover if you ever left. Want me to show you that part?
OBJ.ask: Would you like to see that clause?

OBJ.q: Not interested.
OBJ.means: A reflex to end an unexpected call.
OBJ.reply: That's fine, I haven't really said anything you could be interested in yet. Can I ask one thing, then you decide: is [the problem] something you deal with at all, or not really?
OBJ.ask: Is it the timing, or the topic?

OBJ.q: How did you get my number?
OBJ.means: Suspicion.
OBJ.reply: It's the business number listed on [your website / Google]. Sorry for the interruption. If you'd rather I didn't call, I'll take you off my list right now.
OBJ.ask: Would you like me to take you off my list?

OBJ.q: Remove me from your list.
OBJ.means: Stop contacting me.
OBJ.reply: Done, you're removed. Sorry for the interruption, have a good day.
OBJ.ask: (No question. Remove them immediately and log it.)

OBJ.q: Who is this? What's this about?
OBJ.means: They need context, fast.
OBJ.reply: It's [name], [Dave]. We haven't spoken. I work with [industry] owners who [problem]. Is that something you deal with, or not really?
OBJ.ask: Is that something you deal with?

OBJ.q: I'm in a meeting / driving.
OBJ.means: Bad timing, or a brush-off.
OBJ.reply: No problem, I'll be quick to let you go. Better tomorrow morning, or later this afternoon?
OBJ.ask: What's the best time to reach you this week?

OBJ.q: Are you a robot?
OBJ.means: They suspect an automated call.
OBJ.reply: [If you are a person:] No, real person, calling from [place]. [If it is an AI system, say so plainly at the start. Never deny it.]
OBJ.ask: (Answer honestly and continue.)

OBJ.q: Let me get a few quotes first.
OBJ.means: A normal comparison, or a way to delay.
OBJ.reply: Smart, you should. So you compare like for like, what will you look at besides price? [Listen.] Based on what you told me matters, here's how we stack up on those. If it helps, I'll give you the questions I'd ask each provider.
OBJ.ask: What will decide it for you?

OBJ.q: Send me the contract and I'll review it.
OBJ.means: Interest, with something still unresolved.
OBJ.reply: Happy to. Before I do: on a scale of 1 to 10, how sure are you this is the right fit? [If under 8:] What would make it a 10? [Then:] Let's go through the contract together for ten minutes so nothing is unclear.
OBJ.ask: When will you have read it? Can we book 10 minutes after?

Reply in the same thread with one useful idea or example.
45-second video on their website or Google listing (Module 6).
A short message if connected, or a story reply.
Second call at a different time of day.

Reply by name with one line about their request, then call. Speed matters most.
Short follow-up with two time options today.
Recap of their request and a clear next step.
Second attempt. If voicemail, leave 20 seconds.
New angle: one specific question or a short result.
Third attempt with new information.
Close the loop: keep this open or close it?
Final note. Leave the door open.

Break-up note.
Revive with something new.
Recap, proposal, and the decision date you agreed.
Confirm it arrived. Ask if anything is unclear.

Ask where they are in the decision.

Short, relevant, no pitch, no link.
Thank them and ask one easy question.

Offer a short call or a short video. Then polite close if no reply.
One-line note about their business. No video yet.
Send the 45-second video with one line of context.
Thank them for watching and ask one light question.
If not watched: 'Did my video arrive okay?'
A short plain-text email with a new point.
Close the file and stop.
Thank them and ask for the reason, with no pressure.

A quick question about whether their situation has changed.
Invite them to a refreshed conversation.

SC.label: Opener was short and in my own words
I stated why I was calling
I talked less than half the time
Questions were open and went from problem to impact
I used mirrors, labels or silence
I acknowledged and clarified before answering objections
I asked clearly for the next step or decision
A dated next step was agreed before ending
I logged the call and sent a follow-up within an hour

SCR.body: Hey {{prospect}}, it's {{you}}. We haven't spoken before. I'm calling because {{reason}}. Is that something you deal with, or not really?

SCR.label: Voicemail (20 seconds)
SCR.body: Hi {{prospect}}, it's {{you}} from {{company}}. I'm calling because {{reason}}. I'd like to ask how you handle it at {{business}}. You can reach me on {{phone}}. That's {{phone}}. Thanks, {{prospect}}.

SCR.label: First email

SCR.body:
Hi {{prospect}}, one more thought on {{business}}: {{problem}} Is that something you're looking to fix, or not really a priority right now?
