RP.title: Cold call to a busy plumbing owner
RP.setting: You call a plumbing company owner you have never spoken to. You sell an AI call-answering service.
RP.persona: Dave, owner of a four-truck plumbing company. Busy, direct, tired of sales calls.

beats.p: Yeah, this is Dave.

opts.t: Dave, it's [you]. We haven't spoken. I'm calling because plumbers tell me they lose calls when they're on a job. Is that something you deal with, or not really?
opts.fb: Short, honest about the cold call, names a problem other owners have, and ends on a question with an easy no.

opts.t: Hi Dave, how are you doing today? Hope I'm not catching you at a bad time!
opts.fb: Small talk and an apology mark you as a salesperson in two seconds. Say who you are and why you called.

opts.t: Hi Dave, I'm with [company]. We build AI agents that answer calls for plumbers. Do you have a minute?
opts.fb: Clear, but it leads with your product and ends on a closed question that is easy to refuse.

beats.p: We're slammed right now. I don't have time for this.

opts.t: Sounds like business is good. I'll be quick: when you are under a sink and the phone rings, what happens to that call?
opts.fb: Acknowledges, then asks one easy question about their world. You keep the call alive without arguing.

opts.t: I totally understand, I just need two minutes to explain how our system works.
opts.fb: You ignored what they said and asked for more time. That is pushing.

opts.t: No problem. When is a better time to call back?
opts.fb: Polite, but you leave without a single question. Ask one before you offer to call back.

beats.p: It goes to voicemail. Maybe half get answered.

opts.t: Half. About how many calls a week is that, and roughly what is an average job worth?
opts.fb: Gets the two numbers you need to build the case on their figures.

opts.t: Great, that's exactly what we fix. Our agent answers 24/7 with a natural voice and books the job straight into your calendar.
opts.fb: A pitch dump before you know the size of the problem. Ask first.

opts.t: Wow, that's a lot of missed calls.
opts.fb: A fair reaction, but it is a statement. Turn it into a question about volume and value.

beats.p: Maybe 15 a week. Average job's about four hundred bucks.

opts.t: If even a third of those were real jobs, what would that add up to in a week, roughly?
opts.fb: He does the math with his own numbers. A cost he works out himself is one he believes.

opts.t: Cool. Our plan is a few hundred a month, so you'd earn it back on one job.
opts.fb: The link is good, but you quote a price before they have agreed the problem is real.

opts.t: Okay. Do you want me to send over some pricing?
opts.fb: You skipped the whole point of the numbers. Nothing here has been confirmed.

beats.p: Huh. Two grand a week, maybe. That's more than I thought. So what do you want from me?

opts.t: Ten minutes. I'll show it answering a call for your business and you decide if it is worth it. Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
opts.fb: Small ask, clear purpose, two specific times.

opts.t: Can I just send you an email with the details?
opts.fb: Low commitment, so low value. An email rarely gets read and gives you no next step.

opts.t: Just let me know if you're interested and I'll get something over to you.
opts.fb: You handed control back to a busy owner. Nothing is booked.

RP.title: "Just send me an email"
RP.setting: Early in a cold call the owner tries to end it.
RP.persona: Priya, office manager at a small HVAC business. Polite, wants the call over.
RP.goal: Turn the brush-off into a real conversation or a booked time.

beats.p: Just send me an email.

opts.t: Happy to. So it's relevant, quick question: how are you handling calls that come in while the crew is out?
opts.fb: Agrees, then asks a question that shows if there is any interest at all.

opts.t: Sure, what's your email address?
opts.fb: You accept the brush-off. The email will never be read.

opts.t: I can do that. What would you want it to say?
opts.fb: Better than giving in, but the question is vague. Ask about their situation instead.

beats.p: Honestly, we just let it go to voicemail and call back later.

opts.t: Sounds like a few never get called back, or they've already booked someone else. About how many a week, would you say?
opts.fb: A label followed by a number question. They start thinking about the cost.

opts.t: That's a mistake. Most customers call the next company straight away.
opts.fb: Telling them they are wrong creates resistance. Let them find the cost themselves.

opts.t: Okay. Do you want to hear how we can help with that?
opts.fb: Polite, but a yes or no question that is easy to refuse.

beats.p: Maybe five or six. I never really counted.

opts.t: Since nobody has counted, would it help if I showed you how to track it? Ten minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
opts.fb: Offers something useful, keeps the ask small and gives two times.

opts.t: Then you're losing business. We can fix that. Can I send you a quote?
opts.fb: You jumped to a price before any value was agreed.

opts.t: Okay, I'll send the email and follow up next week.
opts.fb: A follow-up is fine, but no time is agreed and the email still has no reason to be opened.

RP.title: Price and "I'll think about it"
RP.setting: You have run a good discovery call. Now the owner pushes back on price.
RP.persona: Sam, owner of a plumbing and drain business. Careful with money, has been burned by software before.
RP.goal: Keep the deal alive and agree a dated next step.

beats.p: Honestly, four hundred a month feels like a lot.

opts.t: Fair. Let's compare it to one number. You said an average job is four hundred and you miss about seven calls a week. Is it the amount, or whether it would pay back?
opts.fb: Acknowledges, uses their numbers and asks what the concern really is.

opts.t: I can do three hundred if you sign this week.
opts.fb: A discount before you know the objection teaches them that your price is soft.

opts.t: It's actually cheap compared to hiring a receptionist.
opts.fb: Comparing is useful, but it is defensive and about your price, not their gain.

beats.p: I guess it's whether it works. I've been burned by software before.

opts.t: It sounds like you have been burned before. What went wrong last time?
opts.fb: A label and an open question. You learn the real fear.

opts.t: Ours is different. We have great reviews.
opts.fb: Claims without proof, and you did not learn what happened before.

opts.t: Everyone says that until they try it.
opts.fb: Dismissive. You are telling them their concern is not real.

beats.p: It never got set up. Took forever and then nobody used it.

opts.t: So the problem was set-up and follow-through, not the idea. We set it up for you in [N] days and start month to month with one check at 30 days: booked jobs. Would that remove most of the risk?
opts.fb: Addresses the exact fear and makes the risk small and measurable.

opts.t: That won't happen with us.
opts.fb: A promise with nothing behind it.

opts.t: Let me send you some case studies.
opts.fb: Proof helps, but you did not answer the worry or agree a next step.

beats.p: Okay. Let me think about it.

opts.t: Of course. Usually there's one part people aren't sure about. Is it the price, whether it'll work for you, or the timing? And let's put Thursday at 10 in, so you're not left chasing me.
opts.fb: Turns the vague stall into a specific concern, and sets a dated decision call.

opts.t: No problem. I'll check back next month.
opts.fb: A month is too long. The deal will go cold.

opts.t: Sure. Can you tell me what you're thinking about so I can help?
opts.fb: Good instinct, but it is vague and still has no date.

RP.title: Getting past the gatekeeper
RP.setting: Someone answers who is not the decision maker.
RP.persona: Maria, front desk at a roofing company. Protective of the owner's time.
RP.goal: Reach the owner or get a named contact and a time.

beats.p: Good afternoon, [company]. How can I help?

opts.t: Hi, it's [you]. Could you help me? I need to speak with whoever looks after the phones and booking, is that you or the owner?
opts.fb: Calm, asks for help and a role, not a name. Gatekeepers respond to that.

opts.t: Hi, can I speak to the owner please?
opts.fb: Direct, but it triggers the standard screen: "What is it about?"

opts.t: Hi, I'm calling about an opportunity to grow your business. Is the decision maker in?
opts.fb: Sales phrases like "opportunity" and "decision maker" get you screened out.

beats.p: He's not available. What is this regarding?

opts.t: It's about calls that come in while the crew is on a roof. I'll be brief. When is he usually free, so I call when it suits him?
opts.fb: Honest, short reason, and you ask for a time instead of leaving a message.

opts.t: It's a business matter. Can you just put me through?
opts.fb: Vague and pushy. That is exactly what screeners are trained to block.

opts.t: It's about a sales service. Can I leave my number?
opts.fb: Honest, but an owner will rarely call back a number left this way.

beats.p: He's usually in around 8 in the morning.

opts.t: Thank you, that helps. I'll call at 8:05 tomorrow. What's your name, so I can say you suggested the time?
opts.fb: Gets a time, a name and a reason for the owner to take the call.

opts.t: Great, I'll try him some time then.
opts.fb: No time, no name. You will forget and so will they.

opts.t: Thanks. Can I leave an email with you for him?
opts.fb: Possible, but an email from a stranger rarely works. A timed call usually does.

RP.title: "We already have someone"
RP.setting: You sent a cold email. This is the reply.
RP.persona: Tom, owner of a landscaping firm. Replied in two lines.
RP.goal: Keep the thread alive without arguing.

beats.p: We already have a company handling this.

opts.t: Thanks for the reply, Tom. That makes sense. Out of curiosity, how well are they picking up calls after hours? If they do it well, no need to change anything.
opts.fb: Accepts the answer, asks a low-pressure question and gives them a way to be honest.

opts.t: Are you sure they are doing a good job? Many companies like yours still miss a lot of calls.
opts.fb: Challenges them and sounds like a sales sequence.

opts.t: Understood. Would you like me to send some information in case that changes?
opts.fb: Polite, but there is no reason to reply and no question that opens the door.

beats.p: They're okay. Not sure about nights and weekends.

opts.t: That is the gap I hear most. Would it be worth ten minutes to compare how nights and weekends are covered? No obligation to switch. Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
opts.fb: Names the gap, keeps the ask small and gives two times.

opts.t: Then you should definitely switch. We cover nights and weekends.
opts.fb: A pushy leap. They did not say they want to switch.

opts.t: Let me know if you want a quote.
opts.fb: Passive. Nothing moves.

beats.p: Send me something and I'll look.

opts.t: Will do. So I send the right thing, what matters more to you: more booked jobs, or fewer interruptions for your team?
opts.fb: Sends something and uses the moment to learn what to put in it.

opts.t: Sure. Attached is our full brochure and pricing.
opts.fb: A generic dump that nobody opens. You learned nothing.

opts.t: Sure, I'll send a short summary today.
opts.fb: Fine, but no question, and no date to follow up.

RP.title: "How much is it?" in a direct message
RP.setting: You sent a first message on Instagram or LinkedIn. They reply with a price question.
RP.persona: Alex, owner of a home services business. Replying between jobs.
RP.goal: Move to a short call without a price war.

beats.p: Thanks for reaching out. How much is it?

opts.t: Good question. It depends on how many calls you get and what you want connected. Two quick questions: roughly how many calls a week, and what is a typical job worth?
opts.fb: Does not dodge, does not guess a number. Asks the two questions you need to give a real answer.

opts.t: It starts at four hundred a month.
opts.fb: Honest, but the price floats with no value attached and you learned nothing.

opts.t: It's a really great price, I promise it's worth it! Can I call you?
opts.fb: Vague and pushy. Sounds like every other DM.

beats.p: Around 20 a week. Jobs are maybe 500.

opts.t: Thanks. If even 5 of those are missed, that is around 2,500 a week at risk. Easier to show than type. Ten minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
opts.fb: Reflects their numbers and asks for a short call with two times.

opts.t: Great. Plans start at four hundred, and it goes up from there.
opts.fb: Gives the price, but no value or next step.

opts.t: Awesome! Here is a link to our website with all the details.
opts.fb: A link ends most conversations.

beats.p: Thursday at 9 is fine. Can you just text me the details?

opts.t: Yes. I'll send a calendar invite for Thursday at 9 and a text the morning before to confirm. What is the best number?
opts.fb: Locks it in with an invite and a reminder.

opts.t: Sure, I'll text you the details. Talk soon!
opts.fb: No invite and no reminder. No-shows start here.

opts.t: Great. Just show up when you can.
opts.fb: A time without a confirmation is a no-show waiting to happen.

Opening.text: Openers that earn a second sentence

NICHES.name: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical
NICHES.tag: Owners who miss calls while on a job.
NICHES.buyer: The owner or owner-operator. In larger firms, the office or operations manager.
pain: Calls missed while the crew is on a job, after hours and on weekends.
Slow follow-up on web forms and quote requests.
Customers who book the first company that picks up.
NICHES.math: Example only: 15 missed calls a week, a third of them real jobs, 400 average job = about 2,000 a week in jobs that went elsewhere.
NICHES.angle: Speed and coverage. Position the service as the receptionist they cannot afford to keep on 24 hours a day.
NICHES.channels: Call first (owners answer their own phones), then SMS or Facebook message, then email.
NICHES.call: [Name], it's [you]. We haven't spoken. I'm calling because plumbers I talk to tell me they lose calls when they're on a job. Is that something you deal with, or not really?
NICHES.email:
Subject: calls while you're on a job

Hi [Name],

I found [business] on Google. Your reviews mention fast response, which is hard to keep up when everyone is out on jobs.

We [offer]. Is missing calls something that happens at [business]?

If it is, ten minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2 would show you what it looks like on your numbers.

[you]
[company], [postal address]
If you would rather not hear from me, reply stop.
NICHES.dm: Hi [Name], saw [business] has strong reviews around [town]. Quick question: how do you handle calls when the crew is out on jobs?
obj: I already have an answering service.
Good, then you know the value. How many calls does it turn into booked jobs, not messages? That is the number I'd compare.
My customers want a real person.
They do, and so do I. This takes the call when nobody can, books the job and hands it to your team. How many calls go to voicemail today?
Not now, it's busy season.
That is when the missed calls cost the most. Ten minutes now, set-up later, so it is ready when you are quiet?
ask: How many calls do you miss in a typical week?
What is an average job worth?
Who answers the phone after 5pm and on weekends?
What happens to a web form request at 9pm?
NICHES.src: Google Maps: "plumber [city]", "HVAC repair [city]". Check for a phone number only, no website, or few recent reviews. Facebook business pages with posts about "call or text".
NICHES.time: Call 7:30 to 9am or 4 to 6pm local time, before the day starts or when crews are back. Check seasonal peaks: winter for heating and burst pipes, summer for cooling.
NICHES.watch: If you sell AI voice or SMS, check consent and calling-hour rules (lesson 7.6). Do not promise a number of jobs.

NICHES.name: Roofing and exteriors
NICHES.tag: High-value jobs, long quotes, slow follow-up.
NICHES.buyer: The owner or the sales manager. Estimators often handle first contact.
pain: Estimates sent and never followed up.
Storm-season rushes the team cannot keep up with.
Leads from lead platforms that sell the same lead to several roofers.
NICHES.math: Example only: 20 estimates a month, 15 never followed up properly, 2 would have closed at 9,000 = 18,000 a month in value.
NICHES.angle: Follow-up and speed. The lead goes to whoever calls back first and keeps calling.
NICHES.channels: Call, then email with a quote follow-up angle, then a short video.
NICHES.call: [Name], it's [you]. We haven't spoken. Roofers tell me estimates go out and the follow-up slips when jobs are on. Does that happen at [business], or not really?
NICHES.email:
Subject: estimates that go quiet

Hi [Name],

When a roofing estimate goes out and nobody hears back, a lot of the time it is not a no, it is a missed follow-up.

We [offer] so every estimate gets a timed follow-up. Does that gap exist at [business]?

If yes, ten minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?

[you]
[company], [postal address]
Reply stop to opt out.
NICHES.dm: Hi [Name], saw your recent project on [street or town]. Quick question: what happens to estimates that don't reply within a week?
obj: We get plenty of leads.
Good. What percentage of estimates turn into signed jobs? That is where the money is usually lost.
We don't want automated messages.
Fair. I'd write them in your voice and you approve every sequence. Can I show you an example?
I need to talk to my partner.
Of course, that makes sense. When you talk it over, what do you think they will ask first? Would it help if we all spoke for ten minutes?
ask: How many estimates do you send a month?
What share turn into signed jobs?
Who follows up, and how often?
What is an average job worth?
NICHES.src: Google Maps: "roofing contractor [city]". Look at recent reviews and active Facebook pages. Storm-hit areas show demand.
NICHES.time: Call early morning or late afternoon. After storms, call within days while demand is high.
NICHES.watch: Do not use storm damage fear to pressure owners. Keep claims about leads and revenue conditional.

NICHES.name: Dental and orthodontics
NICHES.tag: Front desks that are too busy to answer.
NICHES.buyer: Practice owner or practice manager. The front desk screens everything.
pain: Phones ringing while the front desk checks patients in.
Cancellations and no-shows that leave gaps in the day.
New-patient enquiries that are not followed up.
NICHES.math: Example only: 10 missed new-patient calls a month, 3 booked, new-patient value of 1,500 = about 4,500 a month.
NICHES.angle: New patients and the cost of an empty chair. Always respect the front desk.
NICHES.channels: Email to the practice manager, LinkedIn to owners, call at quiet times.
NICHES.call: Hi, it's [you]. I'm looking for whoever manages new-patient enquiries and bookings. Is that you, or someone else?
NICHES.email:
Subject: new patient calls at [practice]

Hi [Name],

I noticed [practice] gets steady reviews, which usually means a busy front desk. When it is busy, new-patient calls can go unanswered.

We [offer]. Does that happen at [practice]?

If yes, ten minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2 would show how it works without changing your front-desk routine.

[you]
[company], [postal address]
Reply stop to opt out.
NICHES.dm: Hi [Name], I saw [practice] was recently featured in [place]. Quick question: how do new-patient calls get answered when the front desk is busy?
obj: We have patient data to protect.
Rightly. I can walk you through exactly what is handled and what is not. Who handles privacy and compliance at your practice?
My front desk handles it fine.
I'm sure they work hard. How many calls come in at lunch or after 5pm, and who picks those up?
We're not looking for anything new.
Understood. Just so I leave you with something useful: do you track how many new-patient calls are missed?
ask: How many new patients do you want a month?
How are new-patient calls handled at lunch and after hours?
What is a new patient worth over a year?
What is your no-show rate?
NICHES.src: Google Maps: "dentist [city]", "orthodontist [city]". Check for online booking, recent reviews and number of providers.
NICHES.time: Call between 8 and 9am or 1 and 2pm. Avoid the lunch rush and the morning start.
NICHES.watch: Health-privacy rules apply when you handle patient information. Do not handle patient data without a lawful agreement. Check with a qualified advisor.

NICHES.name: Med spa and aesthetics
NICHES.tag: Appointment-driven, high-value, image-conscious.
NICHES.buyer: Owner or clinic manager. Often active on Instagram.
pain: Enquiries from Instagram and ads that are not followed up quickly.
No-shows and last-minute cancellations.
Inconsistent rebooking of repeat treatments.
NICHES.math: Example only: 40 enquiries a month, 10 lost to slow replies, 6 would have booked at 300 = 1,800 a month, more with repeats.
NICHES.angle: Speed to reply, show rate and rebooking.
NICHES.channels: Instagram and Facebook first, then email, then call.
NICHES.call: Hi, it's [you]. Could I speak with whoever handles new enquiries and bookings?
NICHES.email:
Subject: enquiries after hours at [spa]

Hi [Name],

Your Instagram shows strong interest in [treatment]. Enquiries that come in at night tend to book with whoever replies first.

We [offer]. How are late enquiries handled at [spa] today?

[you]
[company], [postal address]
Reply stop to opt out.
NICHES.dm: Hi [Name], love the [treatment] results you shared. Quick question: how do you reply to enquiries that come in at night?
obj: We handle our own bookings.
That is the right instinct for a premium brand. What does a reply look like at 10pm, and how fast does it go out?
We worry about the brand voice.
So do I. I'd write everything in your tone and you approve it first. Can I show you a sample?
Our margin is tight.
Let's check one number: what is a first treatment worth, and how many enquiries do you lose to slow replies?
ask: How many enquiries do you get a week?
How fast do you reply?
What is a new client worth over six months?
What is your no-show rate?
NICHES.src: Instagram search: "med spa [city]". Google Maps: "aesthetics clinic [city]". Check last post date and whether a booking link exists.
NICHES.time: Message mid-morning or early evening. Avoid weekend treatment peaks.
NICHES.watch: Do not make medical claims or promises about treatment results. Keep copy factual.

NICHES.name: Real estate agents and teams
NICHES.tag: Speed-to-lead and follow-up on a long pipeline.
NICHES.buyer: The team lead or a solo agent. Large brokerages: the team's operations lead.
pain: Portal leads that go cold in minutes.
Long-term leads that are forgotten.
Agents who do not have time for first calls.
NICHES.math: Example only: 50 leads a month, 3 percent convert at 9,000 commission = 13,500. Better speed and follow-up might add one deal a quarter.
NICHES.angle: Speed to lead and consistent long-term follow-up.
NICHES.channels: LinkedIn, Facebook, then a call. Agents are active on social.
NICHES.call: [Name], it's [you]. We haven't spoken. I'm calling because agents tell me online leads go cold if the first reply takes more than a few minutes. Is that true for you, or not really?
NICHES.email:
Subject: portal leads that go cold

Hi [Name],

I saw your listings in [area]. Most online leads go to whoever replies first, and it is hard to do that while you are at a showing.

We [offer]. How do you handle new leads when you are out?

[you]

PROMPTS.use: Five-minute research before a call or email.
PROMPTS.p:
Here is the text from a company's website:

[paste text]

Summarise it in four bullets: what they do, who they serve, how customers contact them, and one thing a service like mine could help with. Use only what is in the text. If something is not stated, write "not stated". Do not guess.

PROMPTS.t: Find the true hook in their reviews
PROMPTS.use: A first line that is specific and real.
PROMPTS.p:
Here are recent public reviews for a business:

[paste reviews]

List the three most repeated things customers praise or complain about. For each, quote the exact words from a review. Then suggest one first line for a cold message that refers to a real detail, with no flattery and no claim I cannot verify.

PROMPTS.t: Score a lead against my ideal customer
PROMPTS.use: Rank a list before you start calling.
PROMPTS.p:
My ideal customer is: [describe: industry, size, signs of need].

Here is a lead:
[paste what you know]

Score it 1 to 5 against my ideal customer. Give two reasons for the score and the one fact I should check before contacting them. If information is missing, say so.

PROMPTS.t: Cut my cold email in half
PROMPTS.use: Tighten a draft that runs long.
PROMPTS.p:
Here is a cold email I drafted:

[paste email]

Rewrite it to under 80 words. Keep one idea, one clear question at the end, and no hype words. Do not add claims or numbers that are not in my draft. Show the rewrite, then a one-line list of what you removed.

My email is about [topic] for [role] at [type of business]. Write ten subject lines under 6 words each. Plain language, lower case, no spam words, no clickbait, no emojis. Group them as: question, observation, short label.

PROMPTS.t: Turn a call into a follow-up email
PROMPTS.use: Recap and next step within an hour.
PROMPTS.p:
Here are my notes from a sales call:

[paste notes]

Write a short follow-up email (under 120 words). Include: the problem they described in their own words, the next step we agreed with date and time, and one question to confirm. Do not add anything that was not in my notes.

My first email was:

[paste]

Write three follow-ups for day 4, day 9 and day 16. Each under 60 words, each with a new angle (a question, a small useful idea, a polite close). Never use "just checking in" or guilt. Keep every claim true.

PROMPTS.t: Draft a reply to an objection
PROMPTS.p:
A prospect said: "[objection]".
My service: [one line]. Their business: [one line].

Give me: (1) what the objection may really mean, (2) a reply in three sentences that acknowledges first, then asks one clarifying question, and (3) a second version if they push again. Spoken language, no scripts that sound robotic.

PROMPTS.use: Free roleplay in any AI chat.
PROMPTS.p: Act as [name], [role] at [type of business]. You are busy, a little sceptical, and polite. I am a sales rep who has called you with no warning. Reply in one or two short sentences as the prospect would. Do not help me or break character. After 8 exchanges, stop and score me on: opening, questions asked, handling of objections, and the next step I secured. Give one thing to fix.

PROMPTS.use: Feedback when you have a transcript.
PROMPTS.p:
Here is a transcript of my sales call (Rep and Prospect labelled):

[paste transcript]

Review it against this checklist: short opener, reason for call, talk ratio under 50 percent, open questions, acknowledged objections before answering, clear ask, dated next step. For each, say met, partly or missed, and quote the line. End with the two biggest fixes.

PROMPTS.t: Structure a case study without inventing figures
PROMPTS.p:
Here are the real facts about one client result:

[paste facts]

Write a four-sentence case study: situation, what we did, result, how it was measured. Use only the facts I gave. If a number is missing, leave a [blank] for me to fill. Do not round up or add adjectives.

PROMPTS.t: Clean and standardise a lead list
PROMPTS.use: Before you import to a CRM or sender.
PROMPTS.p:
Here is a lead list as plain text:

[paste rows]

Return a table with these columns: first name, last name, company, role, email, phone, website, notes. Fix capitalisation, remove duplicates, flag rows with missing email or phone, and flag generic emails like info@ or sales@. Do not invent any missing data.

PROMPT_RULES: Never let an AI invent facts about a prospect. Check every claim against a source.
Remove personal data you do not need before pasting anything.
Read it out loud. If it does not sound like you, edit it.
Keep your sending rules: real identity, honest subject, easy opt-out.

templates.body:
Monthly review: {{client}}
30 minutes

1. Results against the goal ({{kpi}} to {{target}}), in your numbers. Value so far: {{valueSoFar}}.
2. What worked: [one or two things to keep]
3. What didn't: [one thing to fix] and the plan
4. Next month: the focus, and any change in scope
5. Feedback: "From 1 to 10, how happy are you? What would make it a 10?"
6. Book the next review.

Next review: [date]

90-day review: {{client}} and {{agency}}
Date: {{d90}} | 45 minutes

1. Where we started (5 min)
   Your goal at kickoff: {{kpi}} to {{target}}. Where you were before: [baseline].
2. What changed (10 min)
   Scoreboard:
@kpirows
   Value in money: {{valueSoFar}} so far, against a fee of {{fee}} a month.
3. What we learned (10 min)
   What worked, what didn't, what we changed.
4. What's next (15 min)

   Our recommendation for the next 90 days: [focus 1], [focus 2].
5. Agree (5 min)

Right after a visible win or a happy review.
templates.body: {{contact}}, I'm glad the results are where they are. Quick question: who else do you know who runs a business like yours and has the same problem we fixed? An introduction by text or email is perfect, and I'll take good care of them.

templates.use: After a win the client has said out loud. Make it easy: offer to draft it from their own words.
templates.body:
Hi {{contact}}, thank you again for saying [their words about the result]. Would you be open to sharing that as a short review?

Three questions make it easy:
1. What was happening before we started?
2. What changed, in numbers if you can?
3. Who would you recommend us to?

If it's quicker, reply with a few lines and I'll turn them into a draft for you to approve. Nothing goes out without your OK.

[REVIEW LINK]

{{me}}

(Never offer anything in return for a review, and ask every client, not only the happy ones.)

templates.use: A 20-minute call with a happy client. Their words become your best sales asset.
templates.body:
Case study interview: {{client}}
20 minutes. Record with permission.

Before
1. What was the business like before we started?
2. What was the problem costing you, in time or money?
3. What else had you tried?

Decision
4. Why did you choose {{agency}}? What almost stopped you?

After
5. What changed? Which numbers moved?
6. What surprised you?
7. What would you tell an owner who is where you were?

Permission
8. May we use your name, business name and these numbers? Anything you want left out?

templates.use: No reply for a week or more. Silence is the most common early warning. Three steps, three channels.
templates.body:
Step 1 (day 7, message)
Hi {{contact}}, haven't heard from you in a bit, so a quick check: is everything OK on your side? No action needed on anything urgent, I just want to make sure we're still working on what matters most to you.

Step 2 (day 10, call)
"{{contact}}, it's {{me}}. I noticed we've been quiet and I wanted to check in properly. How is it really going?"

Step 3 (day 14, short email)
Subject: should I pause anything?
Hi {{contact}}, I haven't been able to reach you, so I want to check: should we keep going as planned, pause anything, or change the focus? A one-word reply is fine.

templates.use: When the client asks for work outside the agreement. Say yes to the goal, put a price and date on the work.
templates.body:
Hi {{contact}}, happy to help with [the request]. It's outside what we agreed for {{service}}, so here are the options:

1. Add it: [price] and ready by [date].
2. Swap it: we pause [something lower priority] this month and do this instead, at no extra cost.
3. Later: we add it to the plan for next term.

Which works best for you?

{{me}}

templates.use: Polite, short and on a schedule. Agree in the contract what happens after 14 days.
templates.body:
Day 1 after due date
Hi {{contact}}, a friendly reminder that invoice [number] for {{fee}} was due on [date]. Here's the link again: [PAYMENT LINK]. Thanks!

Day 7
Hi {{contact}}, invoice [number] is now a week overdue. Is anything holding it up on your side? Happy to help if there's a problem with the invoice.

Day 14

templates.use: When a client signals they may leave. Call, don't email.
templates.body:
Save call: {{client}}

1. Thank and listen
   "Thanks for being straight with me, {{contact}}. Can you walk me through what isn't working?"
2. Find the real reason. Keep asking until it is clear:
   "What else?"  "When did you first feel that?"  "If that were fixed, would you stay?"
   Reason: [results / cost / timing / fit or trust]
3. Say back what you heard
   "So the main issue is [their words]. Did I get that right?"
4. Offer ONE option that matches the reason
   Results:  "Give us 30 days with one change: [change]. We check on [date]. If {{kpi}} hasn't moved, you leave with no hard feelings."
   Cost:     "We can drop to a smaller plan at [price], focused on [the part that works]."
   Timing:   "We can pause until [restart date] and keep your setup ready."
   Fit:      "If this isn't the right fit, I'd rather help you leave well."
5. If the answer is still no
   "I understand. Could you share one thing we should have done differently? And may I check in with you in [month]?"

templates.use: When a client has decided to leave. A clean exit protects referrals and your reputation.
templates.body:
Subject: Confirming your cancellation and handover

Hi {{contact}},

Thank you for letting us know, and for the time we worked together. Your service ends on [end date].

Before then we'll hand over:
- [Data, reports and recordings]
- [Logins, numbers, scripts and files that belong to you]
- [Setup notes the next provider will need]

One favour: what's one thing we should have done differently? Your honest answer helps us improve.

If anything changes, the door is always open.

All the best,
{{me}}

DRILLS.title: Cold call opener
DRILLS.sit: The owner just picked up. Say the opener clearly, at a calm pace.
DRILLS.line: Hi Dave, it's Sam. We haven't spoken before. I'm calling because plumbers tell me they lose jobs when nobody picks up after hours. Is that true for you?

DRILLS.title: Gatekeeper
DRILLS.sit: The office manager answers. Sound like you belong, not like you are selling.
DRILLS.line: Hi, it's Sam calling for Dave. Is he around, or is there a better time to catch him today?

DRILLS.title: Booking the meeting
DRILLS.sit: The owner agreed missed calls cost money. Ask for a short, specific meeting.
DRILLS.line: Let me show you that on your own numbers. Ten minutes on Thursday at nine, or Friday at two?

DRILLS.title: Confirming the meeting
DRILLS.sit: Call the day before to confirm. Friendly, short, with a reason to show up.
DRILLS.line: Hi Linda, it's Sam. I'm calling to confirm our call tomorrow at ten. I'll show you how many after-hours calls you are missing. Does that time still work?

DRILLS.title: Answering "How much?" early
DRILLS.sit: The owner asks the price in the first minute. Stay calm and earn the right to ask questions.
DRILLS.line: Fair question. It depends on how many calls you get, so I'd rather not guess. Can I ask two quick questions, and then give you a real number?

DRILLS.title: Voicemail
DRILLS.sit: No answer. Leave a short voicemail that sounds like a person, not an ad.
DRILLS.line: Hi Dave, it's Sam. I had a quick idea about the calls you miss after hours. I'll send you a short text now, so you have my number. Talk soon.

DRILLS.title: "Who is this?"
DRILLS.sit: You said hello and the owner cuts in.
DRILLS.line: It's Sam, Dave. We haven't spoken before. I work with plumbers on the calls they miss after hours. Got thirty seconds for me to tell you why I called?

DRILLS.title: "Just send me an email"
DRILLS.sit: Twenty seconds into the call, the owner wants you gone.
DRILLS.line: Happy to. So I send something useful and not a brochure, can I ask one quick question? Roughly how many calls go to voicemail in a busy week?

DRILLS.title: "I'm busy right now"
DRILLS.sit: The owner is on a job site.
DRILLS.line: No problem, I'll be quick to let you go. Is tomorrow morning around eight better, or later in the afternoon?

DRILLS.title: "We're not interested"
DRILLS.sit: A fast no before you have said much.
DRILLS.line: Fair enough, most owners say that before they hear why I called. Just so I know, is it that you never miss calls, or that you already have someone answering?

DRILLS.title: "Where are you calling from?"
DRILLS.sit: The owner hears your accent and asks. Be honest and relaxed, then move on.
DRILLS.line: I'm in Pakistan, and I work with businesses in the US. I called because a lot of plumbers lose jobs after hours. Is that something you see too?

DRILLS.title: "Let me think about it"
DRILLS.sit: End of the meeting. The owner stalls.
DRILLS.line: Of course. Usually that means something isn't clear yet. Is it the price, the timing, or whether it will work for your business?

DRILLS.title: Ask for the next step
DRILLS.sit: Dave said he misses about twenty calls a month, and each job is worth about four hundred dollars. Book the next meeting.
DRILLS.line: Twenty missed calls at around four hundred dollars a job is a lot of money. Let's put your numbers into a short demo. Does Thursday at nine or Friday at two work better?

DRILLS.title: Your own voicemail
DRILLS.sit: Leave a voicemail in your own words: your name, one reason for the call, and what happens next. Under 20 seconds.
DRILLS.line: Hi Dave, it's Sam. Quick idea about the calls that go to voicemail after hours. I'll text you a two-line summary so you have my number. Talk soon.

DRILLS.title: Opener built on your research
DRILLS.sit: You checked the practice's hours before calling. Use what you found in the first sentence.
DRILLS.line: Hi Karen, it's Sam. I'm calling because I saw your office closes for lunch, and practices tell me that's when new patients call. Who looks after that for you?

DRILLS.title: "Is this a real person?"
DRILLS.sit: The owner has had a lot of robocalls this week and asks straight away.
DRILLS.them: Is this a real person or one of those AI things?
DRILLS.line: Real person, I promise. I'm Sam, and I work with plumbers on the calls they miss. Fair question though. Can I tell you why I called?

DRILLS.title: "How did you get my number?"
DRILLS.sit: The owner sounds suspicious. Be honest and calm.
DRILLS.them: How did you get my number?
DRILLS.line: It's on your Google listing. I called the business line because I work with HVAC companies on missed calls. If now's a bad time I can call back. Is it?

DRILLS.title: Personal video intro
DRILLS.sit: Read the first lines of a 45-second personal video. Warm, specific, unhurried.
DRILLS.line: Hi Mike, I made this quick video for Apex Roofing. This is your website on a phone. Look how far down the call button is. That's where storm leads drop off.

DRILLS.title: "What's this regarding?"
DRILLS.sit: The receptionist screens the call. Give one honest reason.
DRILLS.line: It's about how you handle calls when the office is busy. I have two quick questions for the owner. Is he in today?

DRILLS.title: "Call me back next week"
DRILLS.sit: The owner is polite but busy. Turn "later" into a time.
DRILLS.line: Will do. Is Tuesday morning better, or Thursday afternoon? I'll put it in my calendar.

DRILLS.title: Framing the meeting
DRILLS.sit: Open a booked discovery call. Calm, clear, no rush.
DRILLS.line: Thanks for the time, Jen. Here's what I suggest: I ask a few questions about how calls work now, you ask me anything, and at the end we decide together if a next step makes sense. Does that work?

DRILLS.title: A consequence question
DRILLS.sit: Ask slowly, then stop talking. The pause is part of the drill.
DRILLS.line: If nothing changes, what does next summer look like for your team?

DRILLS.title: Say back what you heard
DRILLS.sit: Jen said: two people in the office, calls ring out, and her office manager quit partly because of the phones. Sum it up in one or two sentences and check you got it right.
DRILLS.line: So the phones are stretching two people too thin, it's already cost you a good manager, and you want every job booked without burning out the team. Did I get that right?

DRILLS.title: Go one level deeper
DRILLS.sit: The owner gives a vague answer. Ask about a real moment.
DRILLS.line: Annoying how? What happens on the days it's at its worst?

DRILLS.title: "That's more than I expected"
DRILLS.sit: You said the price once. The owner pauses, then pushes back.
DRILLS.line: Fair enough. More than you expected compared to what?

DRILLS.title: "We already have an answering service"
DRILLS.sit: Agree, then ask the one question that matters.
DRILLS.them: We already have an answering service.
DRILLS.line: Good, then you know the calls matter. When they take a call, do they book the job, or take a message?

DRILLS.title: "I need to talk to my wife"
DRILLS.sit: End of the meeting. The owner wants to check with his wife, who runs the money.
DRILLS.them: I need to talk to my wife about it.
DRILLS.line: Of course, that makes sense. What do you think she'll ask first? Would it help if the three of us spoke for ten minutes this week?

DRILLS.title: "Just send me your pricing"
DRILLS.sit: Two minutes in, the owner wants a number by email.
DRILLS.line: Happy to. It depends on how many calls you get, so I'd rather not guess. Roughly how many calls do you miss in a week?

DRILLS.title: Say the price once
DRILLS.sit: Say the price calmly, then stop. Don't explain or apologise.
DRILLS.line: The price is four hundred ninety-seven dollars a month. That includes setup and every call it answers.

DRILLS.title: Ask for the decision
DRILLS.sit: The owner agreed the problem and the fix. Ask clearly.
DRILLS.line: Based on everything you've told me, I think this is a fit. Shall we get it set up this Thursday?

DRILLS.title: No-show call
DRILLS.sit: The owner missed your 10am meeting. You call at 10:08. No guilt.
DRILLS.line: No problem at all, that's the job. Would tomorrow at 7:30 work, or Thursday at 5?

DRILLS.title: Opening a kickoff call
DRILLS.sit: Your first call with a new client. Set the agenda in one breath.
DRILLS.line: Thanks for joining, Dave. Today we'll agree one goal, the three numbers we'll track, who does what, and the first win in the next two weeks. Sound good?

DRILLS.title: Telling a client you're behind
DRILLS.sit: Results are behind plan. Tell the client before they notice, with the cause and the fix.
DRILLS.line: Honestly, we're behind. Bookings are at six against a plan of ten, mostly because calls were transferring too often. We changed that this week, and I'll report the result on Friday.

DRILLS.title: "I think we're going to cancel"
DRILLS.sit: A client calls to cancel. Listen first.
DRILLS.them: I think we're going to cancel.
DRILLS.line: Thanks for telling me straight. Can you walk me through what isn't working?

CLEAR: Am I speaking to Mr. Dave? / What is your good name?
US owners use first names. Formal openers sound like a call centre.
Once is polite. Every line sounds like a script and creates distance.
"Kindly" sounds formal and old-fashioned in the US.
"Revert" means "go back to an old state" to most Americans.
"Prepone" is not used in the US. They will not understand it.
"Query" sounds like a database or a complaint form.
"Out of station" is not used in the US.
Sounds like an order. Suggest instead.
Could you take care of this?
Not used in the US and sounds unclear.
Isn't it? / No? / Na? at the end of every line
Tag questions on every line sound unsure. Make the statement, then ask a real question.
Sorry to bother you / I was just wondering
Apologising tells them the call is a bother. Give the reason instead.
I am / we will / it is / do not (in every sentence)
Contractions sound natural and friendly on the phone. Full forms sound stiff.
CLEAR_FLAGS: Give the reason for the call instead of apologising.
Drop the tag, or ask a real question.
It suggests the rest was not honest. Drop it.
SOUNDS: For V, your top teeth touch your bottom lip. For W, round your lips and do not touch your teeth.
We have very busy vans every Wednesday.
Put your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow air. Avoid replacing it with a hard T or D.
I think this thing is worth three jobs a month.
US listeners find words by their stress. Say the strong part longer and louder: de-VEL-op-ment, ap-POINT-ment, com-PET-i-tor, MAR-ket-ing, a-NAL-y-sis.
Our appointment development work beats any competitor's marketing.
Start "school", "speak" and "small" straight on the S. Avoid "eschool" or "espeak".
Speak to the small staff at the school store.
Finish the last sound of each word, especially -ed and -s: booked, missed, calls, jobs.
He missed six calls and booked two jobs.
Aim for about 130 to 165 words a minute. Pause after your reason for calling and after every question. Silence gives them room to answer.
I'm calling because you might be missing calls. (pause) Is that true for you? (pause)

PL.t: You call a plumbing owner you have never spoken to. Which first sentence is strongest?
o: Hi, how are you doing today?
Dave, it's Alex. We haven't spoken. I'm calling because plumbers tell me they lose calls when they're on a job. Is that something you run into?
Do you have a minute to hear about our AI service?
PL.why: It says who you are, admits the cold call, gives a reason and ends on an easy question.

PL.t: Which cold email opening is strongest?
o: I hope this email finds you well. My name is Alex and I wanted to reach out.
Your reviews mention fast response, which is hard to keep up when the crew is out on jobs.
We are a leading provider of AI solutions for the trades.
PL.why: It is about them and shows you looked. The other two are stock openings that get deleted.

PL.t: Which LinkedIn connection note is best?
o: Hi Sam, I help plumbing companies get 3x more leads. Book a demo here.
Hi Sam, saw your second truck launch. I work with plumbers on after-hours calls. Would be good to connect.
Hi Sam, hope you are well! Would love to connect and chat about growing your business.
PL.why: Specific, short and no pitch. The others sell too hard or say nothing.

PL.t: The owner says, "We miss some calls." What do you ask next?
o: Our system fixes that. Want a demo?
About how many a week, and what is an average job worth?
Have you thought about hiring a receptionist?
PL.why: You need the numbers before you can show what the gap costs.

PL.t: What is the purpose of a consequence question, such as "What happens if this is still going on next summer?"
o: To get the buyer to see the real cost of the problem
To show off your product knowledge
To build rapport before the pitch
PL.why: People act when the cost of the problem outweighs the cost of fixing it.

PL.t: When should you present your offer?
o: As soon as they mention a problem
After they have agreed the gap and what it costs them
On the first call, always
PL.why: Presenting early turns discovery into a pitch they can refuse.

PL.t: A prospect says, "Just send me an email." Your best move?
o: Sure, what is your email address?
Happy to. So it is relevant, how are you handling missed calls today?
Emails get lost. Let me explain it now.
PL.why: Agree, then ask a question that shows whether there is any interest.

PL.t: A prospect says, "It is too expensive." Your best reply?
o: I can give you 20 percent off.
Fair. Is it the amount, or whether it would pay back?
Our competitors cost more.
PL.why: Find out what the objection really is before you answer it.

PL.t: At the end of a good call they say, "I need to think about it."
o: Sure, I will check back next month.
Of course. What would need to be true for this to be an easy yes? Can we speak Thursday at 10?
What is there to think about? It is a great deal.
PL.why: Find the remaining condition and agree a dated next step.

PL.t: How should a good call end?
o: Let me know if you are interested.
Ten minutes Thursday at 9 or Friday at 2?
I will send information and wait for your reply.
PL.why: A specific ask with two choices beats leaving it with them.

o: Send the calendar invite only
Confirm after booking, remind the day before and again on the morning
Call them an hour after the meeting time
PL.why: Several light touches before the meeting keep it in their mind.

PL.t: A lead filled in a web form three minutes ago. What is best?
o: Call within minutes
Email them tomorrow
Wait and call a batch of leads on Friday
PL.why: Speed to lead decides who gets the conversation.

PL.t: How should you show what your offer is worth?
o: Quote general industry statistics
Use their own numbers: calls missed times job value
List every feature
PL.why: Their numbers are believable. Statistics are not about them.

PL.t: When do you quote the price?
o: At the start of the call
After the problem and its cost are agreed in their numbers
Never, always send a proposal
PL.why: Price makes sense only against the cost of the problem.

PL.t: The buyer asks, "Can you do better on price?" Your best move?
o: Cut the price straight away
Ask for something in return, such as a shorter commitment or upfront payment
Say no and end the call
PL.why: A trade protects your price and keeps the deal moving.

PL.t: What talk ratio suits a discovery call?
o: You talk about 80 percent
You talk 40 percent or less
You talk the whole time to keep control
PL.why: The buyer should do most of the talking.

PL.t: You ask a hard question and the buyer goes quiet. What do you do?
o: Fill the silence with another question
Wait. Let the silence do the work
Answer it for them
PL.why: People use silence to think. Interrupting takes the answer away.

PL.t: The prospect sounds rushed. What do you do?
o: Speed up and cram in the pitch
Slow slightly, acknowledge their time, and ask one question
Tell them to calm down
PL.why: A calm pace lowers the pressure and earns you a minute.

TOOLS.title: Funnel planner
TOOLS.desc: Work backwards from the clients you want to how many new people to contact each day across email, calls and social, and see which rate to improve first.

TOOLS.title: Offer builder
TOOLS.desc: Write down who you serve and what you promise. Check your offer on the four things buyers weigh, with a fix for the weakest, and get the one-line offer and target you will use in every message.

TOOLS.title: Message builder
TOOLS.desc: Pick a channel and your market. Get cold emails, LinkedIn, Facebook and Instagram messages, call openers and voicemails, a video script, meeting reminders, or the whole two-week sequence, all from the same details.

TOOLS.title: Cadence builder
TOOLS.desc: Pick a sequence, a start date and your prospect's time zone. Get a dated touch-by-touch plan with the send time in their time zone and yours, ready to copy or add to your calendar.

TOOLS.title: Lead search builder
TOOLS.desc: Type a business type and a place. Get ready-to-use searches for maps, the web, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram and buying signals such as hiring and ads, with links that open in a new tab.

TOOLS.title: Cold email pre-flight checklist
TOOLS.desc: Tick every item before you send a campaign. Catch the setup mistakes that send mail to spam. The numbers match lesson 4.8.

TOOLS.title: Lead tracker
TOOLS.desc: Your pipeline: who, which channel, what stage, what it's worth and what happens next. Import leads from a CSV, search, and export any time. Saved to your account.

TOOLS.title: Reply handler
TOOLS.desc: Paste a prospect's reply from any channel. See what type it is, what it probably means, a reply to adapt and what to do next, then update the lead in one click.

TOOLS.title: Objection bank
TOOLS.desc: 36 objections with what they usually mean, a reply to adapt, and a question to ask. Includes a random drill.

TOOLS.title: Deal qualifier
TOOLS.desc: Check a deal against the course's own questions: five areas before you book (lesson 7.2) and the seven buying beliefs before you give a price (lesson 9.3). Unknowns become your next questions. Keep several deals in one place.

TOOLS.title: Discovery question builder
TOOLS.desc: Generate the full question sequence for your prospect: a call frame, then connect, situation, problem, desired outcome, consequence and commitment questions, plus a summary of the gap to finish. Pick your market to add its own questions.

TOOLS.title: Proposal builder
TOOLS.desc: A one-page, three-option proposal from your discovery notes, laid out as a proper document. Print it, save it as a PDF or download it for Word.

TOOLS.title: Scorecard
TOOLS.desc: Score a call, a cold email or a social message out of 20 against ten habits. See which habit is weakest across everything you score.

TOOLS.title: Contract and invoice kit
TOOLS.desc: Fill in the details and get a plain-language service agreement, a commission agreement, a one-page scope or an invoice. Print it, save it as a PDF, or download it for Word.

TOOLS.title: Client delivery kit
TOOLS.desc: Run every client from one place: a dated delivery timeline from the sale to renewal, go-live checklists per service, 27 templates filled with the client's details, a weekly scoreboard that turns results into money, and a health check that tells you who is at risk and what to do.
